en: The Mahāsāṃghika Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà lóu tán jīng), Scroll One.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Fǎlì and Fǎjù of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Jambudvīpa. Chapter One: Jambudvīpa.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, after the meal, the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall and sat together in discussion, saying:
"How strange and unprecedented! How is it that this heaven and earth are being destroyed?"
"How was it accomplished?
The Buddha, hearing them from afar with his divine ear, saw that after the monks had finished their meal, they were sitting together in the lecture hall discussing this matter.
The Buddha immediately rose and went to sit in the lecture hall, where he asked the monks:
"What was the subject of discussion at the meeting just now?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"After the meal, we were discussing together in the lecture hall:"
"How strange and unprecedented! How is it that this world-system is destroyed?
And how is it brought into being?
Thus they merely discussed these matters together.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to hear from the Tathāgata concerning the times of the formation and destruction of this world-system?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“O God among Gods, now is precisely the time.
You should speak for the sake of the bhikṣus regarding the knowledge of the times of the formation and destruction of the heavens and earth.
Having heard this from the Buddha, the bhikṣus shall immediately uphold it.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall now speak for your sake.
The bhikṣus replied:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear and understand.
The Buddha said:

“O Bhikṣus! Just as a single sun and moon revolve to illuminate the four continents, so too within those worlds of the four thousand continents, there are one thousand suns and moons, one thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, four thousand continents, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great dragon palaces, four thousand great garuḍas, four thousand evil paths, four thousand great evil paths, seven thousand kinds of great trees, eight thousand kinds of great mountains, and ten thousand kinds of great hells; this is called a small chiliocosm.”
As there are one thousand small world-systems, so many thousands of small world-systems constitute what is called a medium-thousand world-system.
As there is one medium-thousand world-system, so many thousands of medium-thousand world-systems constitute what is called a three-thousandfold world-system;
when this is entirely consumed by fire, destroyed, and reformed, it constitutes a single Buddha-field.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus! This earth is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas deep, and its boundaries are limitless.”
That land stands upon water; the depth of that water is four million six hundred thousand yojanas, and its boundaries are without limit or obstruction.
A great wind sustains the water; the depth of that wind is two million three hundred thousand yojanas, and its boundaries are infinite.
"Monks! That great ocean is eight million four hundred thousand yojanas deep; its boundaries have neither shore nor bottom. Monks!"

Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, enters the great ocean; it is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep and also eighty-four thousand yojanas high. It is narrow at the base and gradually widens toward the top, with its summit being perfectly level.
The various groups, comprising four classes, settled above, filling every space without any vacancy.
The great and honored deities also settled above; those most venerable and supreme gods all took up residence there.
The palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is situated atop Mount Sumeru;
above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the Yāma Heaven;
and above the Yāma Heaven is the Tuṣita Heaven.
Above the Tuṣita Heaven is the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
above the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
and above that is the Brahmakāyika Heaven.
Beyond this heaven is the Heaven of Māra.
Its palaces are twenty-four thousand li in breadth and length; they have sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold diamond nets, and sevenfold rows of trees.

The perimeter was entirely composed of the seven treasures, exquisitely painted with gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, red pearls, and musaragalva. There were golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, and musaragalva walls with gates made of all manner of precious jewels; their colors and patterns were wonderfully beautiful, all fashioned from the seven treasures.

The railings were of gold with pillars and beams of gold, and crossbars of silver; the railings were of silver with pillars and beams of silver, and crossbars of lapis lazuli; the railings were of lapis lazuli with pillars and beams of lapis lazuli, and crossbars of crystal; the railings were of red pearls with pillars and beams of red pearls, and crossbars of agate; the railings were of agate with pillars and beams of agate, and crossbars of red pearls; the railings were of musaragalva with pillars and beams of musaragalva—all fashioned from every kind of exquisite jewel.

Where the blades were of gold, the pendants were of silver; where the blades were of silver, the pendants were of gold; where the blades were of lapis lazuli, the pendants were of crystal; where the blades were of crystal, the pendants were of lapis lazuli; where the blades were of red pearls, the pendants were of agate; where the blades were of agate, the pendants were of red pearls; and where the blades were of musaragalva, the pendants were composed of all kinds of jewels.

There are golden trees with golden roots and golden trunks, and silver branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; silver trees with silver roots and silver trunks, and golden branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; beryl trees with beryl roots and trunks, and crystal branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; crystal trees with crystal roots and trunks, and beryl branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; red pearl trees with red pearl roots, agate trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; agate trees with agate roots and trunks, and red pearl branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; musaragalva trees with musaragalva roots and trunks, and branches made of every kind of jewel, with leaves, flowers, and fruits likewise composed of every kind of jewel.
The murals were exquisitely beautiful, all fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
Above the gates were curved awnings, and upon the balustrades were latticed canopies; below the watchtowers were gardens, pavilions, and residences.

In the bathing pools grow lotuses; there are various kinds of trees, various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits, which emit various fragrances; various birds fly about, each warbling its own song.
"Beyond the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is the Brahmakāyika Heaven;
beyond the Brahmakāyika Heaven is the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
and beyond that is the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven."
Beyond this is the Heaven of Calling Out to Break the Void;
beyond this is the Heaven of No Perception of Persons;
beyond this is the Heaven of Ābhāsvara.
Beyond this there are the Sudarśana devas;
beyond this there are those named Sudṛśa devas;
beyond this there are the Sudarśanīya devas.
Beyond this there is the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;
beyond this there is a heaven named Ābhāsvara;
beyond this there is a heaven named Vijñānānantya.
Beyond this there is a heaven named Ākiṃcanya;

beyond this there is a heaven named Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana. Even above these, there are beings subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, whose cycles of coming and going do not exceed that numerical limit.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, has its city constructed from four treasures: lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, and silver."
To the north of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies a world named Uttarakuru; it is forty thousand li in both width and length, and is square.
To the east of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies a world named Pūrvavideha; it is thirty-six thousand li in both width and length, and is perfectly circular in circumference.
To the west of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies a world named Aparagoyānī; it is thirty-two thousand li in both width and length, and is shaped like a half-moon.
To the south of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies a continent named Jambudvīpa, twenty-eight thousand li in both width and length, broad in the north and narrow in the south.
On the northern flank of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, the celestial gold illuminates the continent of the northern quarter;
on the eastern flank of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, the celestial silver illuminates the continent of the eastern quarter.
The crystal heavens on the western flank of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, illuminate the world below in the west;
the lapis lazuli heavens on the southern flank of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, illuminate the world below in the south.

In the northern world there is a tree named Silver Stem (*Rūpyaskandha*), with a circumference of two hundred and eighty *li* and a height of four thousand *li*; its branches and leaves spread out for two thousand *li*.

In the eastern world there is a great tree named Reed Stem (*Vetras-kandha*), with a circumference of two hundred and eighty *li* and a height of four thousand *li*; its branches and leaves spread out for two thousand *li*.

In the world of Godānīya there is a tree named Scale Stem (*Tulā-skandha*), with a circumference of two hundred and eighty *li* and a height of four thousand *li*; its branches and leaves spread out for two thousand *li*, and atop this tree is a stone ox forty *li* in height.

In the world of Jambudvīpa, there is a great tree named Jambu; it is four thousand li in height, its trunk has a circumference of two hundred and eighty li, and its branches and leaves extend over two thousand li.

The King of the Golden-Winged Birds (Garuda) and the dragons have a tree named Kūliśam, four thousand *li* in height, with a trunk circumference of two hundred and eighty *li*, and branches and leaves spreading for two thousand *li*.
The Asuras have a great tree named Śubhadivātikrānta, four thousand *li* in height, with a trunk circumference of two hundred and eighty *li*, and branches and leaves spreading for two thousand *li*.

The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has a tree named Divātikrānta, four thousand *li* in height, with a trunk circumference of two hundred and eighty *li*, and branches and leaves spreading for two thousand *li*.

To the north of the great ocean there is a great tree named Yama, four thousand *li* in height, with a trunk circumference of two hundred and eighty *li*, and its branches and leaves spread over two thousand *li*.
In the sky above the northern lands, there is a grove of trees named Āmra, each measuring two thousand *li* in width and length;
furthermore, there is another grove of trees named Yamapa, also measuring two thousand *li* in both width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Tā, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Natā, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Nara, each two thousand li in breadth and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Women, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Children, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Cypress, each two thousand li in width and length.
Furthermore, there are groves of trees named Candana, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there are groves of trees named Khadira, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there are groves of trees named Panasa, each two thousand li in width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Bilva, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Mahānta, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Āmra, each two thousand li in breadth and length.
Furthermore, there are groves of trees named *dāḍima* (pomegranate), each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there are groves of trees named *cāra*, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there are groves of trees named *avaṭa* (pit), each two thousand li in width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Pailong, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Āmalaka, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Harītakī, each two thousand li in breadth and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named *vibhītaka*, each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named reeds (*vetasa*), each two thousand li in width and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named bamboo (*veṇu*), each two thousand li in width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Tāla, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Khara, each two thousand li in breadth and length;
furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Trapusa, each two thousand li in breadth and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Great Melon (*Mahā-ālābu*), each two thousand li in width and length;
again, there is a grove of trees named Flower Shedding (*Vikīrṇa-puṣpa*), each two thousand li in width and length;
and again, there is a grove of trees named Bathing Pond (*Tīrtha-snāna*), each two thousand li in width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Sumanā, two thousand li in both width and length;
another grove of trees named Pīla, two thousand li in both width and length;
and another grove of trees named Hāsa, two thousand li in both width and length.
Furthermore, there is a grove of trees named Kāyika, two thousand li in both breadth and length;
again, there is a grove of trees named Touxian, two thousand li in both breadth and length;
and again, there is a grove of trees named Pútáo, two thousand li in both breadth and length.

Beyond this empty space, within that empty space, there is further a pool of *utpala* flowers extending for two thousand *li*, a pool of red lotuses for two thousand *li*, a pool of white lotuses for two thousand *li*, a pool of yellow lotuses for two thousand *li*, and a pool of venomous snakes for two thousand *li*.

Beyond this, the ground is empty; within that emptiness lies the sea of Ucchāna, which flows from the east and west into the great ocean. Within that sea of Ucchāna, one sees the tracks of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) as he travels through the world, and it is known that there is a wheel-turning monarch there. To the north of Ucchāna is a mountain named Uttarakā.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"That mountain is exceedingly delightful; its beautiful trees are covered in leaves, and its flowers and fruits are most fragrant. There is no beast or bird that is not found there; nothing can compare to it."
The Buddha said, “Monks!

That Mount Uttarakuru is exceedingly pleasant, beautiful, and magnificent. On Mount Uttarakuru there is a mountain named Suvāhana; on that mountain there are eighty thousand caves, within which dwell eighty thousand elephants. These elephants eat once every seven days; they have six tusks, broad at the top and tapered at the base, with the spaces between the tusks entirely inlaid with gold.”
Passing beyond Mount Sunābha, there is next a mountain named Hemavanta (Winter King), exceedingly high, exceeding one hundred million [yojanas], with a summit four thousand li in height.
Upon it is a body of water named Anavatapta, two thousand li in breadth and length; its bed is entirely of gold, and the water is cool, soft, sweet, and clear.

They constructed moats and embankments made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate; walls were erected on all four sides, likewise paved at the base, with sevenfold railings and sevenfold rows of trees surrounding them on every side, adorned with lattices of the seven treasures, beautifully painted and exquisite.
The waters of the Dragon King Anavatapta have stairways on all four sides:

gold stairways with silver railings, silver stairways with gold railings, lapis lazuli stairways with crystal railings, crystal stairways with lapis lazuli railings, red pearl stairways with agate railings, agate stairways with red pearl railings, and musaragalva stairways with railings of the seven precious gems. These are the stairways.
Above, there are curved canopy-covers, all equipped with railings and balustrades, and there are pavilions with latticed windows;
within the water are blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and yellow lotuses—
flowers that are also fire-colored, golden, blue, crimson, and scarlet.
As for the white variety, its circumference is as large as a chariot wheel and its stem is as thick as a chariot hub;
if one pricks it, the sap exudes like the color of milk, and its taste is like honey.
The palace of the Naga King Anavatapta is within those waters; the palace is named Pañcaśikha.
The Naga King Anavatapta dwells therein.
What kinds of jewels does that dragon possess?

What is meant by the Anavatapta Dragon? Beyond the Anavatapta Dragon, all other dragon kings in the world are scorched by the three heats; the Dragon King Anavatapta is not scorched by the three heats.

Furthermore, beyond the Dragon King Anavatapta, when the rain of hot sand falls upon the bodies of the other dragon kings, it burns their skin until it is charred; once the skin is charred, it burns the flesh; once the flesh is burned, it burns the sinews; once the sinews are burned, it burns the bones; and once the bones are burned, it burns the marrow. This burning and roasting is extremely agonizing. While all the other dragon kings beyond the Dragon King Anavatapta experience this heat, the Dragon King Anavatapta alone does not experience it. For this reason he is named Anavatapta (Without Heat); this is the first matter.

Furthermore, when other dragon kings in the world, having passed beyond the Dragon King Anavatapta, engage in sexual desire toward one another, a hot wind blows upon their bodies, scorching them. They immediately lose their color and assume the form of snakes; thus they become terrified and unhappy.

Among all the dragon kings throughout the world, those who pass by Anavatapta suffer from fever, yet the Dragon King Anavatapta alone is free from fever; for this reason he is named Anavatapta. This is the second matter.

Furthermore, all the dragon kings in the world, with the exception of the Dragon King Anavatapta, and all the other dragon kings as well as the garuḍa kings, enter his palace and are all terrified and devoured by him.

If a garuḍa thinks to himself, "I wish to enter the palace of the Naga King Anavatapta," as soon as he has this thought, countless calamities and transformations afflict his own body; yet while all other naga kings in the world perceive this poisonous heat, the Naga King Anavatapta alone does not perceive it. For this reason, he is named Anavatapta. These are the three matters.
For three reasons, he is named the Dragon King Anavatapta.

To the east there is a great flowing river; following downward for one course, it branches into five hundred tributary rivers that encircle the Dragon King Anavatapta and flow eastward into the great ocean.
To the south of the Dragon King Anavatapta is a great river named Vakṣu; it consists of five hundred tributary rivers that encircle the Dragon King Anavatapta and flow into the Great Southern Ocean.
To the west of the Dragon King Anavatapta is a great river named Sindhu, which has five hundred tributary streams; it winds around the Dragon King Anavatapta and flows into the Great Western Ocean.
To the north of the Dragon King Anavatapta is a great river named Sītā; there are five hundred tributary rivers that wind around the Dragon King Anavatapta and flow into the Northern Ocean.
To the south of Mount Dongwang lies a kingdom named Vaiśālī.

To the north of Vaiśālī are seven Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇagiri). North of these Black Mountains, seven ṛṣis and brahmins dwell; their names are: first, Jijiyou; second, Shini li; third, Yudan; fourth, Chan; fifth, Jiashé; sixth, Youduoluo; and seventh, Bobeitou. There is also a mountain there named Huotanduo.

To the north of the Seven Seers’ Brahmin hermitage, there is a mountain named Gandhamādana. Within it are two caves: one named Citra and the other named Sucitra. They are fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and are as fine and soft as silk brocade.
To the north of the Cave of Excellent Painting, there is a king of trees named Well-Established (*Susthita*), surrounded by eight thousand kings of trees.
Beneath the king of trees, Well-Established, there is an elephant king named Well-Established who dwells there, surrounded on all sides by eight thousand elephants.

To the north of King Supratiṣṭhita’s tree, there is a bathing pool named Manoma. It is surrounded by a moat made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, red pearls, musāragalva, and agate. On its perimeter are eight thousand smaller bathing pools that encircle it. The water in all of them is cool, refreshing, sweet, soft, and clear; the sand on the bottom is entirely gold. There are sevenfold railings, sevenfold networks of bells, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, red pearls, musāragalva, and agate—surrounding the area on every side.
That pond was exceedingly wonderful and beautiful: its golden railings had golden pillars and beams with silver crossbars;
its silver railings had silver pillars and beams with golden crossbars; its lapis lazuli railings had lapis lazuli pillars and beams with crystal crossbars;
its crystal railings had crystal pillars and beams with lapis lazuli crossbars; and its red pearl railings had red pearl [pillars and beams].
The pillars and beams were made of pearls, and the crossbeams of agate; the railings of agate had pillars and beams of agate with crossbeams of red pearl;
the railings of musāragalva had pillars and beams of musāragalva with crossbeams of every kind of jewel;
the golden lattices had silver pendants, the silver lattices had golden pendants, and the lapis lazuli lattices had crystal pendants.
Where the *kinkinījāla* (canopies) are made of crystal, they are hung with pendants of lapis lazuli;
where the *kinkinījāla* are made of red pearls, they are hung with pendants of agate; where the *kinkinījāla* are made of agate, they are hung with pendants of red pearls;
and where the *kinkinījāla* are made of musāragalva, they are hung with pendants of every kind of jewel—all fashioned from the seven treasures and exceedingly beautiful.

The golden trees had golden branches, roots, and silver stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees had silver branches, roots, and golden stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees had lapis lazuli roots and branches with crystal stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees had crystal roots and branches with lapis lazuli stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the red pearl trees had red pearl roots and branches with agate stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and the agate trees had agate roots and branches with red pearl stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

As for the *śaṅkhaśaila* trees, their roots and branches are made of all kinds of jewels, while their stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits are made of the seven treasures; they are all exquisitely beautiful.

The four sides of the circumference of Lake Mānasa are constructed from the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, *śaṅkhaśaila*, and agate—with golden steps and silver railings, silver steps and golden railings, crystal steps and lapis lazuli railings, lapis lazuli steps and crystal railings, red pearl steps and agate railings, agate steps and red pearl railings, and *śaṅkhaśaila* steps with railings made of every kind of treasure; fashioned from the seven treasures, they are exceedingly beautiful.
On the steps above are curved box-shaped canopies; upon the railings are latticed pavilions; below the towers and galleries are gardens, pavilions, and residences, as well as bathing pools.
The trees produce various flowers and various fruits, emitting various fragrances; within them dwell various flying birds, warbling melodiously in harmony with one another.

In the Mānasa Lake, there are blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses; among them are those that are crimson, golden, azure, yellow, scarlet, white, and various other mixed colors.

The circumference of its flowers is as large as a chariot wheel, and the circumference of their stalks is like that of a chariot hub; when the flowers are severed, they exude a sap like milk, and its taste is like honey.
When the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, intending to enter the pond to bathe and enjoy himself, thought of the eight thousand elephant kings,
those eight thousand elephant kings said:
"The Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita has already thought of us."
They immediately went together to where the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita was and stood before him.
At that time, the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita, together with eight thousand elephant kings, went to Lake Mānasa.
Among the elephants, some held parasols for the king, while others fanned him, surrounding him on all sides.
At that time, a sentient being named Kiṇa was at the forefront, dancing, singing, and performing music.
At that time, the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita went to Lake Mānasa to bathe and enjoy himself with music and play. Among the elephants there were some who washed the king’s trunk and mouth;

some who washed his teeth; some who washed his head; some who washed his back; some who washed his belly; some who washed his thighs; some who washed his knees; some who washed his feet; and some who washed his tail. Some pulled up lotus roots, washed them, and gave them to the king to eat. Others took blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses, held them with their trunks, and scattered them over the elephant king’s head.
At that time, after the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita had bathed, enjoyed himself, and finished his meal, he returned to the foot of the Supratiṣṭhita tree.

Each of the eight thousand elephant kings likewise entered their respective ponds to bathe, performed music, enjoyed themselves, and finished their meals, before returning to where the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita was.
At that time, the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded before and behind by eight thousand elephant kings, returned to the foot of the Supratiṣṭhita tree.
Among them were some who held parasols for the elephant king, some who fanned him, and others who performed music, song, and dance in front as they arrived at the grove of the Supratiṣṭhita tree.

The elephant king followed his own will in lying down, rising, and walking; likewise, each of the other eight thousand elephants also followed their own will, lying down, rising, and walking among the trees according to their desires.

Among the eight thousand elephant-trees, some had a circumference of four zhang nine chi; some had a circumference of five zhang six chi; some had a circumference of six zhang three chi; some had a circumference of seven zhang seven chi; some had a circumference of eight zhang four chi; some had a circumference of nine zhang one chi; some had a circumference of nine zhang five chi; some had a circumference of ten zhang five chi; and some had a circumference of eleven zhang two chi.

The trunk of the Bodhisattva Elephant King, Well-Established (*Susthitamati*), is ten zhang and nine chi in circumference; when the branches and leaves of these eight thousand trees fall, the wind blows them away outside.
When the eight thousand elephant kings void their excrement and urine, all the *yakṣas* and spirits clear it away outside.
The Buddha said, "Monks!
Such is the majestic and sublime spiritual power of the noble elephant king Supratiṣṭhita; even among the blood-drinking species of animals, there can be such as this."
Chapter 2: Uttarakuru. In the second chapter of the Mahāsāṃnipāta Sūtra, "Uttarakuru," the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The continent of Uttarakuru is forty thousand li in circumference and breadth."

In the northern region of the world, there are countless various mountains. On both banks of that river stand various trees, and the river flows gently with various flowers drifting in its currents. On both sides of the river are boats, beautifully painted and exquisite, fashioned from the four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

In the center of the northern world there is a bathing pool named Utpalaka, four thousand li in length and breadth; its water is cool, soft, and clear, surrounded by seven layers of walls, and the sand at the bottom is entirely gold.

The Nanda bathing pool has stairways on all four sides, constructed of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden stairways having silver railings, silver stairways having golden railings, lapis lazuli stairways having crystal railings, and crystal stairways having lapis lazuli railings.

In the Nanda Pond, there are blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses; among them are those that are crimson, golden, azure, yellow, scarlet, and white. If their roots and stalks are severed, they exude a sap like milk, which tastes like honey. Their light shines for forty *li*, and their fragrance is likewise perceived for forty *li*.
To the east of the Nanda bathing pool is a river named Yamunā;
to the south of the Nanda bathing pool is a river named Śoṇa;
to the west of the Nanda bathing pool is a river named Mahī.

To the north of the Nanda bathing pool is a flowing river named Śubhavatī; all the waters of these rivers flow gently, and within them grow clusters of floating flowers. On both banks of the river stand various kinds of trees, and the two riverbanks are formed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

To the east of Nanda’s bathing pool is a garden named Bhadraśreṣṭha, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all constructed from the four treasures—gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli—which are exquisitely beautiful.
In the Garden of the Noble Superior, there are fragrant trees that produce flowers and fruits; when split open, they emit various kinds of incense.
There are also trees for powdered incense that produce flowers and fruits; when split open, they emit various kinds of incense.
There are trees of garments, trees of necklaces, and trees of incense.
They produce flowers and fruits; when these are split open, they yield various garments and necklaces, and emit various types of incense.

There are trees of fruit, trees of vessels, and trees of music that produce flowers and fruits; when these fruits are split open, they yield various kinds of vessels, various kinds of fruits, and various kinds of musical instruments.
The trees are seven *li* high; there are those six, five, four, three, two, and even one *li* high.

To the south of Nanda’s bathing pool is a park named Yuxian (With Virtue), surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold lattices, and sevenfold rows of trees, all constructed from the four precious substances. Within it are fragrant trees, incense-grinding trees, clothing trees, necklace trees, inexhaustible trees, vessel trees, and fruit trees, all of which bear flowers and fruit. When the fruit is split open, each yields various kinds of fragrance, incense for grinding, clothing, necklaces, inexhaustibles, vessels, fruits, and various kinds of music. The smallest of these trees are ten *li*, twenty *li*, or forty *li* high, reaching up to seventy *li*.

To the west of the Nanda bathing pool, there is a park named Lāvaṇa, constructed of the four precious substances. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold lattices, and sevenfold rows of trees. The various features arising within it, whether high or low, are also like those of the eastern park.

To the north of the Nanda bathing pool is a garden named Constantly Blooming Flowers (Sadāpuṣpita), which is likewise constructed of the four treasures—gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli—and surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and seven rows of trees. The heights and depths of the various trees produced therein are also like those in the eastern garden.
“In the northern region of the world there is a tree whose branches curve together like a lattice of pearls.
The people of the northern region sleep and rise while remaining below it; men and women occupy separate places.”
There is pure, non-glutinous rice that grows naturally without being plowed or sown, yielding every possible flavor. Those who wish to eat take this pure non-glutinous rice and cook it.

There is a jewel named "Flame Flavor" (Jvālārasa) which, when placed beneath the cauldron, emits light that cooks the rice. People from the four quarters come and all partake of it together; even before they have finished eating, the food is not exhausted. There are no thieves or wicked people, no talk of "my wife and children," and no one who performs the labor of farming.
After they have eaten, their complexions become radiant and they possess majestic spiritual power.

If men or women give rise to thoughts of lustful desire, they gaze at one another without speaking; the man then goes before and the woman follows behind as they proceed to a garden pavilion to enter within and enjoy themselves together. For two days, three days, or even up to seven days, each acts according to their own will; once they have finished, they depart and are no longer bound to one another.
When a woman has been pregnant for seven or eight days, she gives birth to either a boy or a girl and places them in the middle of a crossroads.

If anyone comes from the east, west, south, or north, they give the child their finger to suckle; milk flows forth and the child drinks it. After seven days have passed, by virtue of their own merit, the child immediately grows up, like a person from Jambudvīpa who is twenty or twenty-five years old.

"In the northern region of the world, there is water surrounding the four directions called Anavatapta. During the latter part of the night, clouds arise and the heavens rain down water of eight flavors for the duration of a person's meal. This washes away the dust of the northern region of the world, so that the dust no longer rises."
For example, just as dust does not arise when the ground is smeared with ghee or sesame oil, so it is in the northern continent; dust does not arise from the earth there.

For example, just as a wheelwright or a wheelwright’s apprentice, having fashioned a waterwheel out of various flowers, holds it in his left hand and washes the wheel with water in his right hand so that no dust arises, so it is in the northern continent; dust does not arise from the earth, and there are always flowing waters and growing grasses and trees, which always bear leaves, flowers, and fruit, and among them the grass is ever green.

For example, their wing colors are like those of a peacock; their fragrance is like that of the finest incense. When they step upon it, their feet sink four inches deep, and when they lift them, the ground returns to its original state.

When the people of the northern continent wish to go to the gardens and pavilions of the Sage to play and enjoy themselves, they immediately depart by boat to the shore and strip off their clothes to bathe.

Having thus enjoyed themselves, they left the boat and crossed the river, going to the grove of fragrant trees where they took scents to anoint their bodies; then they went to the grove of clothing trees where they took garments to wear; and finally they went to the groves of inexhaustible trees, necklaces trees, vessels trees, fruit trees, and music trees, taking necklaces and inexhaustible objects to adorn themselves.
Taking their musical instruments, they proceeded to the garden pavilion of Bhadraśreṣṭhin.

At that time of heat, a turbulent wind blew and swept the grounds of Bhadraśreṣṭhin’s garden pavilion; a wind carrying *eranda* pollen arrived, blowing down the flowers until they fell to the ground reaching up to people's knees.

At that time, the people of the northern continent all entered the Garden of Superior Virtue (Bhadrottara) to play and enjoy themselves. After two days, three days, or up to seven days, they each departed, going wherever they pleased without being bound by any ties; they would likewise return to the Garden of Superior Virtue. This was also the case for the Garden of Constant Flowers (Sadāpuṣpita) in Rāvaṇa.

"When the people of the northern world wish to eat, they take pure non-glutinous rice and cook it; beneath it, they use the light of the *jvālā-rasa-maṇi* (flame-flavor jewel) to cook the rice until it is done. Whether someone comes from the east, west, south, or north, all who arrive at that place may eat their fill, yet the food is never exhausted until everyone has finished eating."

In the northern region of the world, there is a tree named Xiangdou; its branches intertwine and curve upward until they meet like a lattice canopy, where the people take up residence and sleep; men and women occupy separate quarters.

The people of the northern region have teeth and hair that are uniformly dark blue-black in color and are eight feet tall; the complexion of the populace is uniform, and their height is likewise equal, as is the case for the women.
The people practiced the ten wholesome deeds and no longer instructed one another in unwholesome conduct; they all lived for a thousand years, with none dying prematurely.
After death, some were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, some in the Yāma Heaven, some in the Tuṣita Heaven, some in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and some in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

When their lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, they descend to be born among humans in Jambudvīpa, immediately taking birth into a family of great wealth and nobility, such as that of a Brahmin or a great householder.
When the people of the northern continent defecate or urinate, they sink into the ground; thus the earth remains clean, without any accumulation of excrement or foul odors.

When men and women of the northern continent die, they are adorned with fine garments and ornaments, and there is no weeping; their bodies are then taken and placed at the intersection of the four main roads.
There is a bird named Uccha that picks up dead people and places them outside the northern continent.
For what reason is it called Uttarakuru?
Because the continent of Uttarakuru is superior to these three continents and is the most excellent of all, it is therefore called Uttarakuru.
The people of the continent of Uttarakuru eat pure non-glutinous rice; there are no thieves and no evildoers.
They do not say, "This is my wife," nor do they say, "This is my son."
Their complexions are excellent and they possess majestic power; none among them are short-lived, and after death they are reborn in auspicious realms.
For this reason, it is called Uttarakuru. Chapter Three:
The Cakravartin Kings The Great Sūtra of the Fire at the End of the Kalpa, Part One of Chapter Three: The Cakravartin Kings. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"When there is a Wheel-Turning King in the world, seven treasures and four virtues naturally arise. What are the seven? First is the treasure of the golden wheel;

second is the treasure of the white elephant; third is the treasure of the dark-blue horse; fourth is the treasure of the bright moon jewel; fifth is the treasure of the jade-like woman; sixth is the treasure of the minister of the treasury; and seventh is the treasure of the minister who guides the way."
What is the nature of the golden wheel of a Wheel-turning King?

On the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full, the king bathes and ascends to sit atop a high tower together with his court ladies. Then he sees a natural celestial golden wheel approaching from the east; it has a thousand spokes, all perfectly complete, fashioned entirely of celestial gold, and stands fourteen feet high.
Having seen this, the king thought to himself:

"I have heard from the former sages that if a king, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, bathes and ascends a high terrace to sit with his court ladies, and sees a golden wheel spontaneously appear in the east, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King."
The king thought to himself that he wished to test the divine golden wheel.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King tested the divine golden wheel; he immediately assembled his fourfold army and proceeded to the place where the divine golden wheel was located.
He adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and holding up his right hand, pointed toward the golden wheel to fly eastward; the golden wheel immediately flew to the east.

The Wheel-Turning King, together with his fourfold army and all his household and kinsmen, followed it as they flew. The gods of the heavens of the Four Great Kings also all flew before the golden wheel.
Wherever the Golden Wheel comes to rest, the Universal Monarch, together with his fourfold army, households, and kinsmen, all takes up residence there.
At that time, the kings of Pūrvavideha in the east fill golden bowls with silver grain and silver bowls with golden grain, and go together to the place where the Universal Monarch is, saying:
"Welcome, Great King! It is most excellent!"

The cities and territories of the eastern regions are prosperous, flourishing, peaceful, and secure; the five grains ripen in abundance, the population is vast, and precious gems are numerous. There is an abundance of skilled artisans, and there is plenty of bright moon pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, white elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, and servants, as well as rice and grain, with storehouses filled to capacity.
"May Your Majesty please remain here; we shall receive and uphold your instructions.
The Wheel-Turning King then addressed the various kings, saying:
"Virtuous ones, each of you must govern your own kingdoms with the True Dharma and do not practice what is contrary to the Dharma."

Virtuous ones, simply do not kill living beings; do not steal; do not violate the wives of others; do not engage in false speech, abuse, harsh words, or double-tongued talk; and do not harbor evil thoughts.
"When one governs with a mind of loving-kindness and fully practices its observance, such a person is truly receiving my teaching.

At that time, the various minor kings brought their realms and offered them to the Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin). The Wheel-turning King then set out to tour the kingdoms of the eastern direction, staying there for countless years, enjoying themselves in pleasure and feasting. Having brought all within the Eastern Sea under his dominion, he returned.
The kings of Jambudvīpa in the southern continent were likewise subdued; together with their households, kinsmen, and the fourfold army, they followed as the golden wheel flew before them.
He proceeded again to Aparagoyānī in the west, where it was likewise; he proceeded again to Uttarakuru in the north, where it was likewise.

All the gods above the Four Heavenly Kings flew ahead of the golden wheel; wherever the golden wheel reached, the Wheel-Turning King, together with his household, relatives, and the fourfold army, would halt there.

At that time, the minor kings of the north filled golden bowls with silver grain and silver bowls with golden grain, and together went to the place where the Wheel-Turning King was, saying: "Welcome, Great King!

In the northern cities and territories, there is great prosperity, joy, and peace; the five grains are abundant, and the people possess many treasures and jewels. Artisans abound, and there is an abundance of bright moon pearls, jade, and lapis lazuli, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, rice, and grain, all filling the storehouses."
"May Your Majesty please remain here; we shall receive and uphold your instructions.
The Wheel-Turning King then addressed the minor kings, saying:
"Virtuous ones, each of you govern your own kingdoms according to the True Dharma (saddharma) and do not practice what is contrary to the Dharma."

"Virtuous ones, do not kill living beings; do not steal; do not violate the wives of others; do not engage in false speech, abuse, harsh words, or double-tongued talk; do not harbor ill will toward others, but should instead cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and practice with right view. Those who act thus are receiving my instruction."

At that time, the various minor kings brought their realms and offered them up. The Wheel-Turning King traveled through the kingdoms of the northern regions, halting there for incalculable years, enjoying themselves with music, pleasure, and fine food and drink, until he had brought the entire Northern Sea region under his dominion.
He then returned to Jambudvīpa with his household, kinsmen, and the fourfold army.

The majesty and spiritual power of Jambudvīpa became even more sublime; its golden wheel was likewise measured at that time as being four hundred and eighty li long from east to west and two hundred and eighty li wide from south to north.

The devas, acting as wheel-turning kings, constructed city walls sevenfold in height, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative lattices, and sevenfold rows of trees surrounding them on all sides. These were exquisitely painted and made entirely of the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musāragalva, and aśmagarbha. Where there was a golden wall, there was a silver gate; where there was a silver wall, there was a golden gate; where there was a lapis lazuli wall, there was a crystal gate; where there was a crystal wall, there was a lapis lazuli gate; where there was a red pearl wall, there was an aśmagarbha gate; where there was an aśmagarbha wall, there was a red pearl gate; and where there was a musāragalva wall, there was a gate composed of every kind of treasure.

The city was surrounded on all four sides by gates. Those with golden railings had pillars and beams of gold and crossbars of silver; those with silver railings had pillars and beams of silver and crossbars of crystal; those with lapis lazuli railings had pillars and beams of lapis lazuli and crossbars of crystal; those with crystal railings had pillars and beams of crystal and crossbars of lapis lazuli; those with red pearl railings had pillars and beams of red pearl and crossbars of agate; those with agate railings had pillars and beams of agate and crossbars of red pearl; and those with musaragalva railings had pillars and beams of musaragalva and crossbars made of every kind of jewel.

Where the golden lattices were, silver tassels hung; where the silver lattices were, golden tassels hung; where the lapis lazuli lattices were, crystal tassels hung; where the crystal lattices were, lapis lazuli tassels hung; where the red pearls lattices were, agate tassels hung; where the agate lattices were, red pearl tassels hung; and where the musaragalva lattices were, tassels made of every kind of jewel hung.

Furthermore, trees were fashioned from the seven precious substances, exceedingly beautiful: the golden trees had golden roots, branches, and silver trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees had silver roots and branches, and golden trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees had lapis lazuli roots and branches, and crystal trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees had crystal roots and branches, and lapis lazuli trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the red pearl trees had red pearl roots and branches, and agate trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the agate trees had agate roots and branches, and red pearl trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and the musaragalva trees had musaragalva roots and branches, with trunks, leaves, flowers, and fruits made of every kind of jewel.
Above the gates were curved box-like canopies and latticed pavilions; there were multi-storied towers and garden houses.
Within the bathing pools were various kinds of trees with various leaves, flowers, and fruits, emitting various fragrances, while various birds sang together in harmony.
Once the city was completed, its majestic power was so sublime that the golden wheel came to a halt; the dimensions of the city were eighty *li* from east to west and forty *li* from south to north.

At that time, the devas, acting as wheel-turning kings, constructed palaces with sevenfold walls of the seven treasures, sevenfold railings, sevenfold jeweled lattices, and sevenfold rows of trees made of the seven treasures, all surrounding them on every side.

Above the sevenfold gates were curved canopies and latticed pavilions; below were pleasure gardens, bathing pools, various trees with diverse leaves, flowers, and fruits, and various birds singing together in harmony.
Once the palace of the wheel-turning monarch had been constructed, the golden wheel stood suspended in mid-air before the palace gate.
At that time, the wheel-turning monarch was filled with great joy and exultation, saying:
"The precious golden wheel has appeared spontaneously for me; now I am truly a wheel-turning monarch."
The Buddha said: "A Wheel-Turning King possesses the natural Golden Wheel Treasure; what is the nature of the White Elephant Treasure possessed by such a Wheel-Turning King?
In the early morning, the Wheel-Turning King assembles with his ministers for consultation."
At that moment, a white elephant spontaneously appeared before him; its entire body was pure white and perfectly formed, and it was capable of flight.
It was upright and handsome with a red head and six tusks—thick at the top and tapering toward the bottom—with the tips of the tusks possessing a golden hue like streaks of gold between brushstrokes.
Having seen this, the Wheel-Turning King thought to himself:
"If this elephant can be tamed, it shall indeed become noble and excellent.
He then entrusted it to an elephant trainer to be properly trained; with a single turn of training, it became well-tamed, becoming as perfectly disciplined as the most well-bred domestic animal.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the white elephant treasure, assembled the fourfold army and had them array themselves in full regalia around the white elephant. Having mounted the white elephant at sunrise, he departed from the palace gate and flew through the air, circling within the four seas, before immediately returning to the palace to sit and enjoy himself.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King was filled with great joy and exultation, saying:
"The white elephant treasure has appeared spontaneously for me; now I have truly become a Wheel-Turning King."
Such is the white elephant treasure of the Wheel-Turning King.
As for the blue horse treasure of the Wheel-Turning King, what is it like?

In the early morning, while the Wheel-Turning King is deliberating with his attendants, he sees a natural blue horse appear before him; its body is greenish-blue with glossy fur, and its head is black.
The Wheel-turning King thought to himself,
"If this horse were tamed, it would be excellent.
He gave it to a horse trainer to tame it, and it was immediately tamed well, becoming as noble and excellent as a superior steed.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the dark-blue horse-treasure, immediately assembled the fourfold army. Having donned his armor and mounted the horse, before he had even passed through the palace gate, he flew with the fourfold army around within the four seas. Returning to the palace on that very day, he sat together with them in enjoyment;
filled with great joy and exultation, he said: "The dark-blue horse-treasure has spontaneously appeared for me; now that I possess it, I am truly a Wheel-Turning King."
Such is the dark-blue horse-treasure of the Wheel-turning King.
As for the bright moon-jewel treasure of the Wheel-turning King, what is it like?
In the early morning, while the Wheel-turning King is seated with his ministers in council, he sees the natural bright moon-jewel appear before him.
That jewel was the color of blue lapis lazuli; it was smooth and lustrous in the eight directions, beautiful, pure, and possessed a brilliant radiance.
Upon seeing it, the Wheel-Turning King thought to himself:
"It would be magnificent if such a jewel were to illuminate my inner palace."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the Moon-Bright Jewel (Candraprabha-maṇi), ordered the fourfold army to assemble; he placed the jewel at the top of a banner and went out from the palace gate at night with the fourfold army.

At that time, the light from the moon-jewel shone forth; the houses of the householders and brahmins began their activities, and the servants were sent to trade in the marketplace, all thinking it was sunrise.

The jewel illuminated the fourfold army with its brilliance, and it traveled forty *li* beyond the palace, flying around within the four seas. That very night, it returned to the palace where he sat; filled with great joy and leaping for delight, he said:
"A natural bright moon-jewel has appeared for me, and I have now become a Wheel-Turning King."
Such is the Moonlight Jewel of the Wheel-Turning King.
