Translated by the Śramaṇas Fali and Faju of the Western Jin, Chapter Three, Part Two:
"The Wheel-Turning King and the Jewel of the Woman.
What kind of person is this Jewel of the Woman that the Wheel-Turning King possesses?

On the following morning, as the Wheel-Turning King sat together with his ministers in council, there suddenly appeared before him a natural *strī-ratna* (jewel of a woman). She was upright and beautiful, with a complexion beyond compare; she was neither tall nor short, neither stout nor thin, and neither too fair nor too dark.

In winter his body is warm, and in summer his body is cool; all the pores of his body emit the fragrance of sandalwood, and his mouth emits the fragrance of the lotus. The Wheel-Turning King holds him in profound esteem and love; he does not give rise to thoughts of lust toward others, much less would he ever act upon them with his body.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King was filled with great joy and exultation, saying:
"The precious jade woman has appeared spontaneously for me; now I have truly become a Wheel-Turning King."
Such is the precious queen-jewel of the wheel-turning monarch.
What is the nature of the precious minister-treasure who is the master of the storehouse?

When the wheel-turning monarch sits in council at dawn, he sees the precious minister-treasure, the master of the storehouse, standing before him—one who is wise, experienced in affairs, and profoundly sincere. He approaches the wheel-turning monarch and says:
"Whatever the Wheel-Turning King desires to seek, I shall provide for him as the Heavenly King; let the King sit in peace.

The Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test the noble minister-treasure of the Treasury, assembled the fourfold army and boarded a ship to enter the water. He addressed the noble minister-treasure of the Treasury:
"I desire gold, silver, and precious jewels; you must give them to me."
The noble minister in charge of the treasury said to the Wheel-Turning King:
"Once he has crossed the water, I shall give it to him according to Your Majesty's wish. The King said:
"I shall now use these here; give me gold, silver, and precious treasures quickly. Once we have crossed the water, I shall have no further need of them.

Hearing and accepting these instructions, the noble minister in charge of the treasury adjusted his robes, ascended the boat, knelt on his right knee, stirred the water with his right hand, and scooped up gold, silver, and precious treasures with a vessel.
It is like insects clinging to a tree; in the same way, various vessels of gold, silver, and precious jewels cling to his hands.
At that time, the holy minister in charge of the treasury takes many precious jewels and places them upon the ship, addressing the Wheel-turning King, saying:
"How much gold, silver, and precious jewels do you wish to have?"
"I shall now give it to you, O King.
The Wheel-turning King said to the noble minister in charge of the treasury, "The gold, silver, and precious jewels I possess are exceedingly numerous; I merely wished to test you!"
Upon hearing this, the noble minister in charge of the treasury returned and placed the gold, silver, and precious jewels back into the water.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King was filled with great joy and exultation, saying:
"The noble minister in charge of the treasury has spontaneously appeared for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning King."
Such is the Jewel of the Minister-Treasurer possessed by a Wheel-Turning King.
What is the kind of Jewel of the Minister-General possessed by a Wheel-Turning King?

At dawn, while the Wheel-Turning King is seated in council, he sees the Minister-General standing before him—one who is wise, courageous, and skilled in affairs. He approaches the Wheel-Turning King and addresses him, saying:
"Whatever you wish to do, I shall provide for it; Your Majesty, simply sit at ease and do not worry!
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test his military minister, summoned the four divisions of the army and addressed the Jewel of the Military Minister, saying:

"Teach those who do not understand the art of war so that they may understand it; teach those who already understand it so that they may know it more deeply; teach those who do not understand how to maintain their positions so that they may know how to maintain them; and teach those who do not understand riding, archery, or horsemanship so that they may master these skills."
The Jewel of the Military Minister immediately accepted the instruction and trained all the soldiers.
The Wheel-Turning King was filled with great joy and exultation, saying:
"The Jewel of the Military Minister has spontaneously appeared for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning King."
"Such is the military minister-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch.
The Buddha said,
"The wheel-turning monarch possesses seven treasures in this manner."
The Buddha said:
"A Wheel-Turning King possesses four virtues.
What are these four virtues?"

First is great wealth: he possesses an abundance of treasures, fields and houses, male and female slaves, pearls and jade, elephants and horses, and many skilled artisans; among all the people in the world, no one is as wealthy as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin). This is the first virtue of a wheel-turning monarch.

Second, the universal monarch is most upright and handsome, with a complexion beyond compare; among all the people in the world, there is none as upright and handsome as the universal monarch. This is the second virtue of the universal monarch.

Third, the wheel-turning king is always peaceful and secure, free from illness; his body is ever in equilibrium, neither cold nor hot, and he finds perfect comfort in both cold and heat. Whatever food and drink he consumes, it is always wholesome for him. Among all the people in the world, there is none who is as free from illness as the wheel-turning king. This is the third virtue of the wheel-turning king.

Fourth, the wheel-turning monarch is always peaceful, secure, and long-lived; among the people of the world, there is no one who is as constantly peaceful, secure, and long-lived as the wheel-turning monarch. These are the four virtues of a wheel-turning monarch.
"The Universal Monarch possesses seven treasures and four virtues in this manner.
The Universal Monarch governs by manifesting the practice of the True Dharma; he does not turn away from what is wholesome, Subhūti, but practices the ten virtuous deeds."
He instructs the minor kings, their ministers, attendants, and the people to practice the ten wholesome deeds.

The Wheel-Turning King pities the people of the various provinces and kingdoms as a father pities his sons, and the people of those provinces and kingdoms love and revere the Wheel-Turning King as sons love their father.

When a Wheel-Turning King governs the world, the continent of Jambudvīpa is level and even, without elevations or depressions; it is free of thorns, poisonous beasts, insects, and ants; it has no mountains, hills, ravines, or valleys; and its ground is free of gravel and stones, consisting instead only of discarded gold, silver, moon-bright pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, amber, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and coral.
"When a Wheel-Turning King governs the kingdom under heaven, it is prosperous, peaceful, secure, and flourishing; the five grains ripen in abundance and the population is vast.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"When a Wheel-Turning King governs the kingdom, there are eighty thousand districts, states, and villages under heaven, where the crowing of roosters can be heard echoing from one to another."
When a Wheel-Turning King governs the realm, water is always present throughout the world; the grasses and trees remain evergreen, and the wood is always covered with leaves and flowers.

The blades of grass on that ground are distributed all around, their color like peacock feathers and their fragrance like the scent of blossoms. When one steps upon them, they sink into the earth four inches; when the foot is lifted, they return to their former state, leaving not even a four-inch gap where the grass does not cover the ground.
There are fragrance trees that constantly produce flowers and fruit; when their fruit is broken open, various kinds of incense emerge.
There are clothing trees that produce flowers, fruit, and various kinds of garments.
There are jewel-garland trees that produce flowers and fruits; when these are broken open, there are within them countless varieties of jewel garlands.
There are "unceasing" flower trees that produce flowers and fruits; when these are broken open, there are various unceasing [sounds] within them.
There are fruit trees that constantly produce flowers and fruits; when broken open, they contain various kinds of fruits.
There are vessel trees that produce flowers and fruits; when broken open, they contain various kinds of vessels.
There are trees of music that produce flowers and fruit; when they are broken open, various kinds of musical instruments emerge.

When the Wheel-Turning King governs the country, at that time, throughout Jambudvīpa, there is no need for plowing or sowing; rice, grains, and all foodstuffs grow spontaneously, pure and free of husks, yielding various kinds of sweet flavors.
When a Wheel-Turning King approaches the end of his life, his body does not experience much pain.
It is just as when a skilled musician eats a large meal, his belly does not feel much pain;
so too, when a Wheel-Turning King approaches the end of his life, his body does not suffer such pain.

After the Wheel-turning King has passed away, the golden wheel and the white elephant treasure vanish; the dark-blue horse and the bright moon jewel also disappear. Then the woman-treasure, the minister-treasure of the treasury, and the minister-treasure who guides the way bathe the body of the Wheel-turning King, wrap it in cotton, and further wrap it in five hundred layers of fine cloth. They place it within an iron coffin, pour clarified butter over it until it is full, cover it, and fasten it with nails.
They carried out the coffin of the Wheel-Turning King, and the multitude together performed music, song, and dance.
Having carried it outside the city, they piled up all kinds of fragrant wood; then, placing the coffin of the Wheel-Turning King upon it, they set fire to it.

After the cremation, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Minister of the Treasury, and the Jewel of the Minister of State Affairs together collected the relics and placed them within a stupa built at the crossroads. It was forty *li* high and forty *li* in length and breadth; a wall was erected all around it, measuring two hundred *li* in length and breadth. It was adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and featured sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees surrounding it on all sides, making it exceedingly beautiful.
Those who came from the four directions to pay homage to the Wheel-Turning King, and those who performed meritorious deeds and erected stūpas, all obtained immeasurable merit.

At that time, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Minister of the Treasury, and the Jewel of the Minister of Statecraft, having erected stūpas for the Wheel-Turning King, then bestowed food upon the hungry, drink upon the thirsty, clothing upon those who desired clothes, incense, perfumes, and flowers upon those who desired them, and wealth, cattle, and sheep upon those who desired them.
Subsequently, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Minister Who Guards the Treasury, and the Jewel of the Minister Who Leads the Way passed away.
**Chapter Four: On the Nirayas (Hells), Part One** The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“There is the Great Iron Ring Mountain, and beyond it lies a second Great Iron Ring Mountain. Between them, it is profound and pitch-black; even the great and venerable radiance of the sun and moon cannot reach to illuminate it.”
Within it are eight great *nirayas* (hells); each *niraya* consists of sixteen sections. The first great *niraya* is named Saṃjīva;

the second great *niraya* is named Kālasūtra; the third great *niraya* is named Saṅghāta; the fourth great *niraya* is named Raurava; the fifth great *niraya* is named Mahāraurava; the sixth great *niraya* is named Tapana; the seventh great *niraya* is named Pratāpana; and the eighth great *niraya* is named Avīci-mahā.
The Buddha said:
"Why is it called 'Perception' (Sañjñā)?

In that Great Perception Hell (Mahāsañjñā-niraya), if someone falls into it, eight-finger-widths of fingernails grow upon them like sharp knives; they seize one another and pierce each other, and their flesh falls away at the touch of the hand. Because they harbor the perception of wanting to kill one another, this place of coarse suffering is called the Hell of Perception."

Furthermore, there are other various causes and conditions. Next, regarding that Great Perception Hell (*mahāsaṃjñā-niraya*): if anyone falls into it, swords and blades naturally appear in their hands with which they hack and stab one another. Because they perceive the desire to kill others, and due to these coarse perceptions, it is called "Perception."

Furthermore, there is another cause and condition: those who fall into this state naturally possess small knives in their hands with which they pierce and flay others, harboring the intent to kill them. Because of these coarse mental conceptions, it is called "conception" (saṃjñā).

Furthermore, there is another cause and condition: those who fall into the Great Perception Hell (Mahāsaṃjñā-naraka) scratch themselves with their hands, peeling the skin from their feet up to their heads; while harboring the thought of wanting to kill others, a cool wind arises and blows upon them, and the wounds on their bodies heal. As they pass the time talking to one another, they say, "We shall surely live again," and among them, some further say to each other:
"We have just been reborn."
For this reason, it is called the Saṃjñā Hell.
Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions by which the lifespan of those in hell is so long that they must emerge from the Saṃjñā Hell before they can run away seeking liberation.

"Furthermore, there is a hell named Black Boundary (Kṛṣṇabandhu), twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All those who enter within it have fire emerge from their bodies, which circles the body three times before re-entering; the agonizing pain is unbearable, yet they do not die because their transgressions and evils have not yet been exhausted."

Furthermore, in the Kālasūtra hell, fire encircles the eastern wall three times and burns the people; the flames reach the western wall, the flames from the western wall reach the eastern wall; the flames from the southern wall reach the northern wall, and the flames from the northern wall reach the southern wall. The upper flames descend to the ground, and the lower flames ascend to the heavens. The person is scorched and roasted within, suffering such agonizing pain that it is unbearable; yet because their transgressions have not yet been expiated, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time before finally emerging from the Kālasūtra hell, whereupon they run away seeking liberation.

“There is a hell named Boiling Excrement, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All those who enter it are submerged up to their necks; the boiling liquid surges and leaps, and people trample them down so that they cannot escape. Their bodies, hands, feet, ears, noses, faces, and eyes are all scorched and cooked; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die.
There are insects called Iron-Mouths that peck at human skulls, peck through human flesh, pierce the bones, and devour the marrow.”

The beings within the Niraya hell roll up excrement with their hands and eat it; their lips and tongues are scorched, and their throats, bellies, intestines, and stomachs are all rotted away, passing through them as they go. The toxic pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time, and only after this do they emerge from the Boiling Excrement Niraya hell, running about seeking liberation.

There is a hell named Five Hundred Nails, twenty thousand li in length and breadth, into which all enter. The attendants of this hell seize each person by their hands and feet, pin them down on the ground, and drive a glowing iron nail through their right palm; they drive an iron nail through their left palm, an iron nail through their right foot, and again an iron nail through their left foot. They then drive an iron nail through their heart, and further drive iron nails all over their bodies until they penetrate the earth. Having been pinned to the body with all five hundred nails, the victim continues to struggle and tries to rise, yet the agonizing pain is unbearable.
The hell-attendant asked,
"What do you seek? They replied:

"I am suffering only from hunger and thirst! A hell-attendant then takes tongs and pincers to force open his mouth, placing glowing, heated iron within his throat; his lips, tongue, and throat are all scorched, and the intestines and stomach within his belly are all seared and rotted away, passing down through the entrails. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because his transgressions are not yet exhausted, he does not die. For this reason, a person remains in hell for an exceedingly long time; only after this does he emerge from the Hell of Five Hundred Nails, whereupon he flees, seeking liberation.
“There is a hell named Chē-tiē, twenty thousand li in length and breadth; all enter into it, and as soon as they do, the attendants of the hell ask them: ‘What do you seek?’”
He replied, "I suffer only from hunger and thirst.

Then the hell-wardens each seized his body, threw him to the ground, took pincers to pry open his mouth, and poured molten copper into it. His lips and tongue were scorched; his five internal organs, intestines, and stomach were all seared, rotted, and burned. The agonizing pain was unbearable, yet because his transgressions were not yet exhausted, he did not die. He remained in hell for a very long time, after which he finally emerged and ran away seeking liberation.
“There is a hell named ‘The Drinker’; they all enter into it, and the wardens of the hell then ask them:
‘What do you seek? They reply:”

"I am merely suffering from hunger and thirst! At once, the hell-wardens each seize the person's body and throw it onto the scorching ground; they pry open the mouth with tongs and place a glowing iron ball inside. The lips, tongue, and throat are all charred; the five viscera, intestines, and stomach are completely consumed by fire as the ball passes through. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time before emerging from the Drinking Hell, whereupon they run away seeking liberation.
“There is a hell named Single Copper Cauldron, twenty thousand *li* in length and breadth, into which all enter.

The hell-wardens then lift the bodies, hands, and feet of the people and place them into the cauldron to boil them; those at the bottom are cooked, and those at the top are likewise cooked. The boiling broth surges and ebbs; even those whose hands and feet are exposed on the surface are cooked when covered. It is like boiling beans: those at the bottom are cooked, and those at the top are likewise cooked; they are cooked when covered and cooked when exposed.”

The beings in the *niraya* hell are likewise; within the copper cauldron *niraya* twenty thousand *li* deep, they are cooked from top to bottom, and their heads, faces, ears, noses, hands, and feet are all seen to be seared and rotten.

The wardens of hell pierce them with spears and thrust them inside; the agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions have not been expiated, they do not die. For this reason, they remain within for an exceedingly long time. Only after that do they emerge from one copper cauldron of hell and immediately flee, seeking liberation.

"There is a hell named Many Copper Cauldrons (*Bahutāmra-kumbha*), twenty thousand *li* in length and breadth. All those who enter it are seized by the hell-wardens, who lift their bodies, hands, and feet and place them into the cauldrons. As the boiling water surges and leaps, they are tossed back and forth between the bottom and the surface; their heads, faces, hands, and feet are all seen to become cooked and rotten. The hell-wardens then pierce the sinners with spears and place them into other cauldrons, where they are boiled in the same manner. The agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time. Only after this do they emerge from the Many Copper Cauldrons hell and run about, seeking liberation."

“There is a hell named Grinding (Cūrṇana), twenty thousand li in length and breadth, into which all enter. The wardens of the hell then each seize a person and place them upon an iron grinding wheel to lie down; they cover them with a lid and seize the wheel to grind them into fragments. Their flesh and blood flow away while their bones remain on the wheel. Fire erupts from within and burns them; the agony is so fierce and unbearable that they do not die because their transgressions have not yet been expiated. For this reason, they remain there for an exceedingly long time. Only after this do they emerge from the Iron Grinding Hell, whereupon they run about seeking liberation.”

“There is a hell named Pus and Blood, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. When people all enter it, pus and blood-flames spontaneously emerge. People try to grasp it with their hands and feet in an attempt to escape, but their heads, faces, ears, noses, bodies, hands, and feet are all scorched. They then take the pus and blood with their own hands and eat it; their lips, tongues, and throats are all scorched, and the intestines, stomach, and five viscera within their bellies are all scorched. It then passes out below, and the poisonous pain is unbearable. Because their transgressions have not yet been expiated, they do not die; they remain therein for a very long time. Only after this do they emerge from the Pus and Blood Hell, running about seeking liberation.”

“There is a hell named Gaojun (High and Steep), twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter into it, and from the flames of the hell, the inhabitants run up and down the mountains on its sides. Their heads, faces, ears, noses, bodies, hands, and feet are all scorched and rotted; the poison and pain are unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time, and only after this do they emerge from the Gaojun Hell, immediately running about seeking liberation.”

“There is a hell named Chopping Boards, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter within it, and the wardens of the hell each seize a person, flinging them onto a ground of glowing iron. They measure their bodies with iron cords and, holding axes in both hands, hack away at their bodies, heads, faces, hands, feet, noses, and ears. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die; they remain therein for a very long time. Only after this do they emerge from the Chopping Boards Hell, fleeing in search of liberation.”

“There is a hell named *Droṇa*, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter into it, and the hell-wardens immediately take burning charcoal and cast the person into the *droṇa* to measure them. They rub the top with their hands until the head, face, body, hands, feet, nose, and ears are all scorched and rotted away. The hell-wardens run the person back and forth over the fire, roasting and searing them; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time, and only after that do they emerge from the *Droṇa* hell, running about seeking liberation.”

“There is a hell named Sword-Leaf Tree, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter within it, where winds arise and blow, causing the leaves of the iron sword trees to fall. As they descend, they sever people’s hands, feet, heads, faces, ears, noses, and bodies; the agony is unbearable. Yet because their transgressions have not been expiated, they do not die. They remain therein for a very long time, after which they finally emerge from the Iron Sword Tree Hell and flee, seeking liberation.”

“There is a hell named the River of Churning (Kṣāranadī), twenty thousand li in length and breadth. On both sides of the river grow the ‘shaving-sword’ grasses; when people enter it, the swords pierce them from above, severing their hands, feet, heads, faces, noses, ears, and bodies, such that the agonizing pain is unbearable.”

"At that time, all people fall into the River of Scorching Boils, where the water boils and surges. At the bottom lie thorns eight inches long; they pierce the bodies of the people so that blood flows and splatters, until nothing remains but bone. Then, the boiling water surges upward again, tossing them back up. The agony is unbearable. Driven by the wind to the grass on the bank, the blades turn inward, severing their heads, faces, ears, noses, bodies, hands, and feet; the agony is unbearable. Yet, because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. The hell-warden then asks the person: 'What do you seek?'"
He replied, "I am merely suffering from hunger and thirst!

Then the attendants of the niraya hell each seized a person and threw them onto the burning ground, pouring molten copper down their throats. Their lips, tongues, and pharynx were scorched; their bodies, five viscera, intestines, and stomachs were all consumed by fire. The liquid passed through and out, yet the agonizing pain was unbearable. Because their transgressions were not yet exhausted, they did not die.

On both sides of the river stand iron trees. As soon as the hell-beings are seized by the attendants, they are hoisted beneath these iron trees. Thorns grow upon the trees and hang downward; they pierce the bodies of the beings, causing flesh and blood to flow away until only bones remain.

When a wind arises, it blows upon their bodies, restoring them to their former state. There are birds called Iron Crows with iron beaks; they peck at the heads of the beings to devour their brains and perch upon their heads to peck out their eyeballs. When the beings wish to descend, the iron thorns point upward to pierce them; when they wish to ascend, the thorns point downward to pierce them.

At that time, people run about seeking liberation, yet they fall back into the River of Scum and Filth. The boiling water surges and leaps as they sink to the bottom, where they are pierced by thorns as before. When they rise to the surface on the scum, the wind blows them toward the banks, where knives slice against the grain, wounding their heads, faces, ears, noses, bodies, hands, and feet. The poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die.
The tree-hell guardians ask them: "What do you seek?"
He said, "I am merely suffering from hunger and thirst!
Thereupon, [the wardens] took molten copper and poured it into his mouth; his lips, tongue, throat, intestines, and stomach were all scorched and rotted away as it passed through and out.
When they reach the edge of the precipice, they are driven back onto the trees at the edge of the *niraya* hell; as they attempt to descend, blades point upward to pierce them.

There is a bird named *Nani-qua* (Needle-beak) that pecks at people’s heads to devour their brains; it pecks at the pupils of those on their heads, attempting to climb up and down while piercing them from every direction. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die.

They fall back again into the River of Scouring and Tossing, where they suffer poisonous pains as before; the wind blows them once more to the riverbank, where grass-blade knives prick and flay them as before. The henchmen of Niraya then ask the person: "What do you seek?"
He replied, "I suffer only from hunger and thirst!

As before, molten copper was poured into his mouth; it burned and scorched him with unbearable agony, and he remained therein for a very long time. Only after that did he finally emerge from the Kṣāranadī River, whereupon he fled, seeking liberation.

There is a hell named Wolf-Jackal (Vṛka-śṛgāla), twenty thousand li in length and breadth. When people enter it, wolf-jackals naturally appear before them; flames issue from their bodies, and they bite off the flesh of human bodies, devouring it as soon as it enters their mouths. The agonizing pain is unbearable. Flying birds also come together to peck and eat the people and pluck out their eyes; the agonizing pain is unbearable. Because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die, remaining therein for a very long time. Only after this do they finally emerge from the Wolf-Jackal Hell, whereupon they run about seeking liberation.

"There is a hell named Cold Ice, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter within it, where cold winds rise from all four sides; they blow upon the bodies of men, penetrating through the skin, flesh, tendons, and bones into the very marrow. For this reason, they die therein."
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is it called the Black-Eared Niraya?

If there are those who fall into the Black-Eared Niraya, black winds and hot sand rain down upon their bodies; as soon as they touch the ground, their skin, flesh, bones, marrow, fat, and pith are scorched. The poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. For this reason, it is called 'Black Ear'."

Furthermore, there is another cause and condition: next, as for the Great Hell of Black Ears (*Kṛṣṇakarṇī*), those who fall into it have their bodies bound with burning iron black ropes, which the wind then tightens and constricts, tearing away the skin and flesh of their bodies, breaking the bones to extract the marrow; the agony is unbearable, yet they do not die because their transgressions are not yet exhausted. For this reason, it is named "Black Ears."

Furthermore, there is a cause and condition for falling into the Great Niraya of Black Ears (*Kṛṣṇakarṇa*). The attendants of that hell wrap the bodies of the inhabitants with cords of black iron heated until glowing red; this scorches their skin, flesh, integument, marrow, and bones. The agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. For this reason, it is named "Black Ears."

Furthermore, there are those who enter the Great Black-Eared Hell (Mahākāla-niraya). There, they are bound on their left and right sides with iron ropes by the hell-wardens, who then saw them apart and split them with axes. The agony is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die; for this reason, it is called the Black-Eared Hell.

Furthermore, a person remains within it for an exceedingly long time, suffering the agonizing pain of being scorched and roasted; only after emerging from this Black-Eared Hell does one run away, seeking liberation.

“There is a hell named Black Fire, twenty thousand li in length and breadth. All people enter within it; black fire issues forth from their very bodies, circles the body three times, and returns back into the body. The agonizing pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. They remain in this hell for a very long time before emerging from the Black Fire Hell, entering successively the sixteen hells as previously described, until they reach the Cold Ice Hell, where their lives finally end.”
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is it called Saṃghāta Niraya?

When there are those who fall into the great Saṃghāta Niraya, two iron mountains spontaneously emerge with fire; these fiery mountains close together and crush the beings within the hell, shattering their bodies. The agony is unbearable, yet they do not die because their transgressions are not yet exhausted; for this reason, it is called Saṃghāta."

Furthermore, there is another causal condition: next, if there are those who fall into the Saṃjīva Great Hell, all such persons enter within it. There are two mountains that strike against each other, and the bodies of the offenders are completely shattered and fall apart; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they do not die. For this reason, it is called Saṃjīva.

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions by which a person remains within it for an exceedingly long time; only after emerging from the great Saṃjīva hell does one run away, seeking liberation.
Furthermore, having entered the sixteen hells as previously described, one finally reaches the Hell of Cold Ice and there passes away.
The Buddha asked:
"For what reason is it named the Lohita (Red) Hell?"

If there are those who fall into the *loutou* (Lohakumbha) hell, the attendants of Niraya each seize them and place them within iron cauldrons; the people cry out loudly in great poison and great pain, and for this reason it is named Loutou.

Furthermore, there are sinful persons who fall into the Raurava hell. The attendants of the hell seize these people and place them within iron cauldrons; they suffer great venomous pain and shriek aloud, and for this reason it is called Raurava.

Furthermore, when there are sinners who fall into the Raurava hell, the wardens of the hell each seize them and place them in iron cauldrons; they wail from great poison and intense pain, and for this reason it is called Raurava.

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions by which a sinner remains within it for an exceedingly long time. Only after emerging from the Lūhaka hell does he run away, seeking liberation; yet he again enters the sixteen hells in succession as before, until he reaches the Arbuda (Ice-Cold) hell, where his life comes to an end.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is it called 'Great Wailing' (Mahāraurava)?

When there are those who fall into the Mahāraurava hell, the wardens of the hell each seize their bodies and place them in large cauldrons to boil them. They suffer such extreme, agonizing pain that they wail loudly; therefore, it is called 'Great Wailing.'"

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions: when there are sinners who fall into the Great Howling Hell (Mahāraurava), the hell-wardens each seize their bodies and place them inside great cauldrons; they suffer excruciating pain and cry out loudly.

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions by which a person falls into the Great Screaming Hell (Mahāraurava). There, the hell-wardens each seize the person and place them in cauldrons and boiling pots to cook them; it is so extremely agonizing that they scream out in great distress.

Therefore, they remain within it for an exceedingly long time. Only after emerging from the Great Shouting Hell do they run about seeking liberation; however, they successively enter the sixteen hells as before, until they finally die in the Cold Ice Hell.
The Buddha said:
“For what reason is it called ‘Scorching and Roasting’?

When there are sinners who fall into the Great Scorching and Roasting Hell (Mahātapana), the hell-wardens each seize them and place them within an iron house. Fire spontaneously breaks out, scorching and roasting them with excruciating pain; therefore, it is called ‘Scorching and Roasting.’”

Furthermore, as for those sinners who have fallen into the Great Hell of Scorching and Roasting, the hell-wardens drag them into an iron lattice pavilion where fire spontaneously arises; they are scorched and roasted with excruciating pain, which is why it is called "Scorching and Roasting. Because their transgressions and evils are not yet exhausted, they do not die.

Furthermore, as for those sinners who fall into the Great Roasting Hell (Mahātapana-niraya), the hell-wardens drag them onto iron platforms where fires spontaneously arise, burning and roasting them with agonizing pain; therefore, it is called "Roasting."

The sinner remains therein for a very long time; having finally emerged from the Scorching Hell, he flees seeking liberation, but in succession enters the sixteen hells as before, until he reaches the Cold Ice Hell and his life comes to an end.
The Buddha said: “For what reason is it called Avīci Mahā?

When there are sinners who fall into the Avīci Mahā Niraya, their eyes see only unwholesome forms and do not see wholesome forms; their ears hear only unwholesome sounds and do not hear wholesome sounds; as for what their mouths eat, they obtain only unwholesome flavors and do not obtain sweet ones; their noses smell only stench and do not smell pleasant fragrances; their bodies experience only unwholesome sensations; and the dharmas they contemplate contain only evil and no goodness. For this reason, it is called Avīci Mahā.”

Furthermore, there are other causes and conditions by which certain sinners fall into the Avīci Mahānaraka hell. There, the flames from the eastern wall reach the western wall, the flames from the western wall reach the eastern wall; the flames from the southern wall reach the northern wall, and the flames from the northern wall reach the southern wall; the flames from above descend to the ground, and the flames from the ground rise to the ceiling. Fire comes from all six directions, burning and scorching the person with such agonizing pain that it is therefore called the Great Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, as for those sinners who fall into the Avīci Mahānaraka hell, there is not even a moment’s pleasure in the time it takes to snap one's fingers; therefore, it is named Avīci Mahā.

The sinner remains within it for an exceedingly long time; only after emerging from the Avīci Mahānaraka does he flee, seeking liberation, and enters the sixteen hells in succession as before, until he dies upon reaching the Arbuda (Cold Ice) Hell.
The Buddha said:

"Outside the Great Iron Ring Mountains, to the south of Jambudvīpa, there is the city of King Yama. It is twenty-four thousand *li* in length and breadth. It is constructed with sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold diamond nets, and sevenfold rows of trees. Parks, pavilions, and bathing pools surround it on all sides. There are golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, and musaragalva walls with gates made of every kind of treasure. Above, there are curved canopies and latticed pavilions; below, there are parks, pavilions, and bathing pools. There are various kinds of trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits that emit various fragrances, and various flying birds that sing together in harmony."
The Buddha said:

"If a person commits evil with their body, speaks evil with their mouth, and harbors evil thoughts in their mind, and after death falls into this Niraya of King Yama, the attendants of the Niraya will bind the sinner in reverse fetters and bring him before King Yama. They address the King, saying:

'These individuals were all unfilial toward their parents, failed to serve śramaṇas and practitioners of the Way, and did not fear the prohibitions of future lives; we pray that Your Majesty shall punish them according to what You know.'"
The king immediately summoned the man before him, examined him with careful scrutiny, and asked:

"When you were formerly in the world, did you not see people aged one hundred and twenty years, with white hair and fallen teeth, wrinkled faces and sagging skin, their physical strength diminished, walking with the aid of a staff, their bodies trembling?"
The person said, "I have seen it. [The Buddha asked:
"Why did you not think to yourself:"
"I too shall likewise reach such extreme old age; there is no one who can escape it.
Why do you not reform yourself in body, speech, and mind to practice what is wholesome?
The person replied:
"I am indeed a lecherous person. The King said:

"Now I shall question you regarding the intent behind your lechery. This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of the gods or the king, nor the fault of your relatives or acquaintances, nor the fault of your deceased ancestors, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You have committed evil; you yourself shall receive its retribution.
This was the first question asked by King Yama. Then the second king, Anati, questioned him with careful scrutiny regarding the truth:

"When you were formerly in the world, did you not see men and women who were ill, weak and exhausted, lying upon their beds, with foul secretions flowing from them, unable to sit up or rise, and dependent on others for sitting, rising, eating, and drinking?"
The man replied, "I have seen it. The king said:
"Why do you not reflect: 'I too shall likewise fall ill and become emaciated,' and thereby reform your body,
speech, and mind toward what is wholesome?"
“I am indeed licentious. The King said:

“Now I shall question you regarding the intent behind your licentiousness. This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of the gods or the king, nor the fault of your relatives or friends, nor the fault of your deceased ancestors, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.”
"You committed the evil yourself; you must now experience the retribution yourself.
This was the second question from King Yama. Then the King asked a third time:

"When you were formerly in the world, did you not see men and women at the time of death, their bodies decaying and broken apart like discarded timber, being devoured by crows, birds, insects, ants, foxes, and wolves, or being cremated or buried?"
The person replied, "I have seen it. [The Buddha said:
"Why did you not think to yourself: "
"I too shall die in this same way.
Should one not then reform one's body, speech, and mind to practice virtue?
"I have indeed committed sexual misconduct."
The King said:

"I shall question you regarding the intent of this lewdness. This is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of the gods or the king, nor the fault of your deceased ancestors, nor the fault of your kinsmen or acquaintances, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You committed evil yourself; you must receive the retribution yourself.
This was the third question from King Yama. Then King Yama asked a fourth time:
"When you were formerly in the world, did you not see infants who, having no knowledge, defecate and urinate upon themselves?"
The person said, "I have already seen it. [The Buddha asked:
"Why did you not think to yourself:..."
"I was originally just like this.
Should one not reform one's own body, speech, and mind to become virtuous?
"I am indeed lustful and disorderly."
The King said:

"Now I shall question you regarding your intent toward lewdness and disorder. This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of the gods, kings, or emperors, nor the fault of your deceased ancestors, nor the fault of your kinsmen or acquaintances, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You committed evil yourself; you must receive the retribution yourself.
This was the fourth question from King Yama. Then King Yama asked again with the fifth question, examining the matter with profound and careful scrutiny:

"When you were formerly in the world, did you not see thieves and criminals who had committed murder in the various provinces, districts, and counties being reported to the king? Did you not see the king issue an edict to have their four limbs severed and their heads hung out as a warning?"
Whether they are boiled in cauldrons, or burned alive;
whether they are confined in prisons and subjected to the agonizing pain of flogging and scourging;
or whether their hands, feet, noses, and ears are severed, or they are impaled alive, or their heads are cut off—such are the various forms of cruel torment.
The man replied, "I have seen it.
[The Buddha said,] "Why did you not think to yourself: "
"If I have committed a transgression, you should likewise take me [to task] in this way.
Should one then reform one's body, speech, and mind to become virtuous?
"I am indeed licentious and disorderly."

"I shall question you regarding the intent of your lustful transgression. This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of gods, kings, or emperors, nor the fault of deceased ancestors, nor the fault of your kinsmen or acquaintances, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You committed evil yourself; you must suffer for it yourself.

Upon this fifth interrogation by King Yama, he hands the person over to the attendants of hell. They then each take the person and cast them headlong into hell. The city of hell is forty thousand li in both width and length, and it is profoundly dark and gloomy.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Four gates face the four directions, The corners are fortified most firmly;
The walls are made of iron, And the top is likewise covered with iron."
The ground there is entirely covered with iron, and fire spontaneously erupts from it.
Within that realm are ten great nirayas:

the first is named Arbuda, the second Nirarbuda, the third Aṭaṭa, the fourth Hahava, the fifth Huhuva, the sixth Utpala, the seventh Padma, the eighth Mahāpadma, the ninth Kumuda, and the tenth Puṇḍarīka.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is it called Ābu?
In the Ābu hell, the bodies of the sinners arise spontaneously, like clouds and mist; therefore, it is called Ābu."
For what reason is it called Nirarbuda?
In the hell of Nirarbuda, the bodies of the sinners are like the solitary flesh of a deer; therefore, it is named Nirarbuda.
For what reason is it called "Agha"?
In the Agha-niraya hell, the sinners suffer such great misery and such intense agony that they cry out; for this reason, it is called "Agha."
For what reason is it called Arbuda?
In the Arbuda hell, the sinners suffer such extreme cruelty and agony that they cry out and wail; therefore, it is called Arbuda.
For what reason is he called Ārava?
In the hell of Ārava, the sinners suffer such extreme pain and agony that they wish to cry out but are unable to do so; they can only move their tongues. For this reason, he is called Ārava.
For what reason is it called *kukūla*?
In the *kukūla* hell, the bodies of the sinners are like yellow fire; therefore, it is called *kukūla*.
For what reason is it called *utpala*?
The sinners in the Utpala Hell have bodies that are blue like the utpala flower; therefore, it is named Utpala.
For what reason is it named Kumuda?
The sinners within the Kumbhīra hell have bodies that are yellowish-white, like the kumbha flower; therefore, it is named Kumbhīra.
For what reason is it named Puṇḍarīka?
In the Pundarika hell, the bodies of the sinners are red like the *pundarīka* flower; therefore, it is named Pundarika.
Why is it named Padma? In the Padma hell, the bodies of the sinners are crimson; therefore, it is named Padma.
The Buddha said:

"Suppose there were a granary with a capacity of one hundred and twenty hu and four sheng, filled to the brim with mustard seeds. A person who lives for a hundred years were to come once every hundred years and remove a single mustard seed."
"Monks! Even when these one hundred and twenty hu (bushels) and four sheng (measures) of mustard seeds are completely exhausted, a person remains within the Arbuda hell without end.
If a person is in the Nirarbuda hell, they must take out one mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting two thousand four hundred and eighty hu of mustard seeds may they finally emerge."
In the Avīci hell, one takes out a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting forty-eight thousand one hundred and sixty hu of seeds does one emerge.
In the Arbuda hell, one takes out a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting nine hundred and sixty-three thousand three hundred hu of seeds does one emerge.
In the Aralu hell, one takes a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting one million nine hundred twenty-six thousand four hundred *hu* of seeds does one finally emerge.

Within the Kṣuramārga Hell, one removes a single mustard seed every hundred years; it takes the exhaustion of three hundred and eighty million five hundred and twenty-eight *hú* (bushels) before one can finally escape.
In the Nīlotpala-hell, one takes out a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting eighty-six billion five hundred and sixty *hu* [of seeds] does one emerge.

In the Pīta-śveta-hell, one takes out a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting one trillion seven hundred and twenty-one billion two hundred million *hu* [of seeds] does one emerge.

In the Kuṇapa-padma hell, one takes out a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after exhausting thirty-four trillion, four hundred and twenty-two thousand four hundred *hu* of seeds will one finally be released.

In the Red Lotus Hell, one must remove a single mustard seed every hundred years; only after sixty million eight hundred and eighty billion four million four hundred and forty-eight thousand *hu* have been exhausted can one emerge.
Twenty minor kalpas constitute half a kalpa. There was a man named Gopāli who fell into the Red Lotus Hell because he sat and slandered Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Buddha then spoke these verses:
"If there is one who initiates [harm], From their mouth issues a blade;
Sitting and speaking evil words, They immediately turn back to cut and wound themselves."
If one slanders those who should be praised and praises those who should be slandered, the verbal expression of evil is a grave transgression;
with such heavy verbal faults, there can be no peace or stability.
For example, one who practices gambling and deception commits only minor evils;
however, to harbor evil intentions toward a virtuous person is the most grave of transgressions.
There are one hundred thousand *niraya* hells, and thirty-five *āpāyika* hells.
Day and night, King Yama three times each undergoes the burning of heated copper;

naturally arising fires appear before him in his palace, and the King, struck with terror, his hair standing on end, immediately exits his palace chambers. Outside as well, [the fires] spontaneously...
Nevertheless, O Great King, [the king] was seized by great terror and retreated back into the palace.
Then the attendants of Niraya each seized King Yama, flaying him upon the ground of glowing iron. Taking iron hooks, they forced open his mouth;
molten copper was poured into the king’s mouth, scorching his throat and gullet, and burning through his belly, intestines, stomach, and five viscera until the copper flowed out.
Below, they are scorched and roasted; the poisonous pain is unbearable, yet because their past evils are not yet exhausted, they do not die.

In this world, those who have committed evil through bodily action, evil through speech, and evil through mental thought fall into the evil realms after death, where they are scorched and roasted with poisonous pain, just like the offenders in the hells.

"Those people in the world who have performed good deeds with their bodies, spoken good words with their mouths, and harbored good thoughts with their minds, will all be reborn in the heavens after death.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"The King’s messenger summoned the deity to question him regarding the evil transgressions committed by the people."
That person is constantly afflicted by sorrow and poison; because of this body, people undergo toil and suffering.
Knowing what must be asked, one does not commit evil; one immediately practices the noble and wholesome Dharma.
If there is fear regarding the causes and conditions of existence, know that birth is nothing but sickness and death.
Without causes or conditions, one is liberated; birth, illness, and death are extinguished.
Attaining peace and supreme happiness, one realizes nirvana in this very life.
"From all terrors and anxieties, one is delivered; in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one alone possesses permanence.
Chapter Five: On the Asuras. *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, Chapter Five: On the Asuras. The Buddha said:
"Forty thousand *li* beneath Mount Sumeru, there dwells an asura named Kāḍaśiri."

Its city walls and moats are each three million three hundred and sixty thousand li in breadth and length; they are fashioned from the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and are exceedingly beautiful, with these materials encircling them on all sides.

There are seven layers of walls and railings, seven layers of diamond moats, and seven rows of trees, eight thousand *li* in height and sixty thousand *li* in length, all fashioned from the seven treasures.
In the four directions there are four gates; each gate is one million *li* high and six thousand *li* wide.

At the side of each gate, there dwell ten *asura* kings, who have constructed palaces out of the seven treasures, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold diamond nets, and sevenfold rows of trees.
There were trees that were blue, red, yellow, and white; there were leafy trees, flowering trees, and fruit-bearing trees.
Birds perched upon the trees—namely cranes, peacocks, mynas, and white doves—all gathered upon the trees, singing together in most harmonious accord.

To the east of Śatapuṣkalaśrī Asura, forty thousand *li* away, there is an asura city and citadel, each thirty-six hundred thousand *li* in breadth and length. It is exquisitely adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—forming sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold diamond-patterned fences, and sevenfold rows of trees, all encircling it on every side.
In the four directions there are gates; each gate is one hundred thousand *li* high and sixty thousand *li* wide, with three hundred asuras dwelling within each.

They are surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of flowing water, exceedingly deep and full, in which there are blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses. The sand at the bottom is entirely gold, and along the edges there are trees—some green, some red, some yellow, and some white—including leafy trees, flowering trees, and fruit-bearing trees. Upon these trees dwell various kinds of birds, which are most beautiful and sing together in harmony.
Forty thousand *li* to the south of Śīrṣavat is an asura realm; there dwells an asura named Pāṭahā.

Its city walls are forty-six hundred thousand *li* in both breadth and length, adorned with the seven treasures in exquisite patterns. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative balustrades, and sevenfold rows of trees.
On the four sides there are gates; each gate is one hundred thousand li high and sixty thousand li wide. Within each gate dwell three hundred asuras.
Surrounding them are seven layers of flowing water, exceedingly deep and full, with sand at the bottom entirely of gold.
Within it are blue, red, yellow, and white lotus flowers; there are seven layers of walls and seven layers of railings, with moats and rows of trees surrounding them on all sides.

There are trees that are blue, red, yellow, and white; there are trees that produce leaves, flowers, and fruit. Each tree is filled with various kinds of flying birds, which sing together in most harmonious accord.
Forty thousand *li* to the west of the Asura Mahāpāśuśrī is an Asura named Pāri.

The city walls and moats are each thirty-six myriad *li* in breadth and length; they are all beautifully adorned with the seven treasures and painted in exquisite colors. There are seven layers of walls, with railings and battlements, and groves of trees and enclosures ten myriad *li* high and sixty thousand *li* wide.

In the four directions there are four gates; each gate is one hundred thousand li in height and sixty thousand li in width. All are constructed of the seven treasures, and at the side of each gate dwell three hundred asuras.

Their palaces were likewise constructed of the seven treasures, with sevenfold walls, railings, moats, and rows of trees. There were seven tiers of flowing water, deep and full, with golden sand at their bottom; there were also blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, as well as blue, red, yellow, and white trees bearing leaves, flowers, and fruit. Above them, various kinds of birds sang together in beautiful harmony.
Forty thousand *li* to the north of the palace of the Asura Śatapuṣkala lies the city of the Asura Rāhu.

Its walls and moats are each three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in width and length; they are likewise adorned with the seven treasures in exquisite patterns, and are surrounded on all sides by walls of the seven treasures, railings, balustrades, and trees.
The walls are one hundred thousand *li* high and sixty thousand *li* wide.
On each of the four sides there are four gates; each gate is one hundred thousand *li* high and sixty thousand *li* wide. Beside each gate, there dwell three hundred Asuras.

Its palaces were likewise fashioned from the seven treasures, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold balustrades, and rows of trees. It was surrounded on all sides by seven layers of flowing water, deep and full, within which were blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses; the sand upon its floor was entirely gold.

Furthermore, it was surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, balustrades, and trees; there were trees of blue, red, yellow, and white that produced flowers, leaves, and fruits, upon which various birds perched, singing most beautifully in harmony with one another.

"In the city of Śatapuṣkala-āsurendra, there is a great tree named Divasasaṃkrānta; it is twelve thousand *li* in height and twelve thousand *li* in circumference. Its roots extend twenty thousand *li* deep, its trunk has a girth of forty thousand *li*, and it is constantly laden with flowers and fruit."

The asura king Śatapuṣkalaśrī is twenty-eight thousand *li* tall; among them, some are twenty-four thousand *li*, some are twenty thousand *li*, some are sixteen thousand *li*, some are twelve thousand *li*, and some are eight thousand *li*. There are those with seven voices, those with six voices, five voices, four voices, three voices, and two voices; the smallest are half a voice in height.
The palace of the asura Śatapuṣkala has four kinds of winds that constantly sustain it. What are these four?
First, the indestructible wind; second, the firmly abiding wind; third, the sustaining wind; and fourth, the upward-moving wind.
"These are the four types of winds that sustain the waters above like floating clouds.

Chapter Six: On Dragons and Birds.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“There are four kinds of nāgas.
What are the four? First, nāgas born from eggs; second, nāgas born from moisture; third, nāgas born from a womb; and fourth, nāgas born by transformation. These are the four kinds of nāgas.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

“There are four kinds of garuḍas: first, those born from eggs; second, those born from water; third, those born from a womb; and fourth, those born by transformation. These are the four kinds of birds.”

At the bottom of the great ocean, to the north of Mount Sumeru, lies the palace of the Naga King Sagara. It is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and is adorned with the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—forming seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, seven layers of balustrades, and seven layers of trees, all of which are beautiful and magnificent on every side.

There were golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, and musaragalva walls with gates made of every kind of jewel; they were beautifully adorned with exquisite paintings.
Its walls extend twenty thousand *li*, with a single gate. The gate is two thousand four hundred *li* high and one thousand two hundred *li* wide.

Five hundred spirits and deities constantly guard the gate. Upon the gate and the walls are railings, lattices, and curved canopies. Beside the gate are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools, where various trees produce all kinds of fragrances; there are various flowers, various leaves, and various flying birds that sing together in harmony.

To the north of the great ocean lies the palace of the Nāga King Dhanada, measuring twenty-eight thousand li in both width and length. It is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, railings, balustrades, and rows of trees, all fashioned from the seven precious gems.

The palace gates were four thousand forty li high and four hundred eighty li wide. Upon the walls were railings, lattices, and curved awnings; surrounding them were gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, and trees, where birds sang in harmonious chorus, like the gardens and pavilions of the Dragon King Sāgara.

"To the north of the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali; its trunk encircles two hundred and eighty *li*, it is four thousand *li* in height, and its branches and leaves extend for two thousand *li*."

To the east of the Kūṭaśālmali tree is the palace of the egg-born Garuḍas, twenty-four thousand *li* in breadth and length. It is adorned with sevenfold walls, railings, balustrades, trees, gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools, where birds sing together in harmony.

To the south of the Kūṭaśālmali tree, there is a palace of the water-born Garuḍas, twenty-four thousand li in breadth and length. It likewise possesses sevenfold walls, railings, balustrades, trees, gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, flowers, and fragrances; and birds fly about, singing in harmonious concert.

To the west of the great tree Śāla, there is the palace of the garuḍas born from eggs, twenty-four thousand li in breadth and length. It likewise possesses sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, as well as railings, balustrades, groves of trees, gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, flowers, and fragrances; birds fly about, singing in harmonious concert.

To the north of the great tree Śāla, there is the palace of the transformation-born Garuḍas, twenty-four thousand *li* in breadth and length. It likewise possesses sevenfold walls, railings, balustrades, trees, and groves made of the seven treasures, as well as gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, flowers, and incense; birds fly about, singing in harmonious chorus.
"When a golden-winged garuḍa of the egg-born kind wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, it descends from an eastern branch of the Kūṭaśālmali tree into the great ocean.

Striking the seawater with its wings, it stirs up waves eight thousand li high; it seizes and devours the egg-born nāgas, but it cannot obtain those of the womb-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born kinds."

When the water-born garuḍa wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, it descends from the great Kūṭaśālmali tree to the great ocean; striking the seawater with its wings, it causes waves eight thousand *li* high, and then seizes the egg-born nāga to devour it.

When the *garuḍa* of the water-born class desires to seize a dragon of the water-born class, it descends from the southern branch of the great *kūṭaśālmali* tree and enters the ocean. It strikes the sea with its wings, causing the waves to surge sixteen thousand *li*; it seizes the water-born dragons to eat them, yet it cannot seize those born from the womb or those born through transformation.

When the garuḍa of the womb-birth (jarāyuja) wishes to seize a nāga of the egg-birth (aṇḍaja), it descends from the eastern branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree into the great ocean; striking the seawater with its wings, it creates waves eight thousand li high, and seizes the egg-born nāgas to devour them.

When the garuḍa born from the womb-kind wishes to seize a dragon of the water-kind, it descends from the southern branch of the great tree Kūṭaśālmali to the great ocean. It strikes the seawater with its wings, causing waves to surge sixteen thousand li, and seizes the water-born dragons to devour them.

When the garuḍa of the egg-born species wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, it descends from the western branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree to the great ocean. It strikes the seawater with its wings, causing waves to surge thirty-two thousand li; it seizes and devours the egg-born nāgas, but it cannot seize and devour the nirmāṇika (transformation-born) nāgas.

When the *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa wishes to seize an egg-born nāga, it descends from the eastern branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree to the great ocean; striking the seawater with its wings, it stirs up waves eight thousand li high and devours the egg-born nāgas.

When the *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa wishes to seize a water-born nāga, it descends from the southern branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree and enters the great ocean. It strikes the seawater with its wings, causing waves to surge sixteen thousand li, and seizes the water-born nāga to devour it.

When the *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa wishes to seize a *garbhaja* nāga, it descends from the western branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree into the great ocean; striking the seawater with its wings, it creates waves thirty-two thousand li high, and seizes the *garbhaja* nāga to devour it.

When the Nirmāṇakāya Garuḍa wishes to seize a Nirmāṇakāya Nāga, he descends from the northern branch of the great Kūṭaśālmali tree into the great ocean; striking the seawater with his wings, he causes waves to surge sixty-four thousand li, and seizes the Nirmāṇakāya Nāga to devour him.
“There are other dragon kings whom the garuḍas cannot catch to eat. Which dragon kings cannot be caught and eaten by the garuḍas? First, the Dragon King Sāgara; second, the Dragon King Anavatapta;

third, the Dragon King Nanda; fourth, the Dragon King Upananda; fifth, the Dragon King Dhṛtarāṣṭra; sixth, the Dragon King Elāpattra; seventh, the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita; eighth, the Dragon King Karkoṭaka; ninth, the Dragon King Aśvatara; tenth, the Dragon King Utpalabhadra; eleventh, the Dragon King Ghaṭotkaca; twelfth, the Dragon King Jambuka. The garuḍas are all unable to seize these dragon kings to eat them.”

All these dragon kings dwell within the mountains. If there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the state of mind of a dragon and fully observes the precepts and conduct of a dragon, he will be reborn among the dragons.
If there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the state of mind of a garuḍa and observes the conduct of a garuḍa while seeking to become one, after death he will be reborn among the garuḍas.
If there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the state of mind of an ulūka bird and fully observes the precepts and conduct, after death he will be reborn among the ulūka birds.
If there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the way of cattle and fulfills the precepts of the bovine mind, after death he will be born among cattle;
if there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the way of dogs and fulfills the precepts of the canine mind, after death he will be born among dogs;
if there is a Brahmin practitioner who seeks the way of deer and fulfills the precepts of the deer mind, after death he will be born among deer.
If there are Brahmin practitioners who practice seeking the way of the chicken, after death they will be reborn among chickens;

if there are Brahmin practitioners who practice seeking the Maṇivatsa devas, those seeking women, those seeking great deities, or those seeking the sun and moon—those who bathe in water three times a day seeking rebirth in the heavens, those who serve the gods, those who serve the sun and moon, or those who seek the celestial realms.
The Buddha said:
"Those who hold such deluded views fall into two evil realms: first, the hells; second, the animal realm.
If there are brahmins or practitioners of the Way who speak of views in this manner:"
"I and the world are eternal," he says;
"my words are the truth, while all others are deluded."
Some say: "The self and the world are impermanent; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded. Others say:
"I and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded. Others say:
"I and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded."
Some say: "I and the world are finite; my words are sincere, while those of others are deluded. Others say:
"I and the world are infinite; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded.
Others say: "I and the world are both finite and infinite; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded."
Some say: "The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; my view alone is true, and all others are deluded. Others say:
"I possess this body and life; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion. Another says:
"When my body dies and becomes something else, my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
Some say: "There is no body or life; my words are the truth, and all others are deluded. Others say:
"Neither is there body and life, nor is there no body and life; my word is the truth, and all others are deluded.
Others say: "Where a person comes from at birth, thither they go after death; my word is the truth, and all others are deluded."
Some say: "There is no place from which one comes to be born, and after death one likewise goes to that [state]. My words are sincere;
all others are deluded. Others say:
"It is born from that which has come from somewhere; it is not born from that which has come from nowhere. After death, it likewise goes there. My [view] is the truth;
all others are deluded. Another says:
"It is neither born from that which has come from somewhere, nor is it born from that which has come from nowhere. My [view] is the truth; all others are deluded."
The Buddha said: "There are certain Brahmin practitioners who say:
'I am eternal in this world; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded.'"
The conduct of such a person is based on perceiving a self, a life-principle, and a body, and perceiving the world as such;
therefore, they say: "The self and the world are eternal. Others say:
"I and the world are impermanent.
Some say: "I and the world are both permanent and impermanent."
Some say: "I and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal. Each says:
"I am the one who speaks with sincerity; all others are deluded.
Such a person, in their conduct, perceives a self, a life-principle, and a body; they perceive the world as such, and therefore say:
"The self and the world are eternal."
There are certain Brahmin practitioners who say:
"I am finite in relation to the world; my words are sincere, while others are deluded.
Such a person perceives a self and a life-principle; for this reason, they speak thus.
"Life is finite and persons are finite.

While in the womb and after death when buried in a grave, they are equal; from the moment of birth, one receives a body, undergoes seven cycles of birth and death, and thereafter attains the Way. For this reason, it is said:
"I and the world are finite."
Some say: "I am infinite with the world; I am the truth, and all others are deluded.
Such a person perceives a self, a life-principle, and a body, and regarding the world, they say:

"There is life and there are people without limit. While they are within the womb, and even after death when buried in the same tomb, from the moment they first receive a body through four stages, if they undergo seven cycles of birth and death, they shall immediately attain the Way."
If a Brahmin practitioner of the Way speaks of his view, saying:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite," then that person's view is that there is a self, there is a life-principle, and there is a body; he perceives the world and says:

"Life is infinite while the person is finite; while dwelling within the human womb, one is equal to others in being buried after death. From the moment of birth, one receives a body composed of four elements; after seven cycles of birth and death, one attains the Way."
Regarding the view held by some people that "both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite," they say: "Life is finite;

while a person is in the womb and after death when buried, these states are equivalent. From the moment one first takes birth and receives a body, one undergoes seven cycles of birth and death before attaining the Way."
Therefore it is said: "Neither finite nor infinite.
If there is a Brahmin or a practitioner of the Way who speaks thus, seeing that this life exists and this body exists, that person says:
"The life-force of this world constantly exists; the life-force of the next world constantly exists.
For this reason, he says:
"I am the one who speaks with utmost sincerity; all others are deluded."
There is a person of the Way who perceives that life is one thing and the person is another; such a person says:
"There is life now, but there is no life in future worlds.
For this reason it is said:
"I am the one who speaks with sincerity; all others are deluded.
If a Brahmin practitioner says:
"I now see that when life ends in death, one proceeds to birth in a future world."
Therefore, he said:
"I am sincere; all others are deluded.
A certain Brahmin practitioner then spoke:
"Neither is there a soul, nor is there a body; when life ends in this world, it is utterly extinguished, and in the next world, too, it is utterly extinguished.
If there is a Brahmin practitioner who holds such a view and says:
"From where one comes into birth, there one also goes to after death—this alone is the truth, and all else is delusion."
That person, seeing that there is body and life in the present world and seeing that there is body and life in future worlds, says:
"I am truthful; all others are deluded."
"If there is a Brahmin practitioner who holds such a view as this:

'There is no place from which one comes to be born; upon death, one likewise goes to that [same state]. One does not perceive a life in the present world, nor does one perceive an absence of life in a future world.'"
"Suppose there is a Brahmin practitioner who asserts: 'There exists that which arises from nowhere and comes from nowhere;

upon death, it likewise proceeds to that [state]. My words are sincere, while others are deluded. Furthermore, he perceives neither the existence of body and life in this present world, nor the existence of body and life in a future world."
"If there is a Brahmin practitioner who asserts:
'That which comes from whence it arises is neither existent nor non-existent; my [view] is the truth, while all others are deluded.'"
"That person is not one who does not see that there is a body and life in this present world, nor is he one who does not see that there is a body and life in future worlds.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Apratihatamukha (Unobstructed Face)."
At that time, he gathered many blind men together and asked them:
"Do you know what an elephant is like?
The blind men replied:
“I do not know, Great King! The king said:
"Do you wish to know what the elephant resembles? He replied,
"I wish to know."
At that time, the king commanded his attendants to bring forth an elephant and ordered the group of blind men to feel it.
Among them, one blind man felt the elephant and grasped its trunk;
another blind man felt the elephant and grasped its tusks.
Among them was a blind man who, feeling the elephant, grasped its ear;
another blind man, feeling the elephant, grasped its head;
and another blind man, feeling the elephant, grasped its back.
Among them was a blind man who, feeling the elephant, grasped its belly;
another blind man felt the elephant and grasped its hind leg;
and another blind man felt the elephant and grasped its knee.
Among them was a blind man who, by feeling the elephant, grasped its foreleg;
another blind man, by feeling the elephant, grasped its tail.
At that time, the king did not show his face but asked the blind men:
"What kind of creature is an elephant?
The one who had grasped the elephant's trunk replied,
"An elephant is like the curved shaft of a cart."
The one who had obtained the elephant's tusk said,
"The elephant is like a pestle.
The one who had obtained the elephant's ear said:
"The elephant is like a winnowing basket.
One who had grasped the elephant's head said,
"The elephant is like a cauldron."
The one who had grasped the elephant's back said,
"An elephant is like a pile [of earth].
The one who had grasped the elephant's belly said:
"The elephant is like a wall.
One who had grasped the elephant's hind legs said:
"The elephant is like a tree."
The one who had grasped the elephant’s knee said,
"The elephant is like a pillar.
The one who had grasped the elephant’s foreleg said:
"The elephant is like a mortar.
One who had grasped the elephant's tail said:
"The elephant is like a snake."
Each of them disputed with the others and did not believe one another; each claimed their own view was correct, saying the elephant was like this, while another said it was not so.
The king laughed with joy.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

There are followers of other paths who do not know from where the Truth of Suffering arises, nor do they know the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, or the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. They do not trust one another's truths, but instead revile each other, claiming themselves alone to be right."
If there are śramaṇas or practitioners who understand from where the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path arise, they shall dwell in harmony together.
Like milk, they shall be blended into one without confusion; they shall speak only the Buddha’s teaching and practice with peace and security.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
You should practice with discernment these truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of its origin, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path."
Chapter Seven: On the Noble Person (*Āryapudgala*). The Great Discourse on the Aggregation of Fire, Chapter Seven, Part One. The Buddha said:
"Ordinary persons have three matters through which they perceive noble matters and understand the thoughts and intentions underlying their conduct."
What are these three matters?
