First, when a person’s mind thinks good thoughts, their speech utters good words, and they practice good deeds with sincerity, even if they were an evil person, others will recognize them as such because of their goodness.
Conversely, if a person’s mind thinks unwholesome thoughts, their speech utters unwholesome words, and they practice unwholesome deeds, noble people will recognize them as being unwholesome.
Why is it called "high"? It is because a person’s mind thinks of what is good, their speech utters what is good, and they sincerely practice what is good with their body.
Such a superior person possesses three qualities in this world by which they obtain merit.
What are these three matters?

First, sitting together with the elderly—whether in a hall, walking through the streets and alleys, or traveling along the roads—to sit with the elderly and together praise the conduct and virtuous deeds of eminent men.
The noble person thinks to himself:
"It would be well if all people were to praise one another!
As soon as there is such a noble person, his mind becomes peaceful; furthermore, hearing these words, his mind is also joyful and his body is likewise at ease.

At times, when high-ranking individuals see thieves and bandits captured by the local authorities, they are subjected to cruel and poisonous punishments: their hands and feet are bound with iron drills and severed; their ears and noses are sliced off; they are whipped with bamboo whips and further hacked limb from limb; they are held out as bait for tigers and wolves; some are ordered to be trampled to death by elephants, some are wrapped in sacks and burned, some are steamed to death, some are slowly starved alive, and some are executed outside the city walls.
When the gentleman saw this, he thought to himself:
"I have done no evil; the King is merely taking away evildoers. Why should I worry?
Until my old age, I shall have no cause for anxiety regarding the government."
Because of this, that noble person’s mind is filled with joy.

This noble person’s thoughts are virtuous, their speech is virtuous, and their bodily actions are virtuous; when they are ill, emaciated, bedridden, and weak, all the virtues they performed during their time of strength and health appear before them for them to see.

A person does not kill living beings, does not take the property of others, does not violate the wives of others, does not deceive others, does not engage in double-tongued speech, does not speak harshly, does not utter falsehoods, is not envious, and does not covet the possessions of others; they believe that performing good deeds brings good results, while performing evil deeds brings evil results.

He immediately saw for himself beings from the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, coming and going to see the Buddha and the Arhats; all the wholesome deeds they had performed during their periods of strength appeared before his eyes.
The sick person thought to himself:

"Is it not because of the good deeds I performed while I was strong and healthy that these many virtues have come to see me on my way? Even if I die, I shall surely ascend to heaven and dwell among the virtuous."
"By means of these three matters, the noble person’s mind is joyful and his body is at ease.
The Buddha said:

"If a noble and virtuous person knows for himself that by performing good he shall obtain good, he will no longer fear birth and death; [the state of] 'not dwelling anywhere' is briefly described thus."

The noble person constantly reflects on their desire to distance themselves from this evil body; within this body there are bones, blood, impurities, and foul-smelling places, and they wish to die soon so as to attain a virtuous body instead.
"Why is this? Because one can recollect the delightful and lovely places; to ascend alone to heaven with joy is itself delightful and lovely, and most worthy of being cherished.
The śramaṇas asked the Buddha:
"May the Buddha please explain to me: what is the nature of the blissful state of the heavens?
The Buddha said, "Listen as I speak of it."
The śramaṇas said, "We shall obey the instruction.
The Buddha said:
"It is, for example, like a Cakravartin King who possesses seven treasures and four attributes that others do not have;
furthermore, he has five kinds of thoughts, such that whatever he desires to obtain appears before him."
The king possesses seven treasures. What are these seven treasures?

First is a golden wheel that appears spontaneously; second is a white elephant; third is a dark-blue horse; fourth is a maṇi jewel; fifth is a noble jade woman; sixth is a noble minister of counsel; and seventh is a noble minister of military affairs.
The Buddha said:
"Do you wish to know what is governed by a single golden wheel?
On the fifteenth day of the month or the final day of the dark fortnight, the king bathes; having bathed, he sits in the main hall together with his women."

From afar he saw a golden wheel flying toward him; the wheel had a thousand spokes, and both the spokes and the hub were perfectly formed and peerless, always hovering three or four *zhang* above the ground.
Upon seeing the golden wheel, the king thought to himself:
"The eminent gentlemen have said:"
"For the sake of the Cakravartin King, a golden wheel flies forth; it always comes from the east.
It has a thousand spokes, and its spokes and hub are perfectly formed. Whoever possesses such a precious golden wheel shall be a Cakravartin King."
"Now, shall I not indeed become a Cakravartin King?
The king thought this to himself and desired to test this golden wheel.
The king rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt upright, and addressed the golden wheel, saying:
"Now that you have come for my sake, you shall tour the various kingdoms according to the ancient laws.
As soon as the King had finished speaking, the golden wheel flew eastward;
the King’s ministers and officials who were by his side all followed it in flight.
Wherever the golden wheel comes to rest, the king’s various officials and attendants likewise follow it to that place.
When the golden wheel arrives at a kingdom or district, the kings of those lands all come forth, kneeling long and bowing their heads, saying:
"This entire realm is the possession of Your Majesty."
Furthermore, he took a silver bowl filled with golden grain and another golden bowl filled with silver grain, presenting them as offerings.
The kings of the various provinces and kingdoms all said:

"This kingdom is abundant and prosperous; grain is plentiful and inexpensive, the rains and winds come in their proper seasons, and the people are flourishing and joyful. Great King, you should accept this kingdom and remain here."

The King then replied to the various kings, saying: "You all shall govern your own kingdoms, but do so solely by means of the True Dharma (saddharma). Do not let established precedents fall into neglect. Be careful never to kill living beings; do not take the property of others without justification; do not violate the wives of others; do not deceive people; do not engage in double-tongued speech; do not speak with harsh words; do not utter falsehoods; do not harbor jealousy; do not covet what belongs to others; and do not give way to anger or malicious intent. You must all practice these ten matters."
"Should anyone among you commit even one of these ten transgressions, do not allow them to remain within the realm.
Having thus instructed the kings of the various provinces and kingdoms in the eastern direction, the Great King followed the golden wheel as it flew to the southern direction.

Wherever the Golden Wheel halts, the Great King stations himself there with a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry. Then the kings of the various provinces and kingdoms to the south all come to prostrate themselves and kneel for a long time, saying:

"We wish to offer the territories of our respective provinces and kingdoms, as well as golden and silver bowls filled to the brim with gold and silver grain; we present these offerings according to the same rites as the kings of the various kingdoms in the east."
The golden wheel flew again toward the western direction, and the attendant ministers and officials all followed wherever the golden wheel came to rest.
The kings of the various states in the west all came forward, prostrating themselves and kneeling for a long time, saying:
"We wish to offer our kingdoms, as well as golden and silver bowls filled with gold and silver grain as tribute, just as was the custom of the kings of the south."
The golden wheel then flew again toward the north; wherever the golden wheel came to rest, the Great King and his various officials and attendants likewise followed where the golden wheel rested.
The kings of all the provinces and kingdoms all came to prostrate themselves and kneel for a long time, saying:

"We offer our realms to Your Majesty. Our people are flourishing and joyful, grain is abundant and cheap, and wind and rain come at their proper seasons. It would be fitting for Your Majesty to govern here."
Furthermore, he filled golden and silver bowls with golden and silver grain and presented them to the Great King.
The Great King would not accept them and addressed the various kings, saying:

"All of you must govern your kingdoms with upright hearts and do not let traditional precedents fall into neglect. Do not kill living beings; do not take the property of others; do not violate the wives of others; do not deceive others; do not engage in double-tongued speech; do not use harsh words; do not speak falsehoods; do not harbor jealousy; do not covet what belongs to others; do not give way to anger; and do not harbor evil intentions. All of you must practice these ten matters."
"Should there be anyone who commits even one of these ten offenses, do not allow them to remain within the kingdom.

The Great King then sent messengers throughout the four seas and the four quarters; subsequently, following the golden wheel, he returned to his capital and ascended the palace hall. The golden wheel remained constantly visible before the King; such was the nature of this King’s precious golden wheel treasure.
"The King further possesses the elephant-treasure.
What is the nature of this elephant-treasure?
That elephant is pure white beyond compare; its body is majestic, and its tusks, hooves, and feet are all perfectly formed and beautiful, with a golden saddle and bridle."
The chest and armpits were all inlaid with gold, while the abdomen, forehead, and body were entirely adorned with white pearls.
When he walked, he flew through the air, moving with sovereign ease wherever he desired to go.
A minister standing by the king’s side addressed the king, saying:
"Congratulations, Great King!

The white elephant-treasure of the kingdom is of such peerless and exquisite whiteness that it is beyond compare; its body, tusks, teeth, hooves, and feet are all white and well-proportioned, and it is equipped with a saddle and bridle made entirely of gold."
"The chest and flanks are all inlaid with gold; the belly and forehead are all adorned with white pearls.
When it walks, it flies through the air, reaching wherever it wishes to go.
Upon seeing the elephant, the king sighed deeply and said:
"The elephant possesses auspicious marks and is beautiful; it should be trained to master its gaits and movements.
Thereupon, the King entrusted him to his skilled attendants, ordering them to instruct it.
Within a few days, they had all learned how to walk.
The King wished to ride and test the elephant; when the sun had risen as high as a single pole, the King mounted it to try it out.
The elephant then circled through the four quarters and the four seas before returning to the palace to eat.
“The Cakravartin King possesses the horse-treasure (*aśvaratna*).
What is the nature of this horse-treasure?

The horse is deep blue in color, with a glossy, well-groomed mane. Its head is like that of an elephant, and it is equipped with golden saddle and bridle. The engraved armlets and girths are all made of pure gold; its chest and forehead are adorned entirely with white pearls.”
It could fly through the air, reaching wherever it desired with ease.
An attendant minister said to the king,
"Congratulations to Your Majesty that such a horse-treasure exists within your kingdom."

His hair was dark blue and glossy, hanging down beautifully; he held his head like an elephant. His saddle, bridle, breastplate, and girth were all of gold, and the front of his chest and forehead were adorned with white pearls.
The King, seeing this, was greatly delighted and immediately ordered his attendants to continue training it.
Within a few days, the horse had mastered the art of walking.

The King wished to test the horse; when the sun had risen only one *daṇḍa*, he mounted the horse, which then flew through the air, circling the four quarters and the four seas before returning to the palace for its meal.
Such is the horse-treasure of the Cakravartin King.
The king possesses the bright moon jewel.
What kind of thing is this bright moon jewel?

The color of the jewel was intensely blue; its eight facets were as sharp as needles. Within the palace, it illuminated everything; where its flames shone, for forty li in every direction, it was as bright as the sun.

The king, desiring to test the brilliance of the pearl, waited until after midnight when the darkness was as pitch-black as lacquer. He fastened the pearl to the tip of a golden staff and went out of the city at night, taking his wife and children along with a thousand chariots and ten thousand horsemen, proceeding to various pavilions and detached palaces within the royal precincts.
The brilliance of the jewel was like the rising sun, illuminating the chariots and cavalry; its light extended far beyond thousands and tens of thousands of riders for forty li all around.
The residents living near the city, seeing the brilliance of the jewel, all said to one another: "Arise! Arise!"
"The sun has risen so high!
Each of you should go to the marketplace to trade; why, on the contrary, do you wish to lie down?
Such was the mani-jewel of the Cakravartin King.
“The King possesses a noble jade maiden.
What kind of being is this jade maiden?

She is neither tall nor short, neither large nor small, neither fat nor thin, neither white nor black; she is perfectly proportioned, of incomparable and supreme beauty. Her breath is like the scent of incense, and every pore of her body emits fragrance like that of saffron.”

In serving the king, he went to bed late and rose early, attending to him without ever failing to please his mind; in winter his body provided warmth, and in summer it was cool, always ensuring that the king remained free from anger—how much more so regarding his own person!
Such was the jade-woman treasure possessed by the Cakravartin King.

The king also had a noble minister who possessed lofty and far-reaching insight; he could discern the nature and disposition of people at a glance. With his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he surveyed the world and foreknew the existence of precious treasures and hidden stores throughout the realm, knowing whether they had an owner or were without an owner.
Those with owners' names were shown to their respective guardians for protection;
those without owners' names were provided for official use.
A minister of the Sage King then addressed the King:
"Enjoy yourself in happiness; there is no need for worry. I myself shall provide the king with wealth and treasures.
The king’s mind was filled with doubt as to whether what the holy minister had requested could indeed be obtained.
The king then boarded a single boat together with his noble ministers; having reached the center of the sea, the king spoke to the noble ministers, saying:
"I desire precious treasures; give them to me here and now."
The noble minister said,
"It can be obtained once I have gone out onto dry land.
The king said:
"I have no need for it on land; I wish to obtain it here.
Thereupon, the noble minister reached down with his hand into the water and retrieved golden treasures as large as chariot wheels, placing them upon the ship until they were beyond counting.
The king said: "Stop! Stop!"
"The ship is full and heavy.
Such were the words of the noble minister of the Cakravartin King.
"What kind of person is the noble minister who wields the military forces and guides the way for the King?"
He was of high talent and courageous strength, knowing all things.
When he wished to raise an army, it would become incalculable; when he did not wish for an army, it would cease.
Bearing arms and leading the way, the minister addressed the king, saying:
"Now, Your Majesty, please enjoy yourself and do not worry about state affairs; if Your Majesty wishes to employ troops, I shall fight them myself.

The King, wishing to test his wise minister, had all the people of the kingdom—men, horses, and elephants—donned armor so that he might have a sufficient force. The infantry were also armored and equipped with swords and weapons. The King thought to himself:
"Would it be pleasant for these troops to go forth on an excursion?"
As soon as the king thought this in his mind, the troops moved forward; when the king thought,
"I wish to make the troops stop," the troops immediately stopped again.
The king thought to himself,
"Let the troops withdraw.
The troops immediately withdrew.
Such is the minister who guides the way and leads the army for a Cakravartin King.
A Cakravartin King possesses the seven treasures in this manner.
"The King has four matters that distinguish him from ordinary people."
What are the four? First, his lifespan is immeasurable; among humans, there is no one whose longevity equals that of a Cakravartin king.

Second, he is always at peace and secure, never suffering from illness; his food and drink are always digested, and his body’s temperature is perfectly suited to the season; among humans, none enjoy such security as a Cakravartin king.
Third, his physical appearance was incomparably handsome, surpassing that of ordinary worldly people, though not yet equal to that of celestial beings;
fourth, all the people loved the king and regarded him as their own parents, while the king loved the people as parents love their children.

Just as he had gone out to the various departments and separate pavilions, the common people said to the king’s charioteer, "Drive the carriage slowly; we wish to gaze upon the king without weariness."
"I pray for the King, that his life may be infinite!
The King spoke again to the charioteer:
"Drive slowly; I wish to see the people of my kingdom, so that their lives may be infinite!"
"The Cakravartin King possesses these four matters which ordinary people do not have.
The king has five aspirations; whatever he thinks of always appears before him.
Whatever his heart delights in, whatever his tongue delights in, whatever his eyes delight in—all that he desires and loves appears before him."
The sounds heard by the ears were songs, music, and auspicious voices;
the fragrances smelled by the nose were those most pleasing to the stomach, all of which were before him;
the flavors relished by the mouth—salty, sour, sweet, and all other delicacies—were likewise all before him.
It is called "Pure and Subtle," for all that he delights in appears before him.
These are the five things contemplated by the Cakravartin King:

his eyes have never seen anything evil, his ears have never heard anything evil, his nose has never smelled anything foul, his mouth has never tasted anything unpalatable, and his body has never worn coarse or inferior clothing.
The Buddha addressed the śramaṇas:
"Such is the Cakravartin King, who possesses seven extraordinary treasures, four distinctive marks, and five kinds of thoughts; do you take pleasure in such a king?"
The śramaṇas replied:
“The king possesses but a single treasure, yet he delights in it;
how much more so would he do if he possessed the seven treasures?”
The Buddha took a small stone and placed it in his hand, then asked the śramaṇas:
"Is the stone in my hand large,
or is the mountain large?"
The śramaṇas said: "The stone in the Buddha's hand is so small; how can it be compared to a mountain?
Even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or a hundred-millionfold [the size of the stone] would still not equal the greatness of the mountain!"
The Buddha said:

"It is like the small stone in my hand; it is not as large as the mountain even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, a billionfold, or ten-billionfold—it is still not as large as the mountain."

Although a Cakravartin King possesses the seven treasures, the four extraordinary marks, and five kinds of wishes, his happiness does not equal that of the heavens by even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or a hundred-thousand-millionfold.
"It is like a small pebble in the Buddha’s hand compared to a great mountain.

The Buddha said, "A person of noble virtue who in this world thinks good thoughts, speaks good words, and acts with sincerity through their body, at the end of their life in this world, after death, will all ascend to the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they will be born as devas."

One hundred years in the human world constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa devas; three thousand years in the human world constitutes one month for the Trāyastriṃśa devas; and thirty-six thousand years in the human world constitutes one year for the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
According to the celestial reckoning, the lifespan of the people in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, is one thousand years.

The outer gate of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is seven hundred li wide; it has seven layers of outer city walls and seven layers of moats. Within these waters are lotus flowers of four colors, and the bottom of the water is entirely covered with golden sand.
On each city wall there are railings made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
the city gates likewise have railings of gold, silver, and crystal. Each of the seven tiers of ground has seven rows of trees:
gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, coral trees, amber trees, and musaragalva trees; the gold trees are [made of] gold.
The gold trees had silver roots, silver stems, silver leaves, silver flowers, and silver fruits; the silver trees had silver roots, silver stems, gold leaves, gold flowers, and gold fruits;
the lapis lazuli trees had lapis lazuli roots, lapis lazuli stems, crystal leaves, crystal flowers, and crystal fruits;
and the crystal trees had crystal roots, crystal stems, lapis lazuli leaves, and lapis lazuli flowers.
The lapis lazuli tree has lapis lazuli roots, coral stems, amber leaves, amber flowers, and amber fruits;
the amber tree has amber roots, amber stems, musaragalva leaves, musaragalva flowers, and musaragalva fruits;
the musaragalva tree has musaragalva roots, musaragalva stems, agate leaves, and agate flowers.
Its fruit is agate.
The city gate is two hundred and eighty *li* deep and six hundred and forty *li* high; its lintels and transoms are all silver, and its two door panels and pivots are made of gold.
There were five hundred spirits guarding the gate outside the palace.
The palace where the devas reside is two thousand li in length and breadth.

Its walls are all the colors of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva. Seven layers of moats surround the walls, and seven rows of precious trees stand like those at the outer gates. They are six hundred and forty li high and two hundred and eighty li deep. The lintels are made of silver and the capitals of gold; the two leaves of the golden gates have thresholds of gold, and five hundred spirits together guard the gate.

The abode of the devas is two thousand li in length and breadth. It is surrounded by sevenfold walls made of the seven kinds of jewels and sevenfold moats of water. The various railings and jewel trees are like those at the outer gates; their height, width, and depth are equal to those of the outer gates, and the number of gate-keeping spirits is the same as that at the outer gates.

To the east of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a place for recreation called Nandanavana, seven hundred million *li* in circumference. It is surrounded by sevenfold walls made of gold, silver, coral, lapis lazuli, amber, musaragalva, and crystal. There are seven channels of water, the beds of which are entirely of gold, and they contain lotus flowers of four colors.

Upon the city walls were railings made of the seven treasures, with sevenfold walls, each adorned with trees of the seven treasures. The golden trees had golden roots and stems with silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees had silver roots and stems with golden leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees had crystal roots and stems with lapis lazuli leaves, flowers, and fruits; and the lapis lazuli trees had lapis lazuli roots and stems with crystal leaves, flowers, and fruits. The great road was six hundred and forty li wide, flanked on both sides by sevenfold walls made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, coral, and musaragalva.

Along each wall there are irrigation channels; within these waters grow lotus flowers of four colors, and the bottom of the water is entirely covered with golden sand. Upon the walls are railings made of the seven treasures, identical to those on the inner side.
There were trees made of the seven treasures: gold trees, silver trees, crystal trees, lapis lazuli trees, amber trees, coral trees, and musaragalva trees.

Within that dwelling were two rocks; one rock was named Nan (Difficult) and the other was named Nanyuan (Far from Difficult). Each was four thousand li in length and breadth; the rocks were soft yet firm, as fine and delicate as silk cords.
Within the hut there were two bathing pools: one was named Nanda and the second was named Nandānī; each was four thousand li in length and breadth.
Within the pools grew lotus flowers of four colors: first, blue; second, red; third, purple; and fourth, white; the sand at the bottom of the water was all gold.
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to sport, they go together to the Eastern Villa (Pūrvavideha) to enjoy themselves to their heart's content; therefore, it is named the Nandanavana Villa.

“Exiting through the southern city gate of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, named Cīrāla, it is seven hundred million *li* in circumference. Its walls are sevenfold: walls of gold, walls of silver, walls of crystal, walls of beryl, walls of amber, walls of coral, and walls of musāragalva.”

On each wall there is a channel of water, within which are lotus flowers of four colors; the sand at the bottom of the water is all gold. There are trees made of the seven treasures—gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, amber trees, coral trees, and musaragalva trees. On those walls are railings made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
The road from Cīrāla to Elāpattra is six hundred and forty li wide; it is entirely enclosed by sevenfold walls made of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.

In one section of the wall, there was a channel of water. Within the water were lotus flowers of four colors—blue, red, purple, and white—and the bottom of the water was entirely of golden sand. There were railings made of the seven treasures: railings of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva. There were also trees made of the seven treasures: trees of gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
Within that hermitage were two rocks, each four thousand li in length and breadth; they were fine and soft like silk cords—the first was named Citra, and the second was named Citrāṅgada.
Within that hermitage were two bathing pools: one was named Citra and the second was named Citta.
Within these two pools grew lotuses of four colors—blue, red, purple, and white—and the bottom of the water in both was entirely composed of golden sand.
Within that palace there are four kinds of precious trees: gold and silver trees, and crystal and lapis lazuli trees.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven come out to the palace of Cūḍikāvatī, where they play and enjoy themselves together; their pleasures are boundless. These four precious substances illuminate the various devas and humans, making their colors brilliantly variegated; for this reason, it is named Cūḍikāvatī.
"Citraratha" refers to the variegated pavilions.

To the north of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a city gate with pavilions called Pāruṣya, measuring seven hundred million *li* in length and breadth. They have sevenfold walls of precious jewels and sevenfold moats; the bottoms of the moats are all of golden sand, and the railings are like those in the south. The width of the path leading to these pavilions is six hundred and forty *li*.
Within the hut are two rocks, each four thousand li in length and breadth; one is named Kāla and the other is named Kālaśīla, both as fine and soft as silk cords.
There are two bathing ponds, each four thousand li in length and breadth. One pond is named Gandhodaka; it contains lotus flowers of four colors: blue, red, purple, and white.

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to play in the Pāruṣyaka grove, their bodies become rigid. Just as a person’s body becomes smooth after bathing, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Pāruṣyaka grove from the north, their bodies all become smooth; for this reason, it is called Pāruṣyaka.

To the west of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a palace named Miśraka-udyāna, seven hundred million *li* in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, seven channels of water, seven rows of jewel trees, and sevenfold railings. There are lotus flowers of four colors, and the bottom of the water consists entirely of golden sand, just as in the north.

Its road is six hundred and forty li wide, with sevenfold walls of precious jewels, seven channels of water, seven rows of jewel trees, and sevenfold railings; there are lotus flowers of four colors, and the riverbed is entirely of golden sand, just as in the north.
Within the hut there were two fine stones, each four thousand li in length and breadth; they were as fine and soft as silk cords. One was named Beiluo, and the other was named Beiluo Yue.

There are two bathing pools, each four thousand li in length and breadth. Within these pools are lotus flowers of four colors—blue, red, purple, and white—and the bottoms of the pools consist entirely of golden sand. One pool is named Pāṃśu, and the second is named Megha.

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to go to the Miśrakāvana grove for recreation, there is no distinction of high or low, rich or poor, noble or weak among them; all are permitted to enter the Miśrakāvana grove. For this reason, it is named the Miśrakāvana grove.

"In the central courtyard before the palace hall in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are objects made of a hundred kinds of precious substances that spread themselves out upon the ground before the King. Within the palace are seven hundred towers with staircases of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; at the foot of each staircase, there are sixteen pillars of lapis lazuli that illuminate it."

Within the palace there were four thrones: a golden throne, a silver throne, a crystal throne, and a lapis lazuli throne. The celestial beings sat upon them, contemplating the virtues of the myriad people and also contemplating the virtues of the various devas.
The palace where the Heavenly King dwells is named Trayastriṃśa.
Upon that palace are one hundred streets; each street has one hundred chambers, and each chamber has seven jade maidens, and each jade maiden has seven attendants.
The palace is the color of dark lapis lazuli, and all the devas surround it.

To the south there is a tree called the Pārijātaka; its roots penetrate two hundred li into the earth, its branches spread in four directions, and the tree is four thousand li high, measuring two thousand li from east to west and two thousand li from north to south.
When the tree is in full bloom, the wind blows from above; the fragrance of the flowers descends for four thousand *li*, and against the wind it travels for two thousand *li*.

When the tree is in full bloom, the various devas sit together beneath the tree and enjoy themselves for one hundred and twenty days; one hundred and twenty days in the heavens is equivalent to twelve thousand years in the world of men.

The devas wished to play with a white jewel elephant named Airāvaṇa; the elephant spontaneously transformed itself into thirty-two heads, each head having seven tusks, and from each tusk were manifested seven bathing pools.
In each bathing pool, seven lotus flowers were fashioned; each lotus stalk had a thousand petals, and upon each petal was a jade maiden performing a dance.
Whatever the King desired appeared before him, satisfying his every whim.

"In this world, although people perform wholesome deeds, they are unable to do so extensively because their mental intentions for wholesome deeds are few, their verbal expressions of goodness are few, and their physical actions of goodness are few. Consequently, even if they are born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they cannot enter the Eastern Sudarśana Hall, nor can they enter the Caitraratha Hall, nor can they enter the Northern Pāruṣyaka Hall; they cannot enter beneath the fragrant and flower-adorned Pārijātaka tree, but may only gaze at it from afar, unable to advance further inside."

It is like the food and drink of a Cakravartin King, which none of the outer palace attendants may enter without permission, and which even the various devas in the heavens may not behold; such is this [state].

If a person performs good deeds in this world—thinking good thoughts with the mind, speaking good words with the mouth, and practicing good conduct with the body with utmost sincerity—then after the end of their life, they shall ascend to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

This noble person ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; at the end of his full lifespan, after death, he was reborn again in the world as the crown prince of a royal house, possessing great wealth and abundant treasures, and being handsome in appearance.

It is like a person who, upon suddenly obtaining large quantities of gold coins, gold, silver, jewels, slaves, horses, carriages, wife, children, fields, and houses, takes note of these possessions and thinks to himself:
"I have not engaged in trade or commerce, nor have I plowed the fields; yet I have come by this wealth of my own accord—it was merely a matter of play!"
"Up to the point that one obtains gold, silver, rare treasures, houses, dwellings, and fields; up to the point that one possesses a name for being wealthy and noble!
The Buddha said:
"If a child at play gains such profit, it is but meager; indeed, it is but meager."
It is better to have good thoughts in the mind, good speech with the mouth, and good conduct with the body; the benefit gained is superior to that of the one who covers his head.
Why is this so? Because by practicing these three things, after death one ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; such a person is a noble being.
The Buddha said to the śramaṇas:
"I shall now explain two paths for you: the path of the deluded and the path of the noble and virtuous.
Which of these paths will you now freely follow?"
"Now that I have become a Buddha, I shall explain for you the difficult and the easy paths. The Buddha said:

"You should, whether in the mountains, beneath a tree, in an empty room, amidst burial mounds, by the water, or in desolate places, contemplate the five internal organs and strive early to seek the path to Nirvana."
The Buddha said,
"This is my teaching. All the śramaṇas joined their palms, received the instruction with words of assent, and each stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha.
Chapter Eight: The Four Heavenly Kings. From the *Mahāsāṃghika Mahāvadāna Sūtra*, Chapter Eight, "The Four Heavenly Kings. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"To the east of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, forty thousand *li* away from Sumeru, there is a city and citadel of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, named the Abode of the Noble King."

It is twenty-four thousand li in length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls made of the seven treasures, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all exquisitely beautiful.

There were golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, and musaragalva walls with gates made of every kind of jewel.

The golden railings have golden pillars and beams with silver crossbars; the silver railings have silver pillars and beams with golden crossbars; the lapis lazuli railings have lapis lazuli pillars and beams with crystal crossbars; the crystal railings have crystal pillars and beams with lapis lazuli crossbars; the red pearl railings have red pearl pillars and beams with agate crossbars; the agate railings have agate pillars and beams with red pearl crossbars; and the musaragalva railings have musaragalva pillars and beams with crossbars made of every kind of jewel.

There were golden lattices with silver hanging tassels, silver lattices with golden hanging tassels, lapis lazuli lattices with crystal hanging tassels, crystal lattices with lapis lazuli hanging tassels, red pearl lattices with agate hanging tassels, agate lattices with red pearl hanging tassels, and musaragalva lattices with hanging tassels made of every kind of jewel.

The golden trees have golden trunks and roots with silver branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees have silver trunks and roots with golden branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli trunks and roots with crystal branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees have crystal trunks and roots with lapis lazuli branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the red pearl trees have red pearl trunks and roots with agate branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the agate trees have agate trunks and roots with red pearl branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and the musaragalva trees have musaragalva trunks and roots with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits made of every kind of jewel.
Above the gates were curved canopies and latticed pavilions; below were gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools.
There were various kinds of trees with various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits.
Various kinds of fragrances waft forth, and various birds sing together in harmony.
Forty thousand *li* to the south of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies the city of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, named Sudarśana (Good-to-See).

It is twenty-four thousand li in length and breadth; the royal residence there likewise features sevenfold walls of the seven treasures, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all surrounding it in a beautiful and magnificent array.
Above the gate is a curved canopy with a lattice screen; below it are gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, and trees, where flying birds sing in harmony.
Forty thousand *li* to the west of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, there is a heaven named Vaiśravaṇa.

There is a city with walls and towers, twenty-four thousand li in breadth and length; the king’s residence likewise possesses sevenfold walls of the seven treasures, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, which surround it on all sides in magnificent beauty.
Above the gates are curved box-like canopies with latticed windows; below are gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, and trees, where flying birds sing in harmony with one another.
"Forty thousand *li* to the north of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is a celestial king named Vaiśravaṇa."

There are three cities and citadels, each twenty-four thousand li in width and length. The king resides in one of them: the first is named Śama, the second is named Pākarada, and the third is named Anīpana. They are also constructed of the seven treasures, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees surrounding them on all sides, beautiful and magnificent.
Above the gate is a curved canopy with a lattice screen; below it are gardens, pavilions, bathing ponds, and trees, where flying birds sing in harmony with one another.
To the east dwells King Aniruddha, and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa has a mountain named Kapiñjala.

It is four thousand li in height, breadth, and length, constructed from the four treasures of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. Surrounding the mountain is a wall, twenty thousand li in breadth and length, made of the seven treasures. It consists of sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, encircling it all around in exquisite beauty.
It has gates on all four sides, constructed from the four precious substances.
Above are curved roof-boxes and latticed canopies; below are gardens, pavilions, bathing pools, and trees, where birds sing together in harmony.
On Mount Kāpiśī, at the abode of King Aniruddha, there is a bathing pool belonging to the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa named Nārī.

It is two thousand li in length and breadth, surrounded by walls. The bottom of the pool consists entirely of golden sand, and the water is cool and clear. Around the bathing pool, there are double-walled enclosures, railings, lattices, and trees made of the four jewels, all exquisitely beautiful. Within it grow blue lotuses, yellow lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses; their light illuminates twenty-four li, and their fragrance is likewise perceived for twenty-four li. Surrounding the bathing pool are steps.
"When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa wished to go to Mount Kāpiñjala to sport and enjoy himself, he immediately thought of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra then said:
'The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa has thought of me.'"

Immediately, he adorned himself with robes and a ceremonial cap, prepared his carriage, and, surrounded on all sides by countless gandharvas and hundreds of thousands of attendants, departed from the city of Bhadraśreṣṭha and went to the abode of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, where he stood before him.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa thought of King Virūḍhaka.
King Virūḍhaka immediately thought to himself:
"King Vaiśravaṇa has already thought of me."

He then put on his robes, cap, and headdress, prepared his carriage, and accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of soldiers and nine classes of spirits, departed from the city of Subhavyūha and went to the abode of King Vaiśravaṇa, where he stood before him.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa thought of King Virūḍhaka.
King Virūḍhaka immediately thought to himself:
"King Vaiśravaṇa has already thought of me."

He then put on his robes and donned his crown and turban; having prepared his carriage, he set out from the city of Mālikā with countless hundreds of thousands of nāgas, surrounding him on all sides, and proceeded to the abode of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, where he stood before him.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, having donned his robes and put on his crown and turban, prepared his carriage and, together with countless hundreds of thousands of celestial kings and spirits, went to Mount Kāpiśī.

At that time, the wind blew and swept the ground of Mount Kāpiṇa; the wind blew the flowers from the trees of the mountain down onto the earth. Then the Four Great Kings entered Mount Kāpiṇa together to enjoy themselves, partaking in food and drink with great pleasure for one day, two days, up to seven days, after which they each departed.
The Mahāsāṃghika Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà lóu tán jīng), Scroll Three;
The Mahāsāṃghika Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇas Fǎlì and Fǎjù of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“At the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which is three million two hundred thousand li in both width and length.”

Above is the city of Śakra-devānām-indra, named Sudarśana, measuring two million four hundred thousand li in both width and length. It is surrounded by sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all of which are exquisitely beautiful. They are all fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.

Where the walls are of gold, the gates are of silver; where the walls are of silver, the gates are of gold; where the walls are of lapis lazuli, the gates are of crystal; where the walls are of crystal, the gates are of lapis lazuli; where the walls are of red pearls, the gates are of agate; and where the walls are of agate, the gates are of red pearls.

The *musāragalva* walls consist of gates made of every kind of jewel. The golden railings have pillars and beams of gold with crossbars of silver; the silver railings have pillars and beams of silver with crossbars of gold; the lapis lazuli railings have pillars and beams of lapis lazuli with crossbars of crystal; the crystal railings have pillars and beams of crystal with crossbars of lapis lazuli; the red pearl railings have pillars and beams of red pearl with crossbars of agate; the agate railings have pillars and beams of agate with crossbars of red pearl; and the *musāragalva* railings have pillars and beams of *musāragalva* with crossbars of every kind of jewel.

Where the golden lattices were, silver tassels hung; where the silver lattices were, golden tassels hung; where the lapis lazuli lattices were, crystal tassels hung; where the crystal lattices were, lapis lazuli tassels hung; where the red pearls lattices were, agate tassels hung; where the agate lattices were, red pearl tassels hung; and where the musaragalva lattices were, tassels made of every kind of jewel hung.

The golden trees have golden roots, stems, and trunks, with silver branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees have silver roots, stems, and trunks, with golden branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots, stems, and trunks, with crystal branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees have crystal roots, stems, and trunks, with lapis lazuli branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the red pearl trees have red pearl roots and stems, with agate branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; the agate trees have agate roots and stems, with red pearl branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and the musaragalva trees have musaragalva roots and stems, with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits made of every kind of jewel.
Its walls are two thousand four hundred li high and one thousand two hundred li wide.
Its gates are two thousand four hundred li high and one thousand two hundred li wide.
The walls are separated by twenty thousand *li* and have a single gate each; at every gate there are always five hundred spirits who guard the gates of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Above the gates are curved awnings and pavilions with latticed windows, while below are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. There are various kinds of trees with diverse leaves, flowers, and fruits that emit all manner of fragrances; various flying birds sing together in harmony.

"In the city of Sutanu, there is the palace of the Naga King Elāpattra, twenty-four thousand *li* in both length and breadth. It is entirely composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and features railings of the seven treasures, sevenfold lattices, and seven rows of trees."

Within the city of Sudarśana, there is the Hall of Deliberation belonging to Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; it is twenty thousand li in both length and breadth, and four thousand li in height. It is constructed of the seven treasures, featuring sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, which encircle it for a total circumference of twenty thousand li.

Above the palace halls were curved box-canopies and latticed pavilions; their covers were made of crystal and lapis lazuli, and their floors were of gold. The central pillars within the halls measured four hundred and eighty *li* in circumference, and the gates were four thousand *li* high, constructed from the seven treasures.
In its center is the seat of Śakra, Lord of Devas, forty *li* in both width and length, fashioned entirely from the seven treasures; the seat is exceedingly soft, with sixteen seats on each side.

To the north of the palace hall is the inner harem of Śakra, Lord of Devas, measuring forty thousand li in breadth and length. It is entirely constructed of the seven treasures, with sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees surrounding it on all sides, which are exceedingly beautiful and wondrous.
"To the east of the palace there is a pleasure garden of Śakra named Karkaśa.
It is forty thousand *li* in extent both ways, and is likewise constructed with sevenfold walls, railings, lattices, and trees made of the seven treasures, surrounding it all around in great beauty."

The gates were twelve hundred li high and eight hundred li wide in length; atop the gates were curved canopies and multi-storied pavilions with open lattices, while below them were gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. Within these were various kinds of trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and various flying birds sang together in harmony.
In the Coarse and Hard Garden (Cūḍakavāṭa), there are fragrant trees seventy *li* in height, all of which produce flowers and fruit; when split open, they emit various kinds of incense.
There are trees twenty, thirty, up to sixty *li* in height, while the shortest are thirteen *li* and one hundred and twenty paces tall.

Next there are garland trees; some are seventy li in height, others twenty, thirty, or up to sixty li, while the shortest are thirteen li and one hundred and twenty paces tall. All produce flowers and fruits, and when split open, they yield various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.

Next there are clothing trees, followed by incense trees, vessel trees, and musical instrument trees. They range in height from seventy *li* down to twenty, thirty, or sixty *li*; even the shortest are thirteen *li* and one hundred and twenty paces tall. All of them produce flowers and fruits; when split open, they yield various kinds of clothing, necklaces, incense, vessels, and musical instruments.
Within the Grove of Coarse Hardness there are two rocks: one named Worthy and the other named Virtuous; they are made of celestial gold, and the stones are exceedingly beautiful.

"To the south of the palace is the celestial garden and pavilion of Śakra-devānām-indra, named Rati-citra. It is forty thousand li in both width and length, and is entirely constructed of the seven treasures with sevenfold walls, railings, decorative nets, and trees."

The gate is twelve hundred li high; atop the gate are curved canopies, lattice pavilions, and watchtowers, while below are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. There are various trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and within the bathing pools are flying birds that sing in harmony with one another.

In the pleasure gardens and pavilions there are two rocks: one is named Zhòu (Day) and the other is named Shànzhòu (Good Day). Each is two thousand li in breadth and length, and the rocks are exceedingly soft.

In the pleasure gardens and pavilions there are fragrant trees, followed by garland trees, inexhaustible trees, and musical trees. Some of these trees are seventy li in height; others are twenty, thirty, or up to sixty li; the shortest are thirteen li and one hundred and twenty paces. All of them produce flowers and fruits, which, when split open, yield various kinds of incense, clothing, garments, garlands, inexhaustible objects, vessels, and music.
"To the east of the Trāyastriṃśa Palace, there is a pleasure garden of Śakra Devānām Indra called Kūṭāgāra.
It is forty thousand li in both breadth and length, and is entirely surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, railings, lattices, and trees, all fashioned from the seven precious gems."
The gates are twelve hundred li high and eight hundred li wide; above them are curved awnings and multi-storied pavilions with latticed windows, while below are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools.

There are various kinds of trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits that emit all manner of fragrances, and various birds sing together in harmony. All that is produced by these trees is also just like that in the southern continent.
In the Garden of Confusion there is a square stone.
To the west of the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is a garden pavilion named Song and Dance.
It is forty thousand li in both length and breadth, and is likewise surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls, railings, lattices, and trees, all fashioned from the seven treasures.
The gates are twelve hundred li high and eight hundred li wide.

Above them are curved awnings, latticed pavilions, and watchtowers; below them are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. There are various kinds of trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits, and various kinds of birds singing together in harmony.

Within the Garden of Song and Dance there are two rocks: one named Nanda and the other named Upananda. Each is two thousand li in length and breadth; both are made of celestial lapis lazuli and are exceedingly soft.

In the midst of this bustling delight, within the painted gardens and pavilions, there is a bathing pool named Nanda, two thousand li in both length and breadth, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of walls; the water of the pool is soft, delicious, and clear.

There are various kinds of trees surrounding it on all sides; the sand at the bottom of the water is entirely gold, and there are sevenfold railings, lattices, and groves made of the seven treasures, encircling it on every side.

Above are curved box-canopies and multi-storied pavilions with latticed windows; below are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. Within are various kinds of trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits that emit diverse fragrances, while various birds sing together in harmony.
Within Nanda’s bathing pool, there were blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and yellow lotuses as large as chariot wheels; their stalks were like chariot hubs, and they exuded sap like milk.
Its light shines for thirty *li*, and its fragrance is likewise perceived for forty *li*.

Amidst the singing, dancing, and tumultuous festivities within the gardens and pavilions, there is a great tree named Zhòu Guòdù (Exceeding the Day). Its trunk has a circumference of two hundred and eighty *li*, it stands four thousand *li* high, and its branches and leaves extend for twenty million *li*.

"The Trāyastriṃśa devas have palaces forty thousand *li* in breadth and length, all constructed of the seven treasures with sevenfold railings, lattices, and groves surrounding them on every side; there are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools, where various kinds of birds warble in harmony."
The various leaves, flowers, and fruits of the trees emit diverse fragrances.

Among the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are those measuring thirty-six thousand li in both width and length; some measure thirty-two thousand li; some twenty-eight thousand li; some thirty-four thousand li; some twenty-four thousand li; some twenty thousand li; some sixteen thousand li; some twelve thousand li; some eight thousand li; and the smallest are four thousand li in both width and length.
Within this, there are further celestial palaces, measuring three thousand six hundred li in width and length, three thousand two hundred li, and down to four hundred eighty li.
All were made of the seven treasures—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—and featured sevenfold railings, latticed pavilions, and groves of trees.
In the gardens and bathing pools, various kinds of birds warble in harmony.
From the front of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are two paths leading to the inner quarters of Śakra, Lord of Devas;
there are also two paths leading to the Kūṭāgāra Garden.
Furthermore, there are two paths leading to the Citraratna Garden;
two paths leading to the Saṃkīrṇa Garden;
and two paths leading to the Gītavādita Garden.
Furthermore, there are two paths leading to the Nanda bathing pool;
another two paths leading to the Great Tree of Day-Passing;
and yet another two paths leading to the palaces of the various devas.
Furthermore, there are two paths leading to the palace of the Naga King Elāpattra.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, desires to go to the Kūṭāgāra garden to observe, play, and enjoy himself, he calls to mind the various heavenly kings.
At that time, the various heavenly kings said,
"The Lord Śakra has thought of us.
They immediately adjusted their robes, donned their crowns and headdresses, adorned their mounts, and together proceeded to where the Lord Śakra was, standing before him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again thought of the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods said:
"Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has already thought of us."
He then put on his garments, prepared various mounts, and went to where Śakra, the Lord of Devas, was.
He then called to mind the Nāga King Elambara.
At that time, the Nāga King Elambara said:
"Śakra, Lord of Devas, has already thought of us.

Thereupon, he manifested thirty-two heads; from each head, six tusks were manifested; upon each tusk, seven bathing pools were manifested; within each bathing pool, seven lotus flowers were manifested; and upon each lotus flower, seven jade maidens were manifested, performing music and dance.
The Naga King Elāpattra, having performed these various supernatural transformations, went to the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and stood before him.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, adjusted his robes, donned his crown and turban, stepped upon the shoulders of the Naga King, and sat upon the crown of his head, with sixteen minor kings attending and sitting on each side.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, then proceeded to the park of the Coarse and Hard (Kharakarkaśa).

At that time, the wind opened the gates of the park of the Coarse and Hard; the sweeping wind then arose and blew across the grounds of the park, and the Ira-wind was produced, blowing the flowers from the trees within the park onto the ground until they reached the knees of the people.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the various devas, entered the pleasure grove and sat upon the Bhadraśilā stone.
On both sides of the Bhadraśilā stone, sixteen minor celestial kings each sat down.
"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to obtain a necklace, addressed the devaputra Viśvabhū.
The devaputra then said:
'Lord Śakra has already thought of me.'"
He then transformed himself into a necklace and went to present it to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven desired that necklace, the devaputra Śabala immediately manifested another necklace and presented it to the various gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There are devas who cannot see the Coarse and Solid Garden-Palace, nor can they enter within it, nor can they enjoy themselves with celestial music. Why is this?

Because of the small amount of merit they performed in previous lives, there are devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who can only see from afar the coarse and solid gardens and pavilions; they cannot enter them, nor can they enjoy themselves with celestial music.
Why is this? Because the merit they had performed in previous lives was slight.
Furthermore, some among them enter [the realm] and enjoy themselves with celestial pleasures.
Why is this? It is because they have fully perfected their merit in previous lives.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, enjoyed themselves and partook of food and drink within the Citraratha Park for one day, two days, up to seven days; then he departed and went to the Nandana Park, where they likewise enjoyed themselves in the same manner.
Furthermore, when they go to the gardens and pavilions of tumultuous song and dance, their enjoyment of food and drink is likewise.
Why, then, are they called "those who dwell in goodness" (*śubha-kṛtsna*)?
When devas enter the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, they contemplate the meaning of goodness and peace; for this reason, they are called "those who dwell in goodness."
Why is it called "Coarse and Hard"?
When the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the park and pavilion named Coarse and Hard, their bodies become coarse and hard; therefore, it is called "Coarse and Hard."
Why is it called the Garden of Delightful Paintings?

When the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the pavilion within the Garden of Delightful Paintings, their bodies naturally manifest various painted colors; therefore, it is called the Garden of Delightful Paintings.
Why is it called "confusion"?

When the devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Grove of Confusion for sightseeing, Śakra, Lord of Devas, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, personally leaves behind his court ladies and wanders alone with the Apsarases.
At that time, the devaputras were mingling with their celestial maidens in a state of noisy confusion; therefore, it is called "confusion.
Why is it called "singing and dancing"?

When the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the pleasure gardens and pavilions for singing and dancing, they immediately sing and dance to amuse one another; therefore, it is called "singing and dancing."
Why is it said that the great tree passes the day?
There is a deva named Māndhātṛ who dwells upon it; because he takes immense delight in the five celestial pleasures, for this reason it is said that the day passes [there].
Furthermore, during the day, it surpasses great trees in its constant production of flowers and fruit, much like the *karnikāra* tree; therefore, it is called "surpassing the day.

On the side of Śakra, Lord of Devas, there are always ten devaputras who protect him: the first is named Mūla, the second Saṃvara, the third Anuvartaka, the fourth Anuvartakagarbha, the fifth Aruṇa, the sixth Pravāha, the seventh Revata, the eighth Lauhitya, the ninth Kokānada, and the tenth Nanda. These ten devaputras constantly protect Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the people of the world.
In the water grow excellent blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses, which are exceedingly fragrant and beautiful;
the flowers on land are also very soft and lovely, known as *atimuktaka*, *campaka*, *sugandhika*, *śata*, and *nūpura*.
The lands of the people of Aparagoyānī, Uttarakuru, and Pūrvavideha are likewise.

As for the nāgas and garuḍas, there are blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses growing in the water—extremely soft, fragrant, and beautiful—as well as various flowers upon the land.
Āsuras, in the waters there are also blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses—soft, exceedingly fragrant, and beautiful—and on the land there are likewise fine flowers;
they are named Mṛdū, Mahāmṛdū, Karka, Mandārava, and Mahāmandārava.
Above the Four Heavenly Kings, lotuses grow—blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses that are exceedingly soft, fragrant, and beautiful; flowers growing on dry land there are likewise beautiful.

In the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, there are also blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses in the water, exceedingly soft, fragrant, and beautiful; flowers on dry land there are likewise beautiful.

"The people here have seven types of complexions: there are those who are red, those who are golden, those who are blue, those who are yellow, those who are purple, those who are white, and those who are black; these are the seven types of complexions among people."
The asuras likewise possess these seven colors, and the devas are the same; they all possess these seven colors.
"The devas have ten matters. What are these ten?"

First, the infinity of flying; second, the infinity of sitting at will; third, the absence of thieves among the devas; fourth, not speaking of one's own virtues nor of others' faults; fifth, the absence of mutual aggression; sixth, the teeth of the devas being even and aligned; seventh, their hair being deep blue-black, glossy, and eight feet long; eighth, those devas with blue-black hair also have bodies that are blue-black; ninth, those who wish to be white become white-bodied;
tenth, those who wish to be black become black-bodied. These are the ten dharmic matters of the devas.
“The brilliance of this human firefly does not equal the brilliance of a lamp;
the brilliance of a lamp does not equal the brilliance of a torch;
the brilliance of a torch does not equal the brilliance of a great conflagration.”
The brilliance of a great fire is not equal to the brilliance of the stars;
the brilliance of the stars is not equal to the brilliance of the moon;
the brilliance of the moon is not equal to the brilliance of the sun.
The brilliance of the sun does not equal the brilliance of the palaces of the Four Great Kings;
the brilliance of the palaces of the Four Great Kings does not equal the brilliance of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
and the brilliance of the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven does not equal the brilliance of the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
In this manner, each successive light is not equal to the next, up to the radiance of the Akaniṣṭha celestial palace.
The radiance of the Akaniṣṭha celestial palace is not equal to the radiance of the Māyābhra Devaputra;
the radiance of the Māyābhra Devaputra is not equal to the radiance of the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of Origination, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path.
The illumination regarding the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path does not equal the illumination of the Buddha.
"The people of Jambudvīpa who are seven feet or eight feet tall wear garments one zhang wide and six chi long;
the people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha who are seven feet or eight feet tall also wear garments one zhang wide and six chi long."
The people of the continent of Uttarakuru are one zhang and four chi tall; their garments are two zhang and eight chi wide and one zhang and four chi long, weighing two and a half *liang*.
The bodies of the *nāgas* and *garuḍas* are forty *li* high; their garments are eighty *li* wide and forty *li* long, weighing two and a half *liang*.
The various *asura*s are themselves forty *li* high; their garments are eighty *li* wide and forty *li* long, weighing two and a half *liang*.
The devas of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings have bodies forty li long, with garments forty li wide and twenty li long, weighing two and a half *liang*;
the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have bodies eighty li long, with garments eighty li wide and forty li long, weighing seven *zhu* and a half;
the devas of the Yāma Heaven have bodies one hundred and sixty li long, with garments one hundred and sixty li wide and eighty li long, weighing half a *liang*.
The devas of Tuṣita Heaven have bodies one hundred and sixty *li* in length; their garments are three hundred and twenty *li* wide and one hundred and sixty *li* long, weighing two *zhu*.

The devas who delight in being free from arrogance have bodies three hundred and twenty *li* in length; their garments are six hundred and forty *li* wide and three hundred and twenty *li* long, weighing one *zhu*.

The devas of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven have bodies six hundred and forty *li* in length; their garments are one thousand six hundred and eighty *li* wide and six hundred and forty *li* long, weighing half a *zhu*. For all the devas above them, the garments they wear correspond to the dimensions of their respective bodies.
“The people of Jambudvīpa have a lifespan of one hundred years, whether longer or shorter;
the people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred years, whether longer or shorter;
the people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of three hundred years, whether longer or shorter.”
The people of the continent of Uttarakuru all live for a thousand years and none die prematurely;
the dragons and garuḍas live for one kalpa, yet some also die prematurely;
the people of the asura realm live for a thousand years, and some also die prematurely.
The devas in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings have a lifespan of five hundred celestial years, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have a lifespan of one thousand celestial years, and likewise there are those who meet with untimely death;
the devas in the Yāma Heaven have a lifespan of two thousand celestial years, and there are also those who meet with untimely death.
The gods and humans in the Tuṣita Heaven have a lifespan of four thousand celestial years, though some also die prematurely;
the gods and humans who delight in freedom from arrogance have a lifespan of eight thousand celestial years, though some also die prematurely;
the gods and humans in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations have a lifespan of sixteen thousand celestial years, though some also die prematurely.
The devas in the Brahmakāyika heaven have a lifespan of one kalpa, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas in the Ābhāsvara heaven have a lifespan of two kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven have a lifespan of four kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely.
The lifespan of the devas in the Yihubu Heaven is eight kalpas, though some may die prematurely;
the lifespan of the devas in the Asaṃjñisattva Heaven and of the hungry ghosts (preta) is seven kalpas, though some may also die prematurely;
the lifespan of the devas in the Avīci Heaven is ten kalpas, though some may also die prematurely.
The devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven have a lifespan of twenty kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven have a lifespan of forty kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas of the Śubhakṛtsnābha Heaven have a lifespan of eighty kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely.
The devas in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven have a lifespan of one hundred kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas in the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven have a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the devas in the Ākiṃcanyāyatana Heaven have a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas, yet there are also those who die prematurely.
Āgnyāyanīputra, among the devas in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the lifespan is forty thousand kalpas, yet there are those who die prematurely;
among the devas in the Heaven of No-thought-yet-with-thought, the lifespan is eighty thousand kalpas, and there are none who die prematurely.
The Buddha said:
“For the sake of sentient beings, four kinds of food sustain the body. What are these four?

First is the nutriment of visible forms, second is the nutriment of temperature, third is the nutriment of mental volition, and fourth is the nutriment of consciousness; these are the four kinds of nutriment.
What is the nutriment that is grasped?
The people of Jambudvīpa eat rice, parched grain, wheat, meat, and fish, and they wear clothing and bathe; they find peace and security through these foods.
The people of Aparagoyānī in the west and Pūrvavideha in the east are likewise.
The people of Uttarakuru eat pure, natural non-glutinous rice; this constitutes their enjoyment of food and bathing.
The nāgas and garuḍas eat fish, turtles, and large fish such as the timi and timitimiṅgila; this constitutes their taking of food, as well as their bathing.
The asuras eat natural food and clothing, and they bathe.
The gods of the Four Great Kings eat natural food and clothing, and they bathe.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven also partake of natural food and wear garments for bathing;
likewise, the gods of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens all partake of natural food and wear garments for bathing.
From the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) upward, beings take the joy of dhyāna as their food and take meditative concentration (samādhi) as their food.
What kind of beings consume "warm food"?
Those of the egg-born class consume warm food; this is what is meant by "warm food."
What is the nutriment of mental volition?
When one has the mental volition of the perception of meat, this is the nutriment of mental volition.
What is the nutriment of consciousness?
The inhabitants of the hells and the gods of the realm of non-perception take consciousness as their food; this is the nutriment of consciousness.
These are the four kinds of nutriment.
For the sake of sentient beings, they arise to sustain and establish life.
“The people of Jambudvīpa conduct trade and commerce using gold, silver, rare treasures, grain, money, and livestock;
the people of Aparagoyānī conduct trade and commerce using oxen, horses, grain, pearls, and jade;
the people of Pūrvavideha conduct trade and commerce using gold, silver, rare treasures, grain, money, and livestock.”
The people of the continent of Uttarakuru have no markets, nor do they buy or sell goods.
It is the same for the various devas.
In Jambudvīpa, however, there are matters of marriage between men and women.

The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha also have the practice of marriage between men and women. The people of Uttarakuru have no such practice of marriage; however, when a man conceives lustful thoughts toward a woman and looks at her, they simply pass each other by, with the man in front and the woman behind. There are trees that bend together like a lattice canopy;

the people of the northern continent stop there, with men and women in separate places, and then go together beneath those trees. If the tree lowers its shade to cover them, they engage in sexual intercourse; if the tree does not cover them, they do not engage in such acts and depart from one another.
As for the nāgas and garuḍas, they also have the practice of marriage between males and females.
The asuras also have the matters of marriage between men and women.
From this point upward, there are no such matters of marriage.
The people of Jambudvīpa, both men and women, dwell together and engage in mutual intercourse; however, [the beings] above do not.
The people of the four continents—Kuru, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru—engage in sexual union as men and women;
the nāgas and garuḍas also engage in sexual union as males and females;
and the various asuras, both male and female, likewise engage in sexual union.
The men and women of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings also engage in the practice of yin and yang;
the men and women of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven take the wind as their practice of yin and yang;
the men and women of the Yāma Heaven accomplish the practice of yin and yang through mutual proximity.
Among the gods and humans of Tuṣita, men and women become male and female by holding hands;
among the gods and humans free from pride, they become male and female by looking at one another;
and among the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, they become male and female by merely thinking of lustful desire.
From this point upward, one is free from desire.

Suppose there is a person who performs evil deeds with the body, speaks evil words with the mouth, and harbors evil thoughts with the mind; when their life in this human realm comes to an end, they fall into the hells (*niraya*), where they receive a lifespan and obtain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and from that name-and-form, they obtain the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Or suppose there is another person who performs evil deeds with the body, speaks evil words with the mouth, and harbors evil thoughts with the mind; when their life in this human realm comes to an end, they fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*), where they receive a lifespan and obtain name-and-form, and from that name-and-form, they obtain the six sense bases.

If there are those who practice evil with their bodies, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds, when they die in this human world, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), where they receive life, obtain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and obtain the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

If there are those who practice good with their bodies, speak good with their mouths, and harbor good thoughts in their minds, when their lives end, they are reborn as humans, where they receive life, obtain name-and-form, and from name-and-form obtain the six sense bases.

If there are those who practice good with their bodies, speak good with their mouths, and harbor good thoughts in their minds, when their lives end in this human world, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), where they receive life, obtain name-and-form, and from name-and-form obtain the six sense bases; they are like a child of one year or one and a half years of age among the people of Jambudvīpa.
When he was first born in the heavens as a son of heaven, all those devas remembered him as "I" or "my son" or "my daughter.
As soon as he was born in the heavens, he immediately knew his own past lives:
"By what causes and conditions have I come to be born here?"
He then spoke of himself:
"By means of three things, I have truly attained birth here.
What are these three?"
The first is generosity, the second is upholding the precepts, and the third is abandoning evil; these are the three.

When my lifespan in the heavens comes to an end, I shall return to be born again in the world; while among humans, I shall likewise practice good with my body, speak good with my mouth, and think good with my mind.
"After my death, I shall return to be born in the heavens.

Having said this, the deva-son thought of obtaining food; immediately, a vessel filled with natural jewels appeared before him with food. For those with little merit, naturally blue rice appeared before them as food;
for those with middling merit, naturally red rice appeared before them as food.
For those of superior merit, white rice appears spontaneously before them, which the devas then take and eat.

At that moment, it is naturally consumed within their mouths; it is like ghee or sesame oil placed upon fire, which is instantly extinguished. When the devas eat, it is just so: it is naturally consumed within their mouths.
When they feel thirsty, vessels of ambrosial nectar spontaneously appear before them, filled to the brim. For those with little merit, naturally blue-colored nectar appears;
for those with middling merit, naturally red-colored nectar appears;
