and for those with superior merit, naturally white-colored nectar appears. They take it and drink, and it dissolves of its own accord within their mouths.
Just as ghee or sesame oil is immediately consumed when placed upon fire, so too does the drink vanish within the mouths of those devas as soon as they drink it.
Once they have finished eating and drinking, they grow large; then, like other devas in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, they proceed to the bathing pools to bathe and enjoy themselves.

Emerging from the bathing pool, he went beneath the fragrant trees, where he took various perfumes and anointed his body. He then went beneath the garland trees; the trees bowed of their own accord, and he took the tree-hats and garlands and put them on.
Next, he went beneath the clothing and inexhaustible trees; the trees bowed of their own accord, and he took the clothing and inexhaustible garments and put them on.
Finally, he went beneath the vessels, fruits, and musical instrument trees; the trees bowed of their own accord, and he took the vessels, took the fruits to eat, and drank their clear juices.

Furthermore, taking up musical instruments and drumming them, he followed along with their singing and dancing, proceeding to enter gardens, pavilions, and mansions. There he saw countless hundreds of thousands of jade maidens performing music, singing, and dancing, enjoying themselves in mutual entertainment.
When he contemplates the jade maidens on the eastern side, he forgets those on the western side;
when he contemplates the jade maidens on the western side, he forgets those on the eastern side.
The Son of Heaven then thought to himself:
"By what causes and conditions did I come to be born in this world in my previous life?
Now, he has completely forgotten the matters of his previous life; because he sat and beheld the jade maidens, he became licentious and lost his composure.
The name of the jade maiden is An-nyan (Non-Thinking). She is called Non-Thinking because she causes men to lose their composure upon seeing her.

When there is a person who practices good deeds with the body, speaks good words with the mouth, and maintains good thoughts with the mind, and at the end of life in this human world is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, his body grows to such a size as if he were a two or three-year-old child from Jambudvīpa.
The devas remember and recognize them, thinking, "This is my son; this is my daughter.
The sons of the gods then reflect upon their past lives:
"For what reason have I been born here?"
"This is because of their practice of giving, maintaining the precepts, and abandoning evil.

When they wish to obtain food and drink, golden vessels spontaneously appear before them, filled according to the superior, middling, or inferior nature of their merit. Food and drink of white, red, or blue colors appear before them, which they take and eat; these vanish of themselves within the mouth.
It is like holding ghee or sesame oil over a fire, which immediately melts away; such is the case when devas and humans eat.
Once they have eaten, their bodies grow large, just like those of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, and they proceed to bathing pools to wash themselves and enjoy themselves.

He went out to the trees that yield fragrance, garlands, clothing, vessels, fruit, and music; the branches lowered themselves of their own accord, so he took the fragrance to anoint his body, took the garlands, clothing, and vessels to wear and use them, took the fruit to eat, and took the musical instruments to play, sing, and dance.

Upon entering the garden and beholding the mansions, he saw hundreds of thousands of countless jade maidens; he immediately forgot his past-life causes and conditions and could no longer recollect them.

"If there are those whose bodily actions are virtuous, whose speech is virtuous, and whose mental thoughts are virtuous, when their lives in this human realm come to an end, they shall ascend to be born in the Yama Heaven to receive their life-span."

At the moment of birth, his body was like that of a person from Jambudvīpa who is three or four years old; the body of the son of heaven naturally grows to such a size, and he likewise reflects upon his previous lives, realizing that it is because of his practice of giving, observance of the precepts, and abandonment of evil that he has attained birth in the heavens.

When they desire food and drink, a natural precious bowl spontaneously appears full before them; they then eat and drink, and it is immediately consumed within their mouths, just as ghee or sesame oil is instantly extinguished when placed upon a fire.

Having finished eating, they enter the bathing pool to wash; emerging, they go among the trees, where the branches bend down of their own accord so that they may take whatever food and drink is there, while making music, singing, and dancing.

Upon entering the garden and beholding his residence, he saw hundreds of thousands of countless jade maidens; his mind became agitated and distracted, and he no longer remembered the matters of his past lives.

There are those who practice goodness in body, speak goodness with their mouths, and maintain goodness in their minds; when such persons exhaust their lifespans in this human realm, they are reborn above in the Tuṣita Heaven. As soon as they are born, their bodies are already fully grown—like children of four or five years of age among the people of Jambudvīpa—and they naturally remember the acts of giving, the observance of precepts, and the abandonment of evil performed in their previous lives. They partake of natural, spontaneous food, and their bodies grow to full maturity just like other devas.

They went to the bathing pools to wash themselves, then emerged and proceeded beneath various trees; each took whatever was available and engaged in music, song, and dance. They entered the gardens, pavilions, and residences, where they beheld hundreds of thousands of countless jade-like maidens, whose sight disturbed their minds so that they could no longer recollect their past lives.

"If there is a person who performs good deeds with the body, speaks good words with the mouth, and maintains good thoughts in the mind, at the end of their life they will be reborn in the Heaven of No Arrogance (Avṛha). As soon as they are born, their body grows large, like a person of five or six years of age in Jambudvīpa."

If one is born in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, as soon as the body is manifested at birth, it is already as large as that of a person in Jambudvīpa who is six or seven years old.
They remembered their past lives, having practiced generosity, maintained the precepts, and abandoned evil.

They partook of food that appeared spontaneously and entered bathing pools to wash themselves. Upon emerging, they went among the trees; the branches lowered of their own accord, and each took whatever garments, robes, and necklaces were available and put them on without ceasing. Taking vessels, they ate fruit, played music, sang, and danced. Entering gardens, pavilions, and dwellings, they beheld hundreds of thousands of countless jade-like maidens, whose beauty disturbed their minds so that they could no longer remember their past lives.
The Buddha said:
“There are three fast days in the fifteenth-day fortnight.
What are the three? They are:”
The eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month constitute the three [fasting days].
What is the fast on the eighth day of the month?
On the occasion of the fast on the eighth day of the month, the Four Great Kings address their messengers, saying:
"I shall travel to inspect the four continents and observe the myriad people.
I wish to know whether there are those in the world who are filial and obedient to their parents,
and whether there are those who serve śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and practitioners of the Way."
Are there those who respect their elders?
Are there those who observe the fasts and guard the Way?
Are there those who practice giving?
"Are there any who have faith in this world and the world beyond?
The messengers received these instructions and traveled throughout the world on all four sides. Upon their return, they reported in full:
"There are many who are unfilial toward their parents, who do not respectfully serve śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, practitioners, and elders, and who do not observe the precepts or practice giving."
When the Four Heavenly Kings heard this, they were immediately displeased and said:
"Now that we have heard these evil words, it will cause the gods to diminish and increase the race of the asuras."

"If there are many śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, practitioners, and elders who are filial toward their parents; who frequently observe the fasts and precepts and practice giving; and who believe in this world and the world beyond—report all of this to him."
Upon hearing this, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with great joy and said:
"We have now heard these virtuous words; because many people practice goodness, the ranks of the devas will increase and the host of asuras will diminish."
This constitutes the fast of the eighth day of the month.

There are four kinds of thunder and lightning.
What are the four? First is the lightning of the eastern direction, named Hundred Masters.
Second is the lightning of the southern direction, named Body Flavor.
Third, the lightning of the western direction is named Ajara.
Fourth, the lightning of the northern direction is named Aśulana.
For what reason do these sounds of lightning arise within the void?
Sometimes the lightning of bodily flavor (*kāyāsvāda*) contends with the *āśulana* lightning; for this reason, a sound issues from the void.
Or, when the lightning of bodily flavor contends with the hundred-masters (*śatapati*) lightning, for this reason, a sound issues from within the clouds.
Sometimes, when the lightning of the *āśulana* and the lightning of bodily flavor contend with one another, a sound issues from the void.
For what reason does a sound issue from the clouds in the void?

At times, the earth element contends with the water element, the earth element contends with the fire element, and the earth element contends with the wind element, just as mountains strike one another and then stand still.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, the earth element contends with the water, fire, and wind elements; for this reason, a sound issues from the void, and this causes the rain to fall."
Furthermore, there are five circumstances by which rain is lost. What are these five?

First, when clouds arise in the sky and thunder rolls with lightning appearing as a sign, people say it is time for it to rain; yet at that moment, a great wind arises, blowing the rain-seeds to distant mountains, ravines, or marshy places where they fall. This is the first circumstance by which rain is lost.

Furthermore, when clouds arise, thunder rolls, and lightning flashes in response, people say that it shall rain. Yet sometimes the fire-element arises and scorches the raindrops; these are the two circumstances by which rain is lost.

Furthermore, when clouds arise in the sky, thunder rolls, and lightning flashes in response, people say that it will rain. At such times, there may be an Asura King who takes the rainwater with both hands and casts it back into the great ocean; this is the third circumstance by which rain is lost.

Furthermore, when clouds arise, thunder rolls, and lightning flashes in response, people say it is about to rain; yet at that time, the Master of Rain instead engages in lewd and chaotic conduct. For this reason, the heavenly rains do not fall according to their proper seasons. This is the fourth cause for the failure of rain.

Furthermore, when a ruler practices unrighteousness, follows deluded teachings, and is full of anger and malice, the heavens do not send rain at the proper times; these are the five matters that cause the loss of rain.

To have the thought of a self, to have the thought of "I," or to have the thought of "mine" is attachment. To think there is no self is also attachment. To have form is attachment; to be formless is attachment; to neither have form nor be formless is also attachment. The gods prevailed and captured the asura Vimalacitra, binding him with the fivefold bonds, and led him before the gods of the Sudarśana heaven to show him to Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
When the asura Vimalacitra came and went with the same conduct as the gods, those who saw him would revile him with harsh words.
At that time, an attendant spoke a verse before Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Is it because Śakra, Lord of the Devas, is afraid?"
"Are you powerless and silent?
Before my very eyes, I have heard Vimalakīrti uttering such coarse and evil words.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied to his attendant with these verses:
“I am tranquil not because I am afraid; my power is no less than that of Vimalakīrti.
How could one who possesses wisdom ever engage in a dispute with the ignorant?”
At that time, the attendant spoke a verse before Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"If fools come to fight, one should not endure such matters;
one should instead take up a staff and strike those fools."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied to his attendant with these verses:
“I have already understood this: One should not speak with the foolish;
If the fool harbors anger, The wise do not wish to quarrel.”
At that time, the attendant spoke a verse before Śakra, the Lord of Devas:
"You should know that this is such tranquility; O Śakra, Lord of Devas, you should see its cause.
Out of delusion, you take what is not wisdom for wisdom, and out of fear, you remain silent."
Out of foolishness he considers himself [victorious], yet out of fear he remains silent;
for this reason he returns to fight again, while the king, terrified, flees like a bull.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra replied to his attendant with these verses:
“Remembering how you came to provoke and insult me, And thinking that I remained silent out of fear— Yet the benefit for one’s own person is supreme; There is nothing equal to patience.”
Those who are wicked and evil, whose bodies give rise to thoughts of anger, should not direct anger toward others;
for those who harbor anger will surely engage in mutual strife.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra again replied to his attendant, speaking in verse:
"There are two causes and conditions for what is done: for one's own sake and for the sake of others.
If there are those who give rise to strife and contention, the wise do not fight with them."
If one performs these two actions for the sake of oneself and others,
people will call this foolishness, because of a failure to understand the Dharma.
Those who are weak claim to have strength; those who possess strength are merely arrogant fools.
But for one who practices the Dharma, there is the strength of their spiritual discipline—none are able to subdue them.
Those who possess such strength of character remain silent toward those who are inferior;
I know that patience is supreme, and thus I endure insults from the inferior with tears.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the Lord Śakra was at that time, it was my own self.
I practiced patience in such a manner then, and I likewise practice patience now."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"In the past, when the asuras fought with the devas and were victorious, the devas were utterly defeated. Then Śakra, the Lord of Devas, mounted a chariot drawn by a thousand horses and fled back."
Seeing Śyāmāka perched upon a great tree with two eggs in its nest, he spoke this verse himself:
"Tell the driver, 'Śyāmāka is here! Turn the horse-drawn chariot and avoid it;
It would be better for an *asura* to destroy me, Than to let these two eggs be destroyed."
The charioteer immediately received the command of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and turned the chariot drawn by a thousand horses away.
When the asuras saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, turning his chariot of a thousand horses back,
they said, "He wishes to come and fight with us."
"Because the asuras were immediately terrified and fled in haste, the devas attained victory.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to know who that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was at that time?"
"I was that very person.
At that time, I maintained a mind of loving-kindness toward all people, as well as toward all classes of creatures, including those that fly and those that crawl.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, when the devas and the asuras were engaged in battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was filled with great joy and returned to construct a great lecture hall, which he named 'Victory' (Jaya)."
For what reason is it called "Victorious"?
Because it surpasses all the asuras.
It is constructed with a hundred tiers of railings, and between each railing, seven hundred lattice windows are fashioned.
Within each of the jeweled nets, there were seven hundred jade maidens.
Each jade maiden had seven hundred attendants.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, no longer worried about the clothing, food, or drink for the jade maidens; each was produced spontaneously according to their former practices.
Within a thousandfold world-system of lecture halls, there was none equal to the lecture hall of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
The Asura King thought to himself:

"My majestic power is so supreme that even all these suns, moons, and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwell and move above me in the void. I wish to seize the radiance of the sun and moon, place it within my ears, and travel to the ten directions."
Having thought this, he became enraged and no longer followed or avoided anything.
At that time, the Asura King called to mind the Asura Vimalacitra.

When Vimalacitra the asura learned of this, he donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up diverse weapons and mounts, and accompanied by hundreds of thousands of myriads of asuras, went to the abode of the asura king and stood before him.
At that time, the Asura King again thought of the Asura Śambara.

The Asura Śambara immediately became aware of this; he then donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up weapons and mounted his steed, and accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of asuras, went to where the Asura King was and stood before him.

At that time, the Asura King again thought of Pūrṇa Asura and Cīra Asura; they immediately knew of his thought, donned various kinds of ornaments and armor, took up weapons, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of asuras, went to where the Asura King was and stood before him.

At that time, the Asura King, having arrayed himself in various ornaments and taken up weapons and mounts, set out from his city surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of asura kings, intending to go and engage in battle with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the Nāga King Nandopananda wound his body seven times around Mount Sumeru, causing it to tremble; he then lashed the great ocean with his tail, sending its waters leaping up to the edge of Mount Sumeru for three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand li. The Trāyastriṃśa devas immediately knew that the Asuras were about to come and wage war against the gods.
At that time, the various nāgas of the ocean, adorned with diverse ornaments and taking up weapons and mounts, all went forth to meet the asuras to fight them.
If they were victorious in battle, they pursued the asuras into their cities and citadels.
If the nāgas were defeated and unable to prevail, they would go to where the kumbhāṇḍas dwell and say to the kumbhāṇḍas:
"The asuras wish to wage war against the devas; come together with us to fight them."
Upon hearing the words of the nāgas, the various kumbhāṇḍa spirits donned various garments and ornaments, took up weapons and mounts, and went together to meet the asuras to engage them in battle.
If they are victorious, they shall pursue the asuras to their city-walls.
If they are not victorious, they shall immediately go to where the flower-bearing spirits reside and say to those flower-bearing spirits:
"The asuras wish to wage war against the devas; we must go together to intercept and pursue them."

Upon hearing these words from the *nāga* and *kūṭa* spirits, the flower-bearing spirits immediately donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up weapons, mounted their vehicles, and went together to meet and engage in battle with the Asuras.
If they are victorious, they immediately pursue them into their city-walls and towers.
If they cannot prevail, they go to the abode of the spirit Caitra-ma and say to him:
"The Asuras wish to battle with the devas; we should go together to intercept and pursue them."

When the spirit Caitasika heard this, he immediately donned various kinds of armor and ornaments, took up weapons, mounted his steed, and went together with others to meet the Asura and engage in battle.
If they are victorious, they pursue the asuras to their city walls.
If they cannot prevail, they go to the Four Heavenly Kings and say to them:
"The various asuras wish to wage war against the devas; we should go together to meet them in battle and drive them away."
When the devas heard this, at that time, the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa thought of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra immediately knew of this; he then donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up weapons and mounts, and, surrounded before and behind by countless hundreds of thousands of *tittira* birds, went to where the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa was and stood before him.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa again thought of King Virūḍhaka. King Virūḍhaka immediately became aware of this;

he then donned various ornaments and took up weapons and mounts. King Virūḍhaka, accompanied by countless devas and hundreds of thousands of them, and further surrounded before and behind by countless hundreds of thousands of nāgas, went to the place where the Great King Vaiśravaṇa was and stood before him.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, adorned with various ornaments and taking up weapons and mounts, went forth surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of spirits and ghosts, together with the other heavenly kings, to engage in battle with the asuras.
If they are able to achieve victory, they shall pursue the asuras to their city walls.
If they do not achieve victory, they shall immediately go to the Suyāma and other devas to inform Śakra Devendra, and address the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, saying:
"The asuras wish to wage war against us; we must go together to meet them in battle and drive them away."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the gods, saying:
"Go to the abode of Suyāma, the abode of Tuṣita, the abode of Nirmāṇarati, and the abode of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and say:
'The Asuras wish to wage war against the gods; you should go together to fight and drive them away.'"
The Brahmā-uttara devaputra immediately received the instruction of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and went to speak thus to the four higher heavens.

Thereupon, each donned various ornaments and took up weapons and mounts to descend from heaven. Together with immeasurable devas, the Suyāma devas went to the eastern flank of Mount Sumeru to protect the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
the Tuṣita devas, together with immeasurable devas, went to station themselves on the southern flank of Mount Sumeru.
The Nirmāṇarati devas, together with immeasurable devas, dwell on the western flank of Mount Sumeru for the sake of protecting the Trāyastriṃśa heaven;
the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, together with immeasurable devas, go to dwell on the northern flank of Mount Sumeru for the sake of protecting the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, called to mind the Vaijayanta spirits.

The Vaijayanta spirits immediately became aware of this; they donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up weapons and mounts, and went to where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was, standing before him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought of the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita.
Supratiṣṭhita, knowing this immediately, adorned himself with various ornaments, took up weapons and mounted his vehicle, and went to where Śakra was, standing before him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again thought of the various kings of the devas.

The kings of the devas immediately became aware of this; they then donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up their weapons and mounts, and went to where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was, standing before him.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again thought of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately became aware of this; they donned various ornaments and accoutrements, took up weapons and mounts, and went to where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was, standing before him.

At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, arrayed himself in various ornaments, took up weapons and mounted his steed; seated upon the flank of the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded before and behind by countless hundreds of thousands of devas, he departed from the celestial palace and went to the abode of the asuras to engage them in battle.

Swords, blades, spears, arrows, bows, and crossbows pierce and wound the bodies of the asuras; the resulting poison and pain are beyond description, yet due to their karmic causes and conditions, they do not die.

The various asuras were likewise; using blades, spears, arrows, bows, and crossbows made of the seven treasures, they pierced and wounded the bodies of the devas, causing unspeakable agonizing pain, yet due to the power of their karmic conditions, they did not die.

It is the same for the gods of the Heaven of Desire (*Kāmadhātu*); when they engage in battle with the asuras, it is because of their desire for concealment and because of the conditions of desire that it happens thus.
Chapter Eleven: The Three Minor Kalpas (*Tri-kṣudra-kalpa-varga*) from the Mahāsaṃvarta-sūtra. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are three minor kalpas.”
What are the three? First, the kalpa of swords and blades; second, the kalpa of famine; third, the kalpa of pestilence. These are the three minor kalpas.
Regarding the kalpa of swords and blades: what is meant by the kalpa of swords and blades?
At that time, people will mostly act contrary to the Dharma; being foolish and holding false views, they will practice the ten unwholesome deeds.
Because people commit these evil acts, all excellent flavors—ghee, sesame oil, honey, and rock sugar—all shall perish.
All fine garments—brocades, white cottons, and the like—will all perish.

On this earth, mountains, forests, valleys, ravines, and cliffs will arise spontaneously, while various jewels such as pearls, lapis lazuli, and crystal will all sink into the ground, leaving only thorny slopes.

During the age of the sword and blade, the people will be unfilial toward their parents, fail to serve śramaṇas and practitioners, and show no respect for their elders; thus, their evil reputation will spread everywhere.
The Buddha said:

"For example, people of the present day who are filial and obedient toward their parents, respectful and compliant in serving śramaṇas and practitioners, and who follow the words of their elders, have their good reputations spread far and wide."

Thus, during the age of the sword-blade calamity, the people will be unfilial toward their parents, will not serve sages or śramaṇas, and will show no respect for their elders; their evil reputation will spread far and wide.
During the Age of Swords (śastra-kalpa), there is no goodness whatsoever; how much less could there be those who practice virtue?

In the Age of Swords, the people of the world have no means of trade or lending. All great trees fall, and the earth is covered only with ditches and pits, uneven with highs and lows. Where there were once rippling waters, the banks collapse; the river water remains deep at the bottom. The population is sparse, and they are filled with such terror that their hair stands on end.
During the age of the sword-blade calamity, when people see one another, they desire only to harm and kill each other, just as hunters in a wild marsh see deer and wish to slaughter them.

Thus, during the kalpa of swords and blades, when people see one another they desire only to harm each other; whatever grass, trees, tiles, or stones they grasp in their hands all transform into swords and blades, and they kill one another in succession.
At that time, the human lifespan was but ten years!
Among them were those who possessed keen intelligence and wisdom; they fled into mountain forests, river valleys, and deep riverbanks to hide there, saying:
"There is no one capable of killing me, nor do I kill anyone."
They then lived there, eating the roots of fruit-bearing trees.
As for those who plundered with swords and blades, they killed one another for seven days before ceasing.
At that time, all the people who died fell into the hells.
Why is this so? During the age of the sword-blade (śastra-kalpa), each person harbors poisonous intent and thinks ill of one another; they die without a single thought of goodwill.
Such is the nature of the age of the sword-blade.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"What is it like during the kalpa of famine?

During the time of the kalpa of famine, the people mostly act contrary to the Dharma; they are ignorant, hold false views, and are envious, stingy, and greedy, guarding their wealth and refusing to practice generosity."
Because of this, the rains do not fall according to the proper seasons.

Due to the untimely nature of the rains, what the people sow and plant withers and does not grow; there are only withered stalks remaining. Consequently, grain becomes expensive, and people must sweep up the fallen grain from the fields to barely sustain their lives.
It is thus during the eon of high grain prices.
Furthermore, during the eon of high grain prices, people sweep the streets and distribute grain evenly throughout the markets and villages to sustain their own livelihoods.
Furthermore, during an eon of famine when grain is scarce, the leaves of trees fall to the ground; people dig into the earth to retrieve these leaves and boil them for food.
Such is the plight of the people during an eon of famine.

In the age of famine when grain is precious, those who die of starvation are many; the skeletons of those who die each year are scattered upon the ground. As all people suffer from hunger, they gather the bones from the markets and streets, boiling them for food. Such is the state of the people’s hunger.
During the kalpa of famine, those who die fall among the hungry ghosts (preta). Why is this?
Because during the kalpa of famine, the people are mutually jealous, stingy, and greedy; such is the kalpa of famine.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"What is it like during the kalpa of pestilence?

During the kalpa of pestilence, the people uphold the sutras and precepts, possess right view and abandon wrong views, and practice the ten wholesome deeds. Because of this, at that time, various ghosts and spirits from other worlds come to harass these people, beating and striking them, and disturbing their minds."
The ghosts and spirits here are licentious and disorderly; for this reason, ghosts and spirits from other regions are able to come and harass people, beating them and disturbing their minds.

It is like a king or a high minister who orders soldiers to guard the city gates; yet while they are thus licentious and disorderly, if powerful bandits from another country come, they will plunder the prefectures, kingdoms, districts, and towns in this manner.

During the kalpa of illness, when the people practice the sutras and precepts, maintain right view and abandon false views, and observe the ten wholesome deeds, ghosts and spirits from other regions come to harass them, beating and striking them to disturb their minds.
During the kalpa of disease, all those who die are reborn in the heavens.
Why is this? During the kalpa of disease, people take turns inquiring after one another’s well-being, saying:
"How is it? Are you at ease? Have you recovered?"
"This is what constitutes the age of disease and calamity;
this is the third minor kalpa.
Chapter Twelve: On Catastrophes. From the Mahākalpaka Sūtra, Chapter Twelve: On Catastrophes. The Buddha spoke to the bhikṣus:
“The heavens and earth undergo three calamitous transformations. What are these three?
First is the calamity of fire; second is the calamity of water; third is the calamity of wind. These are the three calamitous transformations.”
At the time of a cosmic calamity, people gather at three places. What are these three?
When a calamity of fire occurs, all people ascend to the fifteenth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, where they assemble in great numbers.
When the calamity of water occurs, all people ascend to the nineteenth heaven, Pi-jin (Pārśva), where they gather in great numbers;
when the calamity of wind occurs, all people ascend to the twenty-third heaven, Wei-he (Vaṃśa), where they gather in great numbers.
When the calamity of a fire disaster occurs, the people of the world all practice unrighteousness; they hold wrong views and do not perceive the truth, committing the ten evil deeds.
Because the people all practice unrighteousness, uphold wrong views, fail to perceive the three types of conduct, and commit the ten evil deeds, the heavens send rain out of season.
"After the heavens have ceased to rain, all the trees, medicinal herbs, and myriad things in this world will wither and die, never to grow again.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This is impermanent, lacking solidity, and unable to endure; this is the ultimate state of old age. Therefore, you should cultivate weary detachment and strive to deliver all beings, seeking liberation for yourselves."

After an incalculable length of time, a great chaotic wind arises and enters the great ocean for three million three hundred and sixty thousand li, seizing the great city of the sun and ascending to the side of Mount Sumeru at one million six hundred and eighty thousand li, placing it back within its original orbit.
"For this reason, two suns appear in the world; once they have risen, all the canals and small rivers dry up completely, leaving no water behind.

The Buddha said, "This is impermanent, lacking solidity, and unable to endure for long. This is the extreme of old age; therefore, one should cultivate revulsion toward it and proceed until attaining the natural path of liberation."

After a long time, beyond calculation, a great chaotic wind arises and blows upon the waters of that great ocean for three million three hundred and sixty thousand li, entering and seizing the great city-walls of the sun; it then ascends to the side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, for one million six hundred and eighty thousand li, and places the city-walls of the sun within the path [of the mountain].
For this reason, three suns arise in the world, whereby all the great rivers and streams—the Yaśovatī, Airāvatī, Mahī, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, and Gaṅgā—all dry up completely until nothing remains.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Impermanence and lack of solidity are just like this; this is the ultimate state of old age.
Therefore, one should cultivate revulsion for it and distance oneself from it, until one attains the natural path of liberation."

After a further period of immeasurable time, a great chaotic wind arose, blowing upon the seawater until its waves surged three million three hundred and sixty thousand li. These waves entered and seized the great city-walls of the sun, carrying them out to a distance of one million six hundred and eighty thousand li from the side of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and placed them within the path of the sun.

For this reason, four suns arise in the world, whereby all streams, springs, and great fountains—including Lake Anavatapta, the Red Lotus Lake, the Blue Lotus Lake, the White Lotus Lake, the Yellow Lotus Lake, the Great Lake Mānasa, and the Great Lake Nāli—are completely dried up and exhausted, leaving nothing behind.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Impermanence and lack of solidity are thus; they cannot endure for long, and this is the ultimate state of old age.
Therefore, one should cultivate weariness and distance oneself from it, until one attains the natural path of liberation."

After a further period of immeasurable length, a great chaotic wind arose and blew upon the waters of the great ocean, raising waves three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* high. These waves entered and seized the great city-walls of the sun, carrying them up to the side of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, at a height of one million six hundred and eighty thousand *li*, and placed them within the path of the sun.
For this reason, when five suns appear in the world, the waters of the great ocean gradually diminish by four thousand li, eight thousand li, twelve thousand li, and up to twenty-eight thousand li.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Impermanence and lack of solidity are thus; they cannot endure for long; this is the extreme of old age.
Therefore, you should cultivate weary detachment from them and proceed until you attain the natural path of liberation."
When five suns appear, they parch the waters of the great ocean until only twenty-eight thousand li, eighteen thousand li, fourteen thousand li, eight thousand li, or four thousand li remain.

At times, when the ocean waters recede slightly, there remain seven trees, six trees, five trees, four trees, three trees, two trees, or one tree; subsequently, as they recede further, there remain seven men, six men, five men, four men, three men, two men, or one man.

When the remaining seawater is such that it can submerge one person, it gradually recedes until it reaches a person’s waist, then until it reaches a person’s knee, and finally only a small amount remains.

It would be like a drop of water in a cow’s hoofprint after rain; as it gradually diminishes over a long period, the waters of the great ocean will be entirely exhausted, unable even to moisten a person’s finger.
"Just as the essence of fat and grease, when cast into a great fire, leaves no smoke at all," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus, "so too is this [the nature of conditioned things]:
impermanent and lacking solidity. Therefore, one should cultivate revulsion and distance oneself from it, until one attains the natural path of liberation."

After a further period of immense duration, beyond calculation, a great turbulent wind blows upon the waters of the great ocean, raising waves three million three hundred and sixty thousand li high. These waves enter and seize the great city-walls of the sun, carrying it up to the side of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, at a distance of one million six hundred and eighty thousand li, and place it within its proper course.

For this reason, six suns appear in the world; the four great continents and the eighty thousand cities, as well as the great mountains and Sumeru, the king of mountains, are all scorched and emit smoke.
"It is like a great potter who, when first kindling the fire, produces smoke.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"In this same way, when six suns appear in the world, they scorch and bake the four great continents, the eighty thousand cities, and all the great mountains, including Sumeru, the king of mountains, from which smoke issues forth."
"Just as when fat or grease is cast into a great fire, it immediately leaves no smoke," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"because it is impermanent and lacks solidity, one should cultivate revulsion toward it, seek liberation, and attain the Way of spontaneity."

After a further very long time, a great chaotic wind arises and blows upon the waters of the great ocean, creating waves three hundred and thirty-six thousand li high. These enter and seize the great city-walls of the sun, carry it out and up to the side of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and place it within the path of the sun.

Because of this, seven suns appear in the world; the four great continents and the eighty thousand cities, as well as all the great mountains and Sumeru, the king of mountains, tremble with their towering peaks.
It is like a great cauldron over a blazing fire, where the contents boil and surge; such is the state when the seven suns appear.

The palaces of the four continents, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heaven all become ruggedly agitated and tremble.
The wind rises high through the palaces of the various heavens, reaching up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When those newly born devaputras see the fire, they are all struck with terror. The elder devas say to the newly born devaputras:
"Do not be afraid; we have seen it burned before, and the fire never exceeded this."
At that time, the four great continents, the eighty thousand cities, the various great mountains, and Mount Sumeru all shook and trembled with towering majesty.
The King of Mountains, Sumeru, collapsed in sections of four thousand li, eight thousand li, twelve thousand li, sixteen thousand li, twenty-four thousand li, and thirty-eight thousand li.
"It is like fat or grease cast into a great fire; it leaves neither smoke nor residue.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"All that is impermanent and lacks solidity is just like this; this is the ultimate state of old age."
Therefore, one should cultivate a sense of weary detachment and distance, until one attains the natural path of liberation.
Who would believe that there is a time when seven suns arise in the world?
Only those who have seen it themselves would believe it!
Who would believe that the four great continents, the eighty thousand cities, the various great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, would burn and emit smoke?
Only those who have seen it themselves would believe it!
Who would believe that the four great continents and the eighty thousand cities, the various great mountains and Sumeru, the king of mountains, would all tremble and shake;

and that the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmakāyika Heaven would all tremble and shake, as the wind lifts the palaces of these devas up to fifteen āvartas above the heavens?

Only those who have seen it would believe it! Who could believe that Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, would be utterly destroyed until not even a trace of scorched earth remains; that all the *nirayas* (hells) would be completely annihilated; that thereafter the animals and beasts would all perish; that thereafter the *pretas* (hungry ghosts) would all perish; that thereafter the *asuras* would all perish; that thereafter all humans would die out; and that thereafter the gods of the Cāturmahārājika, Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika heavens would all perish? This is called the burning of heaven and earth, when all people gather in one place.

After that, after a very long time, a great cloud arose and released a heavy rain; its drops were as large as chariot wheels, filling all the rivers and seas. Gradually the waters accumulated until they reached the Brahmakāyika heaven, and further ascended to the fifteenth heaven, the Ābhāsvara-svara.

The water is held on all four sides by winds; the first wind is named the Abiding Wind, the second is the Assisting Wind, the third is the Immovable Wind, and the fourth is the Firm Wind—these are the four.
After a long time, and after a further very long time—many tens of millions of years—the waters gradually diminished by hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* beyond measure.
A wind named Saṃkhya arose, blowing from all four directions; as the waters gradually receded, waves rose upon them, producing thick foam that transformed into seven-jeweled lattices.
In this manner, ascending further up to the seventh heaven, they construct palaces.
After a long time of many tens of millions of years, the waters gradually recede by hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, then again by hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.

Turbulent winds arose from the four directions, blowing upon the water and churning it until thick foam was produced; this transformed into the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and red pearls—forming a jeweled canopy.
The Golden Wind sustains the sixth celestial realm, the dwelling place of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas.
After a very long time, many tens of millions of years, the waters gradually recede;

then a turbulent wind named Caijie arises from the four directions, blowing upon the surface of the water so that waves rise and thick foam is produced, which transforms into the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—forming a pavilion of interlaced jewels.
The turbulent winds carry [the materials] up to the fifth heaven above, where they complete the construction of the celestial palaces for the devas.
After a long time—many tens of millions of years—the waters gradually recede;

turbulent winds come from the four directions, blowing upon the surface of the water so that waves arise and thick foam is produced, which transforms into the seven treasures. These are carried upward to construct the palaces in the fourth Tuṣita Heaven and the third Yāma Heaven.
After another very long period of many tens of thousands of years, the water gradually receded by several million yojanas.

Turbulent winds blew in from the four directions, stirring the waves upon the water to produce thick foam, which transformed into four kinds of precious substances: first, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; and fourth, crystal.

The turbulent winds sustain it in the center of the heavens of the world, forming Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in height, and likewise three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in breadth and width; its eastern flank is of celestial white silver, its southern flank of celestial blue lapis lazuli, its western flank of celestial crystal, and its northern flank of celestial gold.
Again, after many tens of millions of years, the water gradually receded by several tens of thousands of *yojanas*.

Turbulent winds blew from the four directions, churning the waters until thick foam rose to the surface, which transformed into the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate—forming intersecting canopies.
These turbulent winds carried them up to the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, where they completed the construction of the second palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
After a further period of many tens of millions of years, the waters gradually receded by many tens of millions of *yojanas*.

Turbulent winds blew from the four directions, churning the surface of the water until waves arose and thick foam was produced; this transformed into the seven treasures, forming intersecting dew-banners (*caitya*).

These turbulent winds carried it up to the midpoint of the hundred sixty-eight million *li* of Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, completing the construction of the celestial palaces for the beings of the First Heaven.
After a further period of many tens of millions of years, the waters gradually diminished.
Turbulent winds blew from the four directions, churning the surface of the water until waves rose and thick foam formed, which transformed into vajra.

These turbulent winds, within the four great continents and beyond the eighty thousand cities, fashioned mountain ranges six million eight hundred thousand yojanas high, encircling them in four layers; these are named the Great Iron Ring Mountains (Mahācakravāḍa).
After a further period of many tens of millions of years, the waters gradually recede;
turbulent winds blow from the four quarters, churning the surface of the water until thick foam arises and transforms into vajra.

These turbulent winds then take up the four great continents and the eighty thousand cities from all around, forming a second great mountain, which is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height.
Thereafter, the water gradually diminished over the course of many tens of millions of years.

Turbulent winds blew from the four directions, churning the surface of the water until waves arose and thick foam was produced, which transformed into the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate. These formed eight concentric mountains surrounding [the central one], reaching a height of 1,680,000 li; they are named Adoli and are exceedingly beautiful.
The water gradually receded by several tens of millions of li;
turbulent winds came from the four directions, blowing upon the surface of the water so that waves arose and thick foam was produced, which transformed into the seven treasures.
Surrounding Mount Adari, they constructed a second mountain named Īṣādhara, one million three hundred and forty thousand *li* in height, which was exceedingly beautiful.
The third mountain is named Yugandhara; it is four hundred and eighty thousand *li* high and also four hundred and eighty thousand *li* wide.
The fourth mountain is named Sudarśana; it is two hundred and forty thousand *li* high and also two hundred and forty thousand *li* wide.
The fifth jewel mountain is named Aparṇī; it is twelve thousand li in height and twelve thousand li in breadth.
The sixth jewel mountain is named Nimindhara; it is forty-four thousand li in height and forty-four thousand li in breadth.
The seventh jewel mountain is named Vinata; it is twenty-two thousand li in height and its breadth is likewise twenty-two thousand li.
The eighth jewel mountain is named Cakravāḍa; it is twelve thousand li in height and its breadth is likewise twelve thousand li.
Afterwards, the water gradually receded;

turbulent winds came from the four directions, blowing upon the water to produce thick foam, which transformed into thick earth and thereby formed the ground. It is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas deep, and its boundaries are limitless.

A violent wind arose with great force, blowing and excavating that ground until it was three million three hundred and sixty thousand li deep and likewise three million three hundred and sixty thousand li long; all the waters of the world flowed into it, filling it completely and thereby forming the great ocean.
"Why is the seawater salty? There are three reasons for its single flavor of saltiness.

First, there are great fish in the sea—some four thousand li long, some eight thousand li, some twelve thousand li, some sixteen thousand li, some twenty thousand li, some twenty-four thousand li, some twenty-eight thousand li, and some thirty-two thousand li—all of whom discharge their pure urine into the sea; therefore, the seawater is salty."

Second, clouds arise and cover all the oceans, releasing great rains; these clouds reach as high as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, raining down drops as large as chariot axles. They wash away Mount Sumeru and the palaces of the various heavens—the Āṭavaka, the Abhāsvara, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, and the Brahmakāyika—down to the Cāturmahārājika Heaven. Because all that salt water flows back into the great ocean, the seawater has but one taste: saltiness.

Furthermore, in the past, there was a man who had attained the state of an immortal (ṛṣi) and possessed the power of incantation; he used his spells to cause the seawater to become uniformly salty in flavor, and thus the seawater is of one salty taste.
These are the three matters.
The Buddha said:

"When heaven and earth together encounter the calamity of a flood, all people in the world practice every kind of good deed and delight in cultivating the Way and its virtue; after death, their spirits, souls, and vital breaths all ascend to the sixteenth heaven above to become celestial beings."

Those within the *niraya* hells, and all sentient beings—whether possessing blood, breath, or moving by crawling—all upon death shall return to human form; having again performed various virtuous deeds and delighting in practicing the Way and its virtue, they shall all ascend after death to the sixteenth heaven above to become celestial beings.

When the Asuras, the devas, and the beings from the first heaven up to those of the fifteenth heaven have all passed away, their spirits and souls descend to return to human form. They practice and accumulate manifold virtues, delighting in the Way and its Virtue; upon death, they all ascend again to the sixteenth heaven to become devas, and only then do the people of the world become extinct.
After a long time, a great cloud arises again and ascends to the fifteenth heaven above.
From that cloud, a heavy rain of boiling ashes falls, with drops as large as chariot axles.

Heaven rains down boiling ashes; thus, for many hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, all the eighty thousand cities throughout the four continents, as well as the great mountains and Mount Sumeru—from the fifteenth heaven above down to the four continents below—are utterly decayed, dissolved, and extinguished, leaving nothing behind.
It is like placing the essence of fat and grease into a great fire; there will be neither smoke nor flame.
Who would believe these words?
Only those who have attained the Way of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) would believe them!
This refers to the essential process by which heaven and earth encounter the calamity of a flood, leading to their destruction and ultimate extinction.
Once heaven and earth have been destroyed and extinguished, there is a further method for them to begin life anew.
Just as when one encounters a calamity of fire, there arises again that which is of the same nature.

Beginning from the fifteenth heaven above, it forms and extends downward to the first heaven, as well as to the Asura heavens; it constructs the four great continents, the eighty thousand cities, the various great mountains, and Mount Sumeru, until the sun, moon, and stars finally become visible.

Downward, including all things that exist under heaven, reaching as far as the Great Iron Ring Mountains at the horizon—this refers to the fundamental principle for the renewed beginning after the destruction and ultimate extinction of heaven and earth during the calamity of the universal flood.
The Buddha said:

"When heaven and earth together encounter the great calamity of the wind-disaster, those people in the world who have practiced service, who are peaceful, kind, and benevolent, and who are always filial and obedient, and who all delight in practicing the Way, will at death have their spirits ascend to the seventeenth heaven above to become celestial beings."

Those in the hells, as well as all sentient beings who breathe and wriggle, upon death shall all return to human form; they shall all again perform various virtuous deeds, all take delight in practicing the Way and its virtue, and at death, their spirits, souls, and spirits shall ascend to the seventeenth heaven to become celestial beings.

From the Asura heavens and the first heaven above, up to the sixteenth heaven, all humans eventually pass away; their spirits, souls, and vital breaths descend to return to human form, where they practice accumulated goodness and delight in the Way and its Virtue. Upon death, they all ascend to the seventeenth heaven to become celestial beings, and only then do the people of the world become extinct.

After a long time, a great wind arose called Kāśa; it ascended to the sixteenth heaven above, where it flashed, shattered, broke apart, dispersed, and was extinguished, leaving nothing remaining—neither sound nor echo.

After blowing for a long time in this manner, the great wind completely exhausts the original abodes of the humans in the sixteenth heaven, and continues downward until it reaches the Āsura heavens without remainder; it is like a great wind blowing upon fine dust, which is carried away, dissipated, and utterly exhausted.
Who would believe these words?
Only those who have attained the Way of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) would believe them!

A great wind blows again, destroying and annihilating all things within the reach of the sun and moon throughout the world; the four great continents and eighty thousand cities, all the great mountains and Mount Sumeru, even the Iron Ring Mountains—all are utterly consumed and extinguished, completely exhausted until nothing remains.
It is like a great wind blowing through fine flour, which is carried away by the current and dissipated until nothing remains.
When heaven and earth together encounter the calamity of the great wind at the end of a kalpa, they undergo the process of being born anew once again.

Furthermore, it is like how after a calamity such as a fire disaster, there is a renewed beginning; once the formation of a kalpa is completed, this is what is meant by the heaven and earth together encountering a great wind that destroys and brings about their final end through three modes, and then they undergo a renewed beginning through those same three modes.
Who would believe these words?
Only those who have already attained the Way of spontaneity (ziran) would believe them!
Heaven and earth undergo a common renewal of birth, just as when they first encountered the calamity of fire, they later underwent a renewed birth.
Turbulent winds arose once more, and when the construction was entirely finished, those of meager merit from the fifteenth heaven above came down and completely filled [the space].

The eleven tiers of heavens, where gods and humans dwell, were completely filled from top to bottom; likewise, the asuras dwelling on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, in their original abodes, were all entirely filled.
