13. Chapter Thirteen: The Reformation of Heaven and Earth The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When heaven and earth are destroyed and subsequently reformed, all people shall dwell in the fifteenth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Heaven of Utmost Purity). The beings in that heaven take joy as their food; each possesses their own radiance and supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and their lifespan is exceedingly long."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, water filled the heavens and the earth.
At that moment, there were neither sun nor moon, nor were there stars; there was no day or night, nor a month or half-month, nor years. It was profoundly dark and obscure, with nothing to be seen."

After heaven and earth were formed, those devas whose merit, fortune, and life-span were thinning and about to end descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to roam this world. They took joy as their food, each possessing natural radiance and the supernormal power of flight; dwelling among humans, they lived for an exceedingly long time.

At that time, the people of the world were exceedingly upright and beautiful; they could not be distinguished as male or female, nor could they be distinguished as rulers or commoners, but instead moved about together as a single multitude.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:

"At that time, the flavor of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) spontaneously arose upon the ground, like the cream on top of white ghee; such was the color of that flavor of the earth, and its taste was like honey."
At that time, there was a certain person who delighted in flavors, and he thought to himself:
"I wish to test this by taking some of the 'earth-flavor' with my finger and tasting it, so as to know what kind it is."

The man then took some of the earth-essence with his finger and tasted it; he found it extremely pleasing and relished it. Having tasted it three times in this manner, he subsequently took a full handful and ate it.
When others saw this, they imitated him, taking handfuls of the essence of the earth (*pṛthivīrasa*) with their hands and eating it.

After people had eaten this essence of the earth, their bodies immediately became coarse and solid, their complexions turned foul, they lost their radiance, and their supernormal power of flight could no longer carry them up to heaven.
The world returns to its former state, and the world becomes profoundly dark and obscure.

After the world has become profoundly dark and obscure, according to the natural law, a great black wind must arise, blowing them into the great ocean at a depth of three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*. It takes the great city-walls of the sun and moon, ascends to the side of Mount Sumeru at a height of one million six hundred and eighty thousand *li*, and places the city-walls of the sun and moon within their proper paths.
By means of these causes and conditions, there are the sun and moon in the world.
At that time, the great city-walls of the sun emerge from the east of Mount Sumeru, circle around the king of mountains, Sumeru, and enter into the west.
Again, it emerges from the east of Mount Sumeru and enters through the west, circling the mountain.
At that time, people say:
"This is the sun of yesterday."
Or someone might say:
"It is not the sun of yesterday.
The solar city then emerges again from the east of Mount Sumeru; after doing this three times, it enters through the west of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, people said,
"This is yesterday's sun. Or some said:
"It is not the sun of yesterday.
The sun-city then emerged again from the east of Mount Sumeru; after doing this three times, it entered through the west of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, people said, "This is what emerged yesterday.
For this reason, it is called the sun; it has three functions: first, it emerges and illuminates the cities and towns.
Second, it is submerged and not visible; its palaces are perfectly square, yet their radiance shines all around, and for this reason they appear circular.
The city walls are constructed from celestial gold and pure crystal. Of these two parts, one part is of pure gold, free from blemish or impurity, shining with brilliant light.
One part is made of crystal, pure, flawless, and free from turbidity, emitting radiance.
The great city of the sun is two thousand thirty li in both width and length, and its height and depth are equal.
Within the city is a golden pavilion palace named Jambū-viśuddha; it is six hundred and forty *li* high and also six hundred and forty *li* wide.

Within the palace pavilions of Jambū, there sits the Sun Deity; it is twenty li in both width and length, and is fashioned from the seven celestial treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
The single body of the Sun Deity emits radiance that illuminates the palaces of Jambudvīpa;
the radiance of these Jambudvīpa palaces, in turn, illuminates the great city walls.
The radiance of the great city walls shines down upon the four quarters.
The Sun Deity does not think,
"I am traveling or not traveling," but constantly delights and enjoys himself with the five kinds of pleasure.

The celestial son has immeasurable devas preceding him as guides; his bliss is infinite as he proceeds with those before and behind escorting and attending him, and for this reason he is called "the One Who Is Guided."

The city walls of the Sun Deity are constructed of the seven treasures, featuring sevenfold enclosures, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold latticed galleries. There are trees, gardens, and pavilions, and bathing pools containing blue, yellow, red, and white lotuses, amidst which various kinds of birds sing in harmony with one another.
The lifespan of the Sun Deity is five hundred years by celestial reckoning; his descendants succeed one another in turn until the very end of an entire kalpa.

From the city-walls of the Sun Deity, five hundred rays of light emerge from below, and there are another five hundred rays of light encircling them, making a total of one thousand rays of light, brought about by the power of virtuous causes and conditions.

From where did you obtain the thousand radiant lights and their wholesome causes and conditions? By what means were they brought about, so that they may illuminate the world and enable all people to behold this radiance, thereby accomplishing all tasks?
Why is this? Because when people see his radiance, they believe it can accomplish all their affairs!

If there are those who give alms to śramaṇas, practitioners of the Way, or the poor and beggars—whether clothing, food and drink, carriages and horses, six types of domestic animals, incense, flowers, beds, couches, rooms, houses, or lamps and torches—they grant whatever is requested immediately. They do not oppose the wishes of others; they are always uninterrupted and never weary in their giving.

To give with single-mindedness and have no regrets afterward; to cause practitioners of the Way to purely uphold the True Dharma with joy; and by means of this, to bring about a peaceful and settled mind, thereby attaining immeasurable wholesome deeds—this is like a Wheel-Turning King who, upon first being established as sovereign, feels immeasurable joy in his heart.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

If there is someone who gives to śramaṇas, practitioners of the Way, and the poor and beggars—providing clothing, food and drink, vehicles and horses, domestic animals, incense, flowers, beds, couches, rooms, houses, and lamps—and who does not refuse what they seek, does not interrupt their single-mindedness, and feels no regret after giving."
Causing those who follow the path of purity to revere the Honored Dharma, they rejoice therein, bringing peace and stability to their minds and attaining immeasurable wholesome deeds.
When such persons' lives end and they die, they go to the abode of peace and are immediately reborn in the presence of the Son of Heaven (Sūrya).
He then swiftly attained mastery over the city-walls of the sun, and its radiance shone down upon the four quarters below.
This is called the "thousandfold light," brought about by virtuous causes and conditions.
Furthermore, from what does one obtain the thousand rays of light?

There are ten causes and conditions for goodness: first, refraining from killing; second, refraining from stealing; third, refraining from violating the wives of others; fourth, refraining from false speech; fifth, refraining from drinking alcohol; sixth, refraining from harsh speech and abuse; seventh, refraining from double-tongued speech and frivolous talk; eighth, refraining from envy; ninth, having no malice in the mind; and tenth, right view.

By contemplating with countless thoughts of goodness, kindness, and benevolence, one will, upon the death of the body, be reborn in the realm of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva). There, one naturally obtains mastery over the city-walls of the sun; this is brought about by the virtuous causes and conditions of the thousand rays of light.
Furthermore, from what does one obtain the thousandfold light of wholesome causes and conditions?
First, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not violating the wives of others; fourth, not speaking falsely; fifth, not drinking alcohol.

The mental activities are immeasurable in their goodness, kindness, and benevolence; they are like a bathing pool at the crossroads of a fine land, filled with cool, refreshing, and delicious water, surrounded on all sides by various kinds of trees.

If there were someone coming from the midst of intense heat, a person suffering from extreme hunger and thirst who enters a bathing pool, bathes, and drinks its water, that person’s mind would experience immeasurable joy.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

Those who refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol, and who cultivate immeasurable goodness in their thoughts, shall upon the death of the body be reborn in the realm of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva). There they will swiftly obtain the governance of the sun’s city and its walls; this is what is called the radiance of a thousand lights brought about by wholesome causes and conditions."

Why is this? Because the great city of the sun causes the world to experience the cold of autumn and winter by means of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). What are these twelve?

First, Mount Sumeru is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* in height; it produces blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses in great abundance, which are exceedingly fragrant and beautiful. When the sun’s great city-wall casts its radiance upon them, the light is eclipsed by them. For this reason, the sun’s great city-wall becomes cold, resulting in autumn and winter;

this is the first matter. Second, Mount Āruda is one million six hundred and eighty thousand *li* in height; within it grow blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses in great abundance, which are exceedingly fragrant and beautiful. They reflect the radiance of the sun’s great city-wall, and because of this, the sun’s city-wall becomes cold; this is the second matter.

Furthermore, the Yūan Mountain (Yugandhara) extends eighty-four thousand *li* in length; within it grow blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, which are exceedingly numerous, vast, fragrant, and beautiful. They further obstruct the radiance of the great city-walls of the sun, and for this reason the world becomes cold;

this is the third matter. Furthermore, the middle of Mount Sudarśana extends forty-eight thousand *li* in length; within it grow blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses, which are exceedingly numerous, vast, fragrant, and beautiful. They obstruct the radiance of the sun, and for this reason they cause the world to become cold; this is the fourth matter.

Outside Mount Sudarśana is next Mount Acchoda; the distance between them is 240,000 li. Behind the five Acchoda Mountains is Mount Nimindhara; the distance between them is 120,000 li. Behind the six Nimindhara Mountains is next Mount Vinataka; the distance between them is 48,000 li. Behind the seven Vinataka Mountains is next Mount Cakravāḍa, which is 24,000 li long. It obstructs the light of the great city-walls of the sun;

for this reason, it causes the world to become cold during the autumn and winter. This is the eighth matter. Furthermore, the flowing rivers of the world obstruct the light of the great city-walls of the sun; for this reason, the great city-walls of the sun become cold during the autumn and winter. This is the ninth matter.

Furthermore, the river flows eastward; those portions flowing toward Jambudvīpa are few, while those flowing toward the continent of Aparagoyānī are many. These strike the radiance of the great city-walls of the sun, and because of this, the days grow cold in the world—this is the tenth matter.

Furthermore, the river flowing toward Aparagoyānī is few, while that flowing toward Pūrvavideha is again many. It further strikes the radiance of the great city-walls of the sun, and thus the world becomes cold—this is the eleventh matter. Furthermore, the river flowing toward Pūrvavideha is few, while that flowing toward Uttarakuru is again many.

That [portion] strikes the radiance of the great city-walls of the sun, and the waters of the great ocean strike the radiance of the great city-walls of the sun; for this reason, the days grow cold in the world, and there are autumns and winters.
These are the twelve matters.
"For what causes and conditions is the great city of the sun hot during the spring and summer?
There are ten reasons."

What are the ten? First is Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains. At its edge is a mountain named Āṭata, one million six hundred and eighty thousand *li* high and likewise one million six hundred and eighty thousand *li* wide. Its boundaries are limitless, and it is exceedingly beautiful, fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate. It obstructs the radiance of the great city of the sun; for this reason, the world becomes hot—this is the first matter.

Furthermore, beyond Mount Āṭata there is a mountain named Isādhara, eighty-four thousand *li* in height and eighty-four thousand *li* in breadth; its boundaries are limitless, it is exceedingly beautiful, and is composed entirely of the seven treasures. It obstructs the radiance of the great city of the sun, and because of this, the world becomes hot—this is the second cause.

Furthermore, beyond Mount Isādhara there is a mountain named Yugandhara, forty-eight thousand *li* in height and forty-eight thousand *li* in breadth; its boundaries are limitless, it is exceedingly beautiful, and is composed entirely of the seven treasures. It likewise obstructs the radiance of the great city of the sun, and the world becomes hot—this is the third cause.

Furthermore, outside Mount Yugandhara there is a mountain named Sudarśana, twenty-four thousand *li* high and twenty-four thousand *li* wide, with its boundaries being limitless; this constitutes the fourth matter.
Furthermore, there is a mountain named Āṭata, twelve thousand *li* high and twelve thousand *li* wide, with its boundaries being limitless; this is the fifth matter.
Furthermore, there is a mountain named Nimindhara, forty-eight thousand *li* high and forty-eight thousand *li* wide, with its boundaries being limitless; this is the sixth matter.
Behind Mount Nimindhara, there is another mountain named Vinataka, twenty-four thousand li high and twenty-four thousand li wide, with its boundaries extending infinitely; this is the seventh matter.

Beyond that, there is another mountain named Cakravāḍa, twenty-two thousand li high and twenty-two thousand li wide, with its boundaries extending infinitely; it is composed entirely of the seven treasures. The radiance of the great city of the sun shines upon its summit; for this reason, the world becomes hot, and the seasons of spring and summer arise; this is the eighth matter.

Furthermore, forty thousand *li* above this, there is a celestial abode made of crystal, situated in the void and sustained by great winds as they move along, like floating clouds. All people in the world collectively call it a "constellation. The largest has a circumference of seven hundred and twenty *li*, the medium-sized one four hundred and eighty *li*, and the smallest two hundred and forty *li*. The radiance of the sun’s great city-walls is all inferior to theirs; for this reason, the world becomes hot. This is the ninth matter.
Furthermore, the earth of the world reflects the radiance of the sun’s great city-walls; for this reason, the world becomes hot during the spring and summer seasons. This is the tenth matter.

“The great city of the sun possesses five kinds of sustaining winds: first, the sustaining wind; second, the stabilizing wind; third, the assisting wind; fourth, the revolving wind; and fifth, the moving wind—these are the five.”
"It travels together through the great city-walls of the day, never resting for a moment.
The Buddha said:

"At that time, the great city-wall of the moon emerges and circles Mount Sumeru, traveling east and entering west; its radiance and majestic power gradually diminish, and for this reason it is called 'the moon' (*candra*)."

The moon has two characteristics: its radiance shines all around, illuminating the four directions, and its great city-walls are perfectly circular, with the radiance encircling them in perfect circles. The city-walls of the moon are constructed of celestial silver and celestial lapis lazuli.

The Great City of the Moon is one thousand nine hundred and sixty li in both width and length, and its height and depth are equal; within the city is the celestial lapis lazuli palace of the Moon Deva King, six hundred li in height and also six hundred li in width.

Within it there is a celestial palace where a son of heaven sits; it is twenty li in both width and length, and is fashioned from the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearls, musaragalva, and agate.
From the body of the Moon Deity, light emanates everywhere to illuminate his palace; this light further radiates out to shine upon the great city walls.
The light from these city walls descends to illuminate the four directions entirely. The Moon Deity does not think to himself:
"I am traveling" or "I am not traveling."
He constantly enjoys the pleasures and delights of the five celestial musical instruments.
Countless devas precede and follow the Moon Deva-son; because he is always joyous and gladdened by these hundredfold attendants, he is called "Yù" (the Guided).
The lifespan of the Moon Deity King is five hundred celestial years, during which his descendants succeed one another in turn.

His city walls and ramparts are fashioned from the seven treasures; there are sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all of which encircle the perimeter and are likewise constructed from the seven treasures.
There are pleasure gardens and bathing pools, within which grow blue, yellow, white, and red lotuses; various kinds of birds sing together in harmony.

The Moon Deity has five hundred rays of light below and another five hundred rays of light surrounding it, making a total of one thousand rays of light, brought about by the power of virtuous causes and conditions.
From what source do these thousand rays of light and their excellent causes and conditions arise?

If one gives to śramaṇas, practitioners of the Way, and the poor who beg—whether clothing, food and drink, carriages and horses, domestic animals, incense, flowers, rooms, houses, or lamps—and does not refuse what they seek, giving with a single-minded heart without later regret, thereby enabling pure practitioners of the Way to uphold the True Dharma and abide in peace, one shall attain immeasurable wholesome deeds. It is like when a Wheel-Turning King first ascends the throne; his heart is filled with immeasurable joy.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

If there are those who give robes, food and drink, and various necessities to śramaṇas, practitioners of the Way, and the poor and destitute, they will cause immeasurable virtue, peace, and joy to arise. When such a person's life ends, they shall immediately be reborn in the abode of the Moon Deity (Candradeva) and swiftly obtain the great city-walls of the Moon."
Therefore, it is said that those thousand rays of light are brought about by virtuous causes and conditions.
Furthermore, from what source are these virtuous causes and conditions for the thousand rays obtained?

If there are those who, in this regard, do not kill, steal, or engage in sexual misconduct; who do not speak falsely, use frivolous speech, harsh words, or abuse; who do not use double-tongued speech; and whose minds are free from envy, anger, and delusion—practicing these ten wholesome deeds with a mind constantly joyful and immeasurable.

It is like a bathing pool situated at the crossroads of a fertile land, its water pure, soft, and sweet, surrounded by trees. If there is a person suffering from hunger and thirst who comes from the midst of the scorching heat, enters the pool to bathe, and partakes of food and drink, they will experience immeasurable joy.
The Buddha said: "It is so.

If there are those who practice the ten wholesome deeds, upon the death of their bodies they will be reborn in the abode of the Moon Deva King, and shall swiftly come to uphold the great city-walls of the moon."
This is called the attainment of those thousand rays of light through the power of virtuous causes and conditions.
Furthermore, from what source does one obtain these virtuous causes and conditions for the thousand rays of light?

If there is one who does not kill, does not steal, does not violate the wives of others, does not speak falsely, and does not drink intoxicants, that person will rejoice; upon the death of the body, they will be reborn in the abode of the Moon Deity (Candradeva) and will swiftly come to possess the city-walls of the moon.
This is called the thousand rays of light brought about by virtuous causes and conditions.

"In the time it takes to snap the fingers sixty times, one cuts seven feet of thread; cutting twenty-one feet constitutes one 'time' (muhūrta); and snapping the fingers one hundred times constitutes cutting ten feet."
The sun’s great city-walls move gradually southward; after traveling sixty li for one hundred and eighty days, it then returns northward again for another full one hundred and eighty days.
The sun travels for one hundred and eighty days before it sets; the moon travels for fifteen days and then returns.
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, it is night in Pūrvavideha to the east, sunrise in Aparagoyānī to the west, and midnight in Uttarakuru to the north.
When it is midday in Godānīya, Jambudvīpa is in darkness; when it is sunrise in Uttarakuru, it is midnight in Pūrvavideha.
When it is midday in Uttarakuru, Godānīya is in darkness; when it is sunrise in Pūrvavideha, Jambudvīpa is in the middle of the night.
When it is midday in Pūrvavideha, it is night in Uttarakuru; when the sun first rises in Jambudvīpa, it is midnight in Aparagoyānī.

Thus, when it is midday for the people of Jambudvīpa, it is night for the people of the world of Pūrvavideha to the east, sunrise for the people of the world of Aparagoyānī to the west, and midnight for the people of the world of Uttarakuru.
When it is midday for the people of Aparagoyānī, it is midnight for the people of Jambudvīpa; when the sun rises in Uttarakuru, it is midnight for the people of Pūrvavideha.
The Buddha said:
"By what causes and conditions does the moon gradually appear diminished?
It is deficient for three reasons."
What are the three?
First, because it moves along its horns, it gradually manifests as diminished; this is the first matter.

Second, on the perimeter of the great city of the moon, there are devas whose bodies are blue and who wear blue garments and blue ornaments; wherever they station themselves facing the moon, that portion of the lunar face appears diminished; this is the second matter.

Third, the great city-walls of the sun, by means of sixty rays of light, illuminate the surface of the great city-walls of the moon; because of this illumination, that surface appears diminished. These are the three matters.
Since the sun eclipses the radiance of the moon, for what reason does the moon appear full again?
It is due to three factors being complete. What are these three?
First, the moon gradually moves through three directions; for this reason, the moon gradually appears full—this is the first matter.
Second, on the fifteenth day of the month, the various beings who are blue in color and wear blue garments enter the city of the moon to enjoy themselves together.
At that time, the moon illuminates all the devas and humans with its radiance, just as when a great fire is lit in the midst of many lamps, the light of that fire outshines all the other lamps.
The Buddha said:

"In this way, on the fifteenth day of the month, the devas at the edge of the Great City of the Moon—those whose complexions are blue and those whose garments are blue—enter [the city] to enjoy themselves together with the Moon Deva King. Its radiance illuminates all the devas and humans; for this reason, on the fifteenth day the moon appears full. This constitutes the second matter."

Third, on the fifteenth day of the month, the sun illuminates the great city-walls of the moon with sixty rays of light; yet the moon does not receive them. For this reason, the moon appears full. These are the three matters.
“The great city of the moon has five kinds of winds that constantly sustain it. What are these five?
First is the sustaining wind, second is the stabilizing wind, third is the assisting wind, fourth is the rotating wind, and fifth is the moving wind; these are the five winds.”
They constantly travel together through the city walls of the moon, never resting.
For what reason does the moon also manifest a milky color?
There is a tree named Jambū; for this reason, this world is called Jambudvīpa.
Beneath that tree is a mountain made entirely of the seven treasures, eight hundred *li* in height and also eight hundred *li* in circumference.
The tree is four thousand *li* in height, two thousand *li* in circumference, five hundred and sixty *li* in girth, and its roots extend eight hundred and forty *li* deep.
Because its reflection appears within the moon, it causes the great city-walls of the moon to appear milky-white and lack clarity.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu: “Noble son!

In practicing your conduct, you should be like the moon illuminating the world; cast aside the mind of arrogance, distance yourself from pride in your lineage, and always maintain a sense of shame and remorse.
On the great trees of Jambudvīpa there are fruits that resemble large jars; their flavor is as sweet as honey, and their color is as white as clarified butter.
"To the north of the great tree of Jambudvīpa, there are seven tiers of mountains and seven tiers of trees, where there are seven hermitages for the *brahman* sages.
The Buddha said:

"At that time, the people sustained their lives by eating the essence of the earth (*pṛthivīrasa*). Eating this essence of the earth in such a manner, they lived for an exceedingly long and limitless lifespan."

Among them, those who ate much of the essence of the earth had their complexions turn foul, while those who ate little had fine complexions. Those with beautiful complexions then became arrogant and mocked those with ugly complexions.
Because they were arrogant on account of their appearance and mocked one another, the essence of the earth then vanished and did not arise again.
Furthermore, thin cakes (apūpa) spontaneously arose, which were exceedingly fragrant and delicious, yet they were not as excellent as the previous *pṛthivīrasa*.
People gathered together in council, grieving and beating their breasts, sighing and weeping, longing for the former *pṛthivīrasa* which was so exquisite, now lost to them.
The Buddha said:
“It is like this: suppose there were a person here with delicious food, and he gave it to someone else to taste.
That person would then say:”
"How exquisite is its flavor!
Thus they craved its taste without end.

At that time, people deliberated together in this manner; they were filled with sorrow and grief, beating their breasts, sighing and wailing as they longed for the former *pṛthivīrasa* (earth-flavor).
At that time, the people again took up the thin cakes from the ground and ate them to sustain their lives, and so it continued for a very long time.

Those who ate many of the thin cakes from the ground eventually had their complexions turn ugly, while those who ate little had fine complexions. Those with fine complexions would mock those with ugly complexions;
because they were arrogant due to their appearance and mocked one another, the thin cakes from the ground then vanished and did not grow back.
The *pāra* fruit is also fragrant and delicious, yet its flavor is not as good as that of the previous thin cakes; it is like the *kṛmuka* flower, whose taste is like honey.
At that time, people gathered in council, grieving and beating their breasts, sighing and weeping as they remembered the taste of the former earth-cakes.
People then took the *pāla* fruit and ate it to sustain their lives; thus, their lifespans became exceedingly long.

Those who ate much of the *pāra* fruit had their complexions turn foul, while those who ate little had their complexions remain fine and handsome. Those with handsome complexions became arrogant on account of their appearance and mocked one another; as a result of this, the earth's *pāra* trees then vanished and ceased to grow.

Furthermore, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously; its flavor was fragrant, delicious, and exquisite, and its various pure qualities produced every possible taste, yet it was not as good as the *pāla* fruit.

People gathered together in consultation, filled with sorrow, sighing and weeping, remembering the former taste of the *pāra* fruit as they beat their breasts; it was like people here in this world who, encountering a most agonizing state, sigh and weep.
The people of that time were like this.

At that time, people gathered and ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice; after eating the naturally grown non-glutinous rice, men and women throughout the world began to look at one another, and thus the thought of lust arose. They went to secluded places to engage in impure acts together, practicing defiled and turbid ways.
Others who saw him immediately said:
"Why do you perform such an unlawful act?
Would anyone else ever dare to do such a thing before others?"
He kept his distance from the man and did not converse with him.
Only after two or three months did he finally call him to meet, saying:
"Formerly, this person had nothing to which he was attached; now, this person has begun to have some attachments."
Thereafter, he took the young girl and gave her in marriage to her husband; they sang, danced, played, and laughed, pronouncing wishes for the couple to always remain peaceful and secure.
At that time, people engaged in unrighteous sexual desire, and after practicing such unrighteous lust, they began to build houses.
"Because of this unrighteousness, houses were first constructed.
Thereupon the Buddha spoke in verse:
"At first the kingdom of Campā was built; Next the city of Vārāṇasī arose."
"By means of this day, light was produced, and only then did the city of Rājagṛha come into being.

At that time, the people subsequently became unrighteous and attached to sensual desire. From among the beings in the fifteenth heaven, Ābhāsvara, those whose merit and fortune were exhausted and whose life-span ended, died and descended to the human world; they entered a mother’s womb and formed a fetus. For this reason, women first began to conceive and give birth to sons and daughters.

At that time, the people ate this pure non-glutinous rice together; they would go to gather it in the late afternoon, yet by the following morning it had grown back as before. When they went to gather it in the morning, by evening the non-glutinous rice had grown again just as it was.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, people gather and take up non-glutinous rice morning and evening; as it grows, it returns to its former state, so that they do not perceive the place from which it was taken.
At that time, there was a man who thought to himself:"
"I am weary of going back and forth every morning and evening to fetch pure non-glutinous rice; it would be better to go and fetch enough for two days at once.
He then went and fetched it.
When others saw this, they called out to him, saying, "Come with us to fetch non-glutinous rice."
He replied, "I have already brought two days' worth of non-glutinous rice;
you may take as much as you need. At that, the man was pleased and said:
"That person is truly clever; he went to fetch two days' worth of non-glutinous rice.
I shall go again to fetch enough for two or three days.
Another person saw this and said:
"Let us go together to fetch pure non-glutinous rice.
The man replied, "I have already taken enough non-glutinous rice for two or three days; you may take as much as you wish."
When that person heard this, he approved it and thought to himself,
"I shall go and fetch enough non-glutinous rice for four or five days. You,
therefore, should immediately go and bring back pure non-glutinous rice sufficient for four or five days.

Because people began to emulate one another and went to harvest the pure, non-glutinous rice in great quantities, the stalks thereafter produced coarse, glutinous rice; and once a portion was harvested, it no longer grew in that place.
At that time, the people all gathered together to deliberate; filled with sorrow and displeasure, they beat their breasts, wept, and lamented, saying:
"In the past, we took joy as our food; our bodies possessed radiance, and we could fly with supernormal powers, abiding in peace and security."
At that time, the flavor of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) spontaneously appeared; it was exceedingly fragrant and delicious, its color like that of white ghee or fat, and its taste like honey.
Those who were foolish took it and ate it, and others followed their example, taking the flavor of the earth to eat; consequently, they all lost their radiance and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
Those who ate much had their complexions turn foul, while those who ate little had fine complexions. Those with fine complexions became arrogant and mocked those with foul complexions.
Because they mocked one another in this way, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) immediately vanished and did not arise again.
When the thin cakes were exhausted, *pāla* grew; when the *pāla* were completely consumed, non-glutinous rice (*śāli*) grew.
Because they compared their physical forms with haughty pride and mocked one another, even the pure non-glutinous rice that had been gathered ceased to grow in certain places;
thus, they decided to divide the land and establish boundaries.
For this reason, the people of the world began to practice a way of life never before seen: they divided the land into boundaries and each began to cultivate their own plots.
At that time, a foolish man, while possessing his own non-glutinous rice, went and stole the non-glutinous rice from another's house.
When the master saw this, he said:
"What you have done is improper and contrary to the Dharma!
You have rice of your own that you do not take, yet instead you go about stealing the rice of others!"
"You, sir, must not do such a thing again.
Although the man was thus addressed three times, he continued to set aside his own non-glutinous rice and steal the non-glutinous rice from another's house.
When the owner saw him once more, he spoke again:
"What you have taken is most improper; you placed your own non-glutinous rice there, yet you instead stole from another's house.

This was repeated two or three times, whereupon he struck him with his hand and led him away to the village. There, he sat him down before the assembly and said, "This man placed his own non-glutinous rice there, yet he went so far as to steal from another."
The thief addressed the assembly, saying, "This man struck me with his hand.
Thereupon, the people deliberated together; filled with sorrow and displeasure, they beat their breasts, weeping and wailing in lamentation, saying:
"Now, evil and unwholesome states have arisen in the world; the knots of enmity grow daily, resulting in suffering and pain.
Having been repeatedly burned, one's life is consumed by old age, sickness, and death.

Regarding matters concerning the evil realms and matters that people must undergo in this very life, they proceeded to strike and beat one another; having witnessed these things, they immediately began to reflect upon them.
The multitude then deliberated together:
"Where shall we find a worthy man whom we may collectively establish as our sovereign and leader to preside over our affairs?"
"What we do shall depend upon you. If there are those who act contrary to the Dharma, they shall be punished.
As for the non-glutinous rice we cultivate, each of us shall contribute to provide you with food and clothing."

At that time, within that assembly, there was a person who was most eminent, handsome and fair, and possessed of majestic and towering spiritual power. The multitude then addressed that person, saying:
"You shall act as our presiding lord and sovereign; we shall receive your instructions and teachings, and if anyone acts contrary to the Dharma, they shall be punished."
"The non-glutinous rice harvested from our fields shall each be provided for your clothing and food.
The man then replied, "Yes."
They then established him together as their sovereign and leader; all that they did, they received his instructions upon.
If anyone acted wrongly, they would immediately execute or punish them.
The non-glutinous rice planted by the people was each brought in together to the lord.
Because he issued all commands and the people called him "Great King," and because he took the tax in accordance with the Dharma, he was named Kṣatriya.
For this reason, the Kṣatriya caste first arose in the world, and all the kingdoms existing in the world were subject to the Great King.

At that time, this land of Jambudvīpa was level and even, without mountains, hills, valleys, or gorges; it was free from thorns and brambles, and likewise devoid of mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice, as well as gravel and stones. The earth yielded moon-bright pearls, jade, lapis lazuli, gold, and silver.

"When the Great King ruled over Jambudvīpa, the world was wealthy and joyful, flourishing, peaceful, and secure; the five grains ripened in abundance, the population was vast, the land was excellent, and water was plentiful—just as when the ground is smeared with ghee, sesame oil, or oil, dust does not rise, and lush green grass grows in great profusion."
It was perfectly circular all around; its color was like that of a peacock’s tail, and its fragrance was like that of the finest incense.
It was as soft and supple as fine silk; when one stepped upon it, the ground sank down four inches, and as soon as the foot was lifted, it returned to its original state.

There was not even a space of four inches on the ground that was not covered; there were fragrant trees, garland trees, clothing trees, incense-burning trees, jewel trees, vessel trees, and musical-instrument trees. These trees produced flowers and fruits, and when these were split open, they each yielded all manner of various things.
Among them, some were seven tones high, while others descended to six, five, four, three, two, or one tone; the lowest was half a tone high.

"When Your Majesty ruled the world, there were eighty thousand kingdoms in Jambudvīpa where people lived in villages and settlements, such that the crowing of roosters could be heard echoing from one to another."
In the world there was no illness, nor excessive heat, nor excessive cold; furthermore, there were no people suffering from hunger or thirst.
Your Majesty governed by means of the Dharma and practiced the ten wholesome deeds, instructing all the people throughout the land to conduct themselves as a father loves his son.
The people of the world revere the King as children revere their father.
The Great King had a son named Zhen; Zhen Wang had a son named Qi.
The King of Qi had a son named Dingsheng.
King Dingsheng had a son named Zheliu. King Zheliu had a son named Heying.
King Samavartin had a son named Ruruka. King Ruruka had a son named Āditya.
King Āditya had a son named Punarvasu.
King Pāṇa had a son named Mahāpāṇa. King Mahāpāṇa had a son named Sāgara.
King Sāgara had a son named Mahāsudassana.
King Mahāsudarśana had a son named Tiyaṇa.
King Tiyaṇa had a son named Rañña. King Rañña had a son named Meru.
King Meru had a son named Mālu. King Mālu had a son named Vīryabala.
King Vīryabala had a son named Dṛḍhavarman.
King Dṛḍha had a son named Daśaratha. King Daśaratha had a son named Śara.
King Śara had a son named Daśānana.
Daśāṅgula-rāja had a son named Śatāṅga.
Śatāṅga-rāja had a son named Nahuṣa. Nahuṣa-rāja had a son named Ṛkṣa.
King Cīna had a son named Pāyana. Later, the kings became very numerous.

There are ten lineages of the *cakravartin* kings: first, the Kāṇva; second, the Tālujita; third, the Āpa; fourth, the Gandhāra; fifth, the Kalinga; sixth, the Cāpa; seventh, the Kauravya; eighth, the Pañcāla; ninth, the Mithila; and tenth, the Amamahi. These are the ten lineages.

There are five *kanuca*, five *taliu*, seven *apā*, seven *gandhārī*, nine *kalinga*, fourteen *cāpa*, thirty-one *kaurava*, thirty-two *vatsa*, eighty-four thousand *miśrī*, and one hundred and one *mamī*.
After that, there was a king named Mahāsammata, whom people called Imā.
King Imā had a son named Ullabha. King Ullabha had a son named Buni.
King Anīka had a son named Siṃha. King Siṃha had a son named Śuddhodana.
King Śuddhodana had a son named Bodhisattva Siddhārtha.
"Siddhārtha Bodhisattva had a son named Rāhula.
The Buddha said,
"By these causes and conditions, from antiquity until now, the Kṣatriya caste has arisen."
At that time, the people thought to themselves:
"I am afflicted by disease, swelling, and sores; I wish to cast off all such afflictions and go to dwell in a secluded, empty chamber."
He immediately cast off his attachment to illness and sores, went to a secluded place, and sat there contemplating the Way.
Rising early today, and rising early again at dawn tomorrow, he entered a village to beg for alms. When the people saw him, they all gave with joy, saying: "Excellent!"
"Having cast off diseases, swellings, and sores, and having abandoned all attachments, they go to dwell in secluded places and sit in meditation, contemplating the Way.
The Buddha said: "These people merely practice evil and unwholesome dharmas; for this reason, they are called 'Brahmins'."
At that time, that person was unable to sit in meditation and contemplate the Way, nor could he attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because he could neither sit in meditation nor attain concentration, he rose from his seat and entered a village for alms, reciting this prayer:
"I am unable to sit in meditation, nor can I attain concentration."
Together with those of deviant conduct, they entered villages and towns to beg for alms; thus, they were called *grāma* (villages).
Because they practiced deviant dharmas, they were called *vaṃśa* (clans).
In this way, the Brahmin caste was first created and established in the world.
At that time, the people each practiced various dharmas; for this reason, there were craftsmen in the world.
At that time, people each committed the taking of life; for this reason, it was called the "species of killing."
By these causes and conditions, killing first arose in the world.
Because these four types [of practitioners] had already arisen in the world, the fifth type, the śramaṇa, subsequently appeared in the world.

If one of the Kṣatriya caste performs evil deeds with the body, speaks evil words with the mouth, and harbors evil thoughts with the mind, after committing such evils, they will fall into states of suffering upon the death of the body;

the same applies to those of the Brāhmaṇa caste, the Śūdra caste, and those of the slaughterer caste—if they perform evil deeds with the body, speak evil words with the mouth, and harbor evil thoughts with the mind, they will fall into suffering upon the death of the body;

whereas if one of the Kṣatriya caste performs good deeds with the body, speaks good words with the mouth, and harbors good thoughts with the mind, they will again fall into a place of happiness upon the death of the body.

Whether one belongs to the Brahmin caste, the artisan caste, or the butcher caste, if they perform good deeds with the body, speak good words with the mouth, and maintain good thoughts with the mind, upon the death of the body, they will again fall into a place of happiness.

Whether one belongs to the Kṣatriya caste, the Brahmin caste, the artisan caste, or the butcher caste, if they perform two types of actions with the body, and two types of actions with the mouth and mind, upon the death of the body, they will fall into a state of mixed suffering and happiness.

As for the Kṣatriya caste, if there are those who shave their hair and beards, don the kāṣāya robes, believe in the Way, leave the household life, practice as śramaṇas, and uphold the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ).

Having practiced this, sons and daughters of good family, because they have faith in the Way, leave their homes to become śramaṇas and practice the unsurpassed pure deeds. Before long, they personally realize the Way through their own merit, bringing an end to birth and death, fulfilling the holy life (brahmacarya), accomplishing what was to be done, and no longer undergoing further existence.

Whether one is of the Brahmin caste, the artisan caste, or the butcher caste, if they shave their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and practice as a śramaṇa, upholding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; and if, out of faith as a son of good family, they renounce the household life to become a śramaṇa and cultivate the unsurpassed, pure practice—then before long, through their own merit, they will realize the path for themselves, bring an end to birth and death, fulfill the holy life, accomplish what was to be done, and no longer have anything further to do.
"Among these four types of persons, there are those who practice to achieve wisdom; they attain the venerable state of an Arhat, free from attachment.
At that time, the Brahmā Sahampati spoke in verse:
"The Kṣatriya caste is the most honored among men; among all people, it is the lineage of conduct."
"From the arising of faith, one accomplishes the practice of wisdom; such a person is honored among gods and humans.
Thus did the Brahmā Sanatkumāra receive these verses and not what was unwholesome; he spoke of virtuous matters and did not utter evil words, thereby encouraging and assisting [the Buddha].
The Buddha said:
"I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have also spoken this verse on this meaning:
'Among all people who follow the lineages of birth, the Kṣatriya caste is the most honored among men.'"
"From this, one attains the perfection of wisdom-conduct and becomes a venerable one among gods and humans.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, eighty-four thousand devas and humans distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them;
countless bhikṣus gave rise to the state of nirvana without remainder and attained liberation of mind, no longer subject to birth and death.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus rejoiced; they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
Beneath this earth, extending for two hundred billion *yojana*, there is another layer;
further below that, for two hundred billion *yojana*, there is the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*).
Below that is again yellow gold for two trillion yojanas;
below that is again hard iron for two trillion yojanas;
below that is again water for eight hundred billion yojanas.
Below this there is further wind extending for five hundred and twenty billion *li*;
furthermore, there is another world-system below, from this human realm up to the Brahma Heaven, which likewise measures five hundred and twenty billion *li*.
Question: "Why is it specifically named 'kalpa' (aeon)? Answer:

"A kalpa is called the period of destruction; there are four causal conditions for it: first, after the earth has endured for a long time, fire arises and exhausts it; second, after fire has endured for a long time, water arises and exhausts it; third, after water has endured for a long time, wind gradually arises and exhausts it; finally, heaven and earth are reformed. From their formation they are again destroyed, revolving like a ring without beginning or end; therefore, it is called a kalpa."

When the duration of heaven and earth has reached its ultimate limit and the cycle of time is exhausted, all those whose karmic offenses have been fully expiated will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven; that heaven is near.
At that time, those with remaining offenses who have not yet reached their end will be reborn in the evil realms within the lands of the Buddha-realms in other directions.
The reason why kalpas have their arising and ceasing is that they manifest impermanence and decay; thus, their nature must necessarily be so.
If death were the arising [of suffering], one would not know suffering at its cessation; and if one does not know suffering, one would likewise not know how to seek the Way.
Why is this? Because fire arises from exhaustion. Why is this?
Because it arises from the exhaustion of water. Why?
Because it arises from the exhaustion of wind.
Why is this? Because it arises throughout the entire earth.
*Mahāsāṃghika-lokānuvartana-sūtra*, Scroll Six.
